the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking all my colleagues for the work we have done together on this issue, which has enabled all the political groups in this parliament to reach a common position and to be led to put an oral question and to draw up a resolution accompanying the voluntary partnership agreements. the subject is important. as you all know, the forest is retreating. every two seconds, the equivalent of a football field is destroyed worldwide, and in one year, the equivalent of the territory of greece is deforested, and this is obviously dramatic. this is dramatic from the point of view of biodiversity: only a few thousand plant and animal species are endangered, while the most affected forests - tropical forests - comprise half of the world's biodiversity. this is of course also dramatic from the point of view of climate change: deforestation contributes up to 20% to the greenhouse effect. and deforestation is endangering the lives of some hundreds of millions of people who live in or on the forests. the logging and forestry industry are among the main causes of deforestation, particularly in the area of interest to us today, the congo basin. it is estimated that 20 to 40 percent of the timber harvested and traded worldwide is illegal. so the question we are discussing today is obviously a vital one. these voluntary partnership agreements were approved under the approval procedure in the committee on international trade. this procedure, thanks to the treaty of lisbon, allows the european parliament to express its views, but at the same time it can only say yes or no. that is why this debate is extremely important, because it allows us to go into more detail and allows you, commissioner, as the commission's representative, to answer the questions put to you by parliament. these agreements are important, they allow for the traceability of the wood. they also set up independent verification procedures and support forest policies and governance in the countries concerned. today we are talking about congo brazzaville and cameroon. but first, before we go into these agreements and the questions in parliament, we must make a distinction between legal and sustainable timber. of course, we are talking about the legality of timber here, but the legality of timber does not mean the sustainability of logging. so the first general question i would ask the commission is: how does the commission commit itself to ensuring overall coherence around the question of forests - 2011 is the international year of forests - taking into account what was said in nagoya, taking into account what was also decided in cancun, notably on the redd-plus mechanism and also taking into account the negotiated trade agreements which sometimes, by liberalizing the timber trade, contribute to deforestation? secondly, we are still waiting for a response from the european commission on the question of agrofuels and indirect land use change. you know that parliament has asked you to include these issues in the criteria for assessing the sustainability of agrofuels. with regard more specifically to voluntary partnership agreements, there are many positive elements: we highly appreciated the work of negotiation and, in particular, of association of civil society actors in cameroon and the republic of congo; we know that it is not easy and from this point of view it seems that these voluntary partnership agreements are a success. but as i said earlier, a number of questions and requests remain: commissioner, are you prepared to come to us, for example, every six months or six months after an agreement has been signed, to report on the implementation of the agreement? because it is obvious that there can be a big difference between the quality of the negotiation and the implementation. we would therefore like to know from you whether the stakeholders, in particular civil society actors, continue to be involved in implementation. in countries where it is not always easy to complain, especially when there is corruption, are there any complaint mechanisms - especially independent ones - that would allow these civil society actors to denounce poor implementation, to say that their voice is no longer heard? in the same way, we would like you to report regularly on the impact of the implementation of these agreements, so that you can tell us where we are, both in terms of the overall coherence of the commission's action on forests and in terms of specific implementation on the question of the legality of timber. finally, you say that there is no budget in these agreements. but obviously budgets will have to accompany these policies, so can you clarify the budgetary issue around these voluntary partnership agreements?
member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to start by thanking the rapporteur, mr jadot, for his support for the voluntary partnership agreements on forest law enforcement, governance and trade with congo and cameroon. i hope this house will follow the recommendations for consent to conclude these two agreements. this would also encourage the parliaments in both cameroon and congo to complete their consideration. it is important that both the european union and our partner countries endorse the vpas, since illegal logging is a problem for all. i know that illegal logging is just the visible tip of the iceberg. basically we are talking about starting to work together for sustainable management of forestry resources. and, to answer one of the rapporteur’s suggestions immediately, i could say that, yes, i am ready to come here every six months, as parliament calls me, to monitor the implementation of these agreements. it is true that this is a commitment. there are risks but this is the only way, in my opinion, to achieve really sustainable management of this resource, because if we do not do this, we will not manage to be successful through declarations alone. for our partner countries there is a lot of commitment, but i believe that one important factor is the loss that results from illegal logging. each year, usd 10-15 billion is lost in revenue. illegal logging also has extremely negative consequences for indigenous peoples, for biodiversity and in terms of climate change. at the same time, it is also important to emphasise that the eu is one of the biggest markets for tropical wood. this means that our approach is extremely important in how the whole issue is being addressed. of the tropical wood arriving in the eu, 20% comes from illegal sources, so we have an obligation to ensure that we source only legal wood. the climate change issue is another concern for everyone, and the protection of forests needs to start somewhere. it is very simple to say that we need to pay to protect forests: it is a simple formula, but applying it requires a lot of commitment from both sides. i shall try to answer a couple of questions that have been put to me. on enforcement and implementation, the vpa establishes a joint committee to monitor implementation of the agreement. it will also establish an independent audit to analyse the legality assurance system and its effectiveness and efficiency. there is also an annual reporting mechanism, and the annual report will be made public and will definitely be available to the european parliament. moreover, in preparation for the vpas, we have involved civil society and indigenous peoples. until now they had been completely left out of the process, so we have agreed, under the new agreements, to set up multi-stakeholder committees to monitor, or guide, the implementation process where indigenous people are involved. in addition, the vpas include a complaints mechanism, and the independent auditor will have access to, and will rely on, information from a wide array of sources, including civil society and communities. there is a definite cost in terms of resources. between 2002 and 2008, the eu contributed eur 544 million to forestry in general in the developing world, some of it directed to flegt work in individual countries. the commission has so far spent a further eur 35 million to support flegt more generally, and we will spend eur 35 million more between 2011 and 2013. i would emphasis, too, that member states also make fiscal contributions. we have also dedicated human resources to the implementation of flegt. i have seven civil servants dealing with this, and they are working closely with the european forest institute and national forest authorities. an additional effort has been made in the form of the illegal timber regulation, adopted in 2010 as a key element of the flegt action plan, and this will complement the vpa approach. it will discourage unregulated, unsustainable exploitation of forests. the recent agreement in cancún on action to reduce emissions due to deforestation and forest degradation (known as ‘redd’) will facilitate further commission support for developing countries. our future work on forest governance through vpas will be helped by the fact that redd makes provision for governance and for observance of the rights of indigenous peoples and members of local communities. i take note of the human rights situation in partner countries. i agree with the draft motion for a resolution that the commission should continue to focus on these issues. i can assure you that we keep human rights issues at the centre of our political dialogue with the partner countries, and i can assure you that the fight against corruption is one of the issues we address when dealing with the partner countries. but i would emphasise one particular point that represents encouragement for the whole process: the fact that partner countries feel engaged. without real engagement from our partner countries, given all the weaknesses at administrative level, we cannot protect forests more effectively. i know that this is the start of the process, but it is a start being made by both sides, and i am always ready to come to parliament to report on how the implementation is going. however, with flegt we are definitely not taking a wrong step. it is a step in the right direction: we are not increasing the risk. perhaps we are not providing entirely sufficient solutions, but at least it is a decent step that we can be proud of.
the committee on development and cooperation has tabled a number of amendments. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, these partnership agreements between the european union, cameroon and the congo should in principle be good news for these populations, good news for biodiversity. but this is only one step in a long process which the european parliament will follow closely. if we want this agreement to allow the establishment of a regulated, transparent and environmentally friendly timber trade, for the benefit of local people and not just a few more or less legal groups, the european union must ensure that the rights of local and indigenous people are fully respected and that their participation in the consultations is effective. it must help to strengthen the capacities of the actors, to fight against corruption, and to establish genuine forest governance. the agreements must not be a pretext for perpetuating the plundering of the natural resources of the developing countries, but must allow a rebalancing of relations between the european union and these countries.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, once again i thank the members who have spoken. i think we have all been working in the same direction: to recall this essential point through the vpa, which is the link between development, the environment and the strengthening of civil society. i believe that today, if there is a lever on which we can build sustainable development in these countries, especially african countries, it is obviously the strengthening of civil society. as long as the only or the main element of democracy in these countries is the vote for the president, as we can see clearly - as the history of côte d'ivoire sadly reminds us - we will not make enough progress. so it is essential to strengthen civil society, to have it as a permanent participant in the implementation of these agreements, in the monitoring of logging, in the discussion on the conditions of logging and on the sharing of the revenues linked to logging. it is also through this strengthening of civil society that we best respond to the argument that is often presented to us on the question of china. why should we have to meet the criteria of strong cooperation with europe, social, democratic and environmental criteria, when china offers us a freeway in terms of corruption or pillage? the strengthening of this civil society is the best defence against the system which china is trying to impose in particular in the countries of the south. and then, as you said, commissioner, europe is a big market for tropical wood, but it is also - and this is essential for all loggers, for the whole industry - a stable and profitable market, and this is very important also as a lever in these countries. thank you for your interest in working with the european parliament. we are very excited about this upcoming collaboration.
in writing. i welcome the fact that after five years of negotiations, the voluntary partnership agreements (vpas) under the forest law enforcement, governance and trade (flegt) action plan are being concluded, one with cameroon and the other with the republic of congo. these agreements will help to ensure good forest governance by granting a flegt licence to forest products from these countries and thus ensuring sustainable exploitation and management of forests. it is more than necessary to have a system which allows the monitoring of the movements of wood and its products from harvest to export. 20% to 30% of the world's industrial timber production is of fraudulent origin and 60% of logging in africa has been illegal over the past ten years. these vpas will help to preserve the forests of these countries by fighting illegal logging, which is responsible for significant environmental, economic and social damage. the great advantage of these vpas is that they will apply to all exports between the eu and these countries as well as to all other timber importing countries. i hope that this vpa system will be rapidly extended to other forestry countries.

i'm the reporter. - mr president, i will allow myself four minutes and reserve the two minutes for the end of the debate. mr president, madam president of the council, commissioner, 'finally!' i would say, we see the end of the tunnel on this important subject for patients. we could no longer continue in a confused situation where the law was enacted by the court of justice of the european union. the directive now lays down clear rules for the mobility of patients across europe. what kind of care is available abroad? how and on what grounds can you be reimbursed? how are responsibilities divided between the member state of affiliation and the member state of treatment? all the answers to these questions are now contained in the draft directive. let me first of all thank the belgian presidency for its excellent work throughout the negotiations. its ability to persuade was decisive because - it must be stressed - many member states did not want this directive. i think that was irresponsible. i also want to pay tribute to my friend and former member of parliament john bowis who is in the gallery. as rapporteur for the first reading, he was also the architect of this directive and has always campaigned for the rights of patients. of course, i also thank commissioner dalli and my fictitious rapporteurs, who have contributed very actively to the outcome of the negotiations, and without whom nothing would have been possible. what is at stake for patients here? medical progress means that the supply of all pathologies can no longer be strictly national and that sometimes it is necessary to cross borders to seek treatment. this may be the case for patients living in border areas, where care provided abroad may be closer to home. this may also be due to the fact that there are more resources and expertise available in another member state, such as for certain highly specialised treatments. finally, for some europeans, it may simply be more convenient to receive care outside their country of affiliation because they have family living in another member state. consumers, employees, students and now patients will therefore be able to benefit from mobility rights within the union through clear legislative provisions. of course, this is not to encourage any kind of medical tourism, since social security schemes, their organisation and management remain the sole responsibility of the member states. patients will therefore now generally be able to receive in another member state all the care to which they are entitled in their home country and be reimbursed up to the amount of reimbursement provided for by their own system. for hospital care involving an overnight stay, or using specialised or expensive technology, the member state may set up a system of prior authorisation. this will take into account the planning and investment needs of member states in their care structure. parliament has succeeded in having the conditions for refusing prior authorization limited and set out in a closed list, in order to ensure legal certainty for patients. parliament also made further progress: each member state will have to set up national contact points to provide information and guidance to patients in accordance with their needs. each national contact point will operate as a single point of contact and will need to network with the other national contact points. this will provide the patient with clear and accurate information. the issue of reimbursement, which is in fact a major obstacle, has been greatly improved and either a compensation mechanism can be used as is currently the case with regulation 883/2004 on social security, or the patient will have to advance the payment and be reimbursed as soon as possible. we also ended up getting patients with rare diseases to be less isolated and to have access to outside expertise that will diagnose the disease and allow for prior authorisation for care. i would like to conclude by saying that, thanks to european cooperation in areas such as the european reference networks, patients will thus have access to highly specialised care, with the aim of encouraging the sharing of experiences, in order to improve performance, diagnostics and therapeutics in the interests of patients. so today we can say that we have achieved our goal and i thank all my colleagues for that. i would say that the health europe is being built through this directive.
mr president, commissioner, madam president, first of all, let me say that we are pleased with the progress made by this directive which we are going to vote on tomorrow. for years, only the court of justice of the european communities has been able to arbitrate disputes concerning crossborder healthcare and patients' rights. patient mobility is no longer a marginal phenomenon in europe but has become a daily reality. crossborder treatment now accounts for 1% of total health expenditure in europe. however, patient mobility should not be confused with medical tourism, which has developed in recent years. the latter is organized and, alas! is proving increasingly lucrative. health care is gradually becoming a competitive market. a german goes to hungary for dental treatment, an englishman - if he can afford it - goes to france to have surgery faster. there are many examples. but we have to make sure that health is not treated as a commodity, so that we are all equal. and that is why, over the last three years, we have defended the principle of prior authorization by the member state of affiliation for both hospital and non-hospital care. i would like to congratulate the rapporteurs here - mrs grossetête and our socialist rapporteur, dagmar roth-behrendt, to whom i would like to pay special tribute - for the work they have done, which has made important progress in, for example, reimbursement of medical care, the establishment of national contact points and european reference networks, the treatment of rare diseases and increased cooperation between member states. mr president, commissioner, our work is not finished. we must go further, beyond this breakthrough, to help close the gaps we still have in europe and i know that we can all work together to ensure that the patient and the european citizens are treated equally.

in writing. compared to the commission's initial proposal, which facilitated the mobility of patient-clients in a market-based view of health, i welcome the progress made in this agreement. the introduction of a system of prior authorization for hospital or other expensive care was essential to safeguard our social protection systems. similarly, the reference to article 168 of the treaty was necessary to ensure respect for the prerogatives of the member states in the organisation of their public health system. finally, there is commendable progress in cooperation and information for patients. however, major gaps remain: the lack of reflection on the mobility of professionals, medical demography, or the ageing of the population. other legislative proposals should address this problem, in particular the one on vocational qualifications, where it will be important to reaffirm that health is a sector with its own specificities and that it is not a commodity governed by the laws of the market alone, but the most valuable asset of citizens.

member of the commission. − madam president, may i also join you in expressing sympathy to those affected and their families. a year ago, we witnessed in haiti one of the worst natural catastrophes in recent history but this also triggered one of the best displays of solidarity, with people whose resilience in the face of disaster and disorder is a lesson of courage to us all. one year after the disaster, we would like to pay tribute to those who died, but also to those who have survived. we promised them our help, and we stand by our promises. the eu is a critical part of the global solidarity effort for haiti. we have mobilised all the means available to provide both humanitarian assistance and, as commissioner piebalgs will outline later, development aid to rebuild the country. after the earthquake, the eu pledged more than eur 320 million in pure humanitarian aid, of which the commission provided eur 130 million for last year, 2010. these funds allowed us to touch the lives of more than four million haitians through food assistance, sanitation and shelter. close to 1.5 million people have been provided with a place to stay: a basis from which to re-start their life. our assistance targeted not only port-au-prince but also other affected cities – léogâne and jacmel – and we followed, with aid, the 500 000 haitians who left port-au-prince to live with relatives in rural areas, bringing food, water and medical care, clearing the roads and supporting cash-for-work programmes. our current humanitarian assistance is focusing on cholera, using eur 22 million to cover the most essential needs in terms of healthcare, access to proper water supplies and sanitation, information campaigns, epidemiological surveillance and logistics. we have funded treatment for 158 000 people so far but, more significantly, we have provided clean water for half a million and access to safer sanitation for 900 000 people, we have raised awareness among one million haitians about what cholera is, how to avoid getting sick and how to treat cholera, and we have distributed 1.3 million soaps and chlorine tablets to affected communities. we had hoped that one year after the earthquake the situation would be better, but it is not. for this reason we are budgeting for this year, 2011, eur 33 million. we stand ready to provide more if more help is necessary. for 2011, our priorities will be housing, sanitation and healthcare. we will continue to tackle poor sanitation because it is obviously a risk in terms of cholera spreading and affecting communities. we will also continue to assist with healthcare, but the healthcare system of haiti is a shambles. it is not there to help people. in this process we have relied on humanitarian aid workers and i want to express my gratitude to those who have been risking their lives to help the haitian people. we are also supporting commissioner piebalgs in linking relief to rehabilitation and development. for instance, some of the 9th edf ‘b’ envelope funds will be allocated for housing programmes in close coordination with our humanitarian support. i want to stress here that we have been looking at the situation in haiti comprehensively with a view not only to helping people in immediate need but also to building the foundation for longer-term recovery.
member of the commission. − madam president, we are also delivering on the reconstruction front. the eu as a whole – that is the union and the member states – has already committed eur 600 million out of its eur 1.2 billion pledge in new york, and has already disbursed eur 330 million. as part of the overall eu commitment, the union’s pledge was initially announced at eur 460 million, and we consider it necessary to increase that to eur 522 million. out of this pledge we have already committed eur 327 million. ongoing programmes were adjusted, by extending their duration and/or by increasing the financial envelopes, to respond better to revised priorities. new programmes were put in place to address additional needs. disbursements strictly linked to the pledge amounted to eur 74 million in 2010. i believe that, given the situation in haiti, this is quite a good result. one has to realise that the situation there, which was already very difficult before the earthquake, working in quite difficult conditions. other factors which we need to bear in mind include, firstly, the fact that medium-term to long-term reconstruction assistance is implemented over three to five on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, madam commissioner, mr commissioner, one year after the earthquake, haiti is still in a state of emergency and reconstruction is still in the early stages, which is due to the structural deficiencies of the haitian state, the lack of political will and decision by the haitian authorities and the lack of support from the international community. without a major decision from the haitian authorities, including expropriation, the millions of rubble blocking reconstruction efforts will not be cleared. i would like to commend the efforts and the work of the humanitarian organizations. progress is being made and millions of lives are being saved. however, humanitarian actors cannot continue to overcome the weaknesses of the haitian state. the european union must therefore do everything in its power to strongly support a legitimate and transparent electoral process in order to guarantee the stability and political will required for reconstruction. it is imperative that it should accompany the future haitian authorities in the organization of their institutions towards a new balance at all levels, towards a fully functioning democracy throughout the reconstruction process. it is also essential that the european commission, as a member of the interim commission for the reconstruction of haiti, and in view of its financial contribution, intervene to accelerate the implementation of the latter's mandate and to ensure its functioning. after the earthquake, the international community decided to rebuild haiti in a different way, without making the same mistakes of the past. it is time to tackle, once and for all, the root causes of poverty in haiti.

president of the european council. − first of all i wish you a happy new year. as simple as that and i wish it for you personally and i wish it for our union, in these difficult times. as the last european council is already a month behind us, let me remind you that i already give a full report each time to your conference of presidents on the results of the european council just a few hours after every meeting. at the december european council, we focused on the first day on economic issues and on the second day on foreign policy. on economic policy, we reached some important conclusions. first, we decided on the proposal for a limited treaty amendment required to establish a permanent mechanism to safeguard the financial stability of the euro zone as a whole. following our agreement, in principle, in our october meeting that such a treaty change is needed, i had consulted the members of the european council about its possible wording and content. i secured agreement on a text consisting of two sentences, to be added to article 136 of the treaty. i quote:‘the member states whose currency is the euro may establish a stability mechanism to be activated if indispensable to safeguard the stability of the euro area as a whole. the granting of any required financial assistance under the mechanism will be made subject to strict conditionality.’ it is an essential piece in our efforts to make europe more crisis-proof. it is important, not just for legal certainty, but also for market credibility. as this amendment will not increase the competences of the union, all members of the european council agreed that it was appropriate to use a simplified revision procedure. this now requires an opinion from your parliament, as well as from the european commission and the central bank. we hope to secure your approval. i need hardly remind you of the importance of proceeding as rapidly and as smoothly as possible in this matter in a period where market volatility remains a concern. i know that you, and your responsible committees, have been following this matter closely, not least during the work of the task force on economic governance which i chaired and which gave rise to meetings between myself and the seven chairs of the parliamentary committees most involved. i would like to thank president buzek for his contribution on this at the european council and for informing us of parliament’s willingness to proceed quickly in considering this matter. with the benefit of your opinion, the european council will be able to turn this draft decision into a full decision at its march meeting. then the treaty amendment will have to be approved in each member state. the aim is for the amendment to enter into force on 1 january 2013 at the latest, so that the permanent mechanism itself can be in place in june 2013. the european council also examined what could be the key features of the future mechanism. already in october, we had asked the commission to undertake the preparatory work. this resulted in a statement by the eurogroup finance ministers on 28 november, which was fully endorsed atthe european council meeting. it foresees that the future european stability mechanism will be designed on the basis of the current mechanism, so imf involvement is provided for. the eu will continue to adhere strictly to standard imf and international practices. concerning the role of the private sector, decisions will be taken on a case-by-case basis, so private sector involvement will not be a prior requirement for support under the future stability mechanism. finally, the european council also had a very good and in-depth exchange of views on recent economic developments and on how to deal with the challenges for all european economies, short-term and long-term. the president of the central bank was also present and a statement by the heads of state or government of the euro zone and the eu institutions present was welcomed by the european council. this discussion confirmed the sense of determination and unity amongst the member states and the institutions. everybody around the table shared the basic analysis. i insist: all 27 agree, even if the analysis focuses particularly on the current 17 euro countries. we thus have a joint will to make our economies more resistant to crises and to enhance structural economic growth in europe. let me mention the elements of this joint approach, which reflects the statement adopted. three points concern work to be done by the national governments: first, fiscal responsibility; second, stimulating growth; and third, the two countries with support programmes are forcefully implementing the necessary measures and we all welcome the efforts of those two governments, of greece and ireland, and their populations. two other points concern work to be done by the member states and the institutions of the european union together. firstly, the european council asks the other institutions, not least your parliament, to make sure that the agreements reached in october, on the basis of the task force which i chaired, regarding the stability pact and macro-economic surveillance, are in place by the summer. it is our common duty. secondly, we agree to conduct new stress tests in the banking sector to ensure full transparency in the broader context of the eu annual exercise. our determination is clear. the heads of state or government of the euro zone and the eu institutions ‘stand ready to do whatever is required to ensure the stability of the euro zone as a whole’. work is going on to develop these elements of this overall approach. on the second day of our meeting, we focused on our relations with strategic partners. cathy ashton presented progress reports on how to deal with strategic partners and i briefed colleagues about the positive outcome of three recent summit meetings, namely: the summit with president obama, where we opened new avenues for transatlantic cooperation on growth, jobs and security, such as green growth and cyber-security; the summit with president medvedev in which we reached the bilateral agreement onrussia’s wto accession, a major achievement; and the summit with prime minister singh of india, which showed good progress for an ambitious and balanced free trade agreement, hopefully with a result in the first semester of this year, and which also produced a joint declaration on international terrorism. these meetings all showed that, for our partners, the european union is not only an economic union and a trade bloc, but also a geopolitical partner. the european council also decided to give montenegro the status of candidate country. it underlines the conviction within the european council that the countries of the western balkans have a european vocation. finally, we agreed also on the position on côte d'ivoire, in line with what the ministers of foreign affairs decided a few days previously, sending a clear signal on the need to respect the results of democratic elections. as you know, the european council on 4 february will deal principally with our growth agenda. innovation and energy – especially energy security – are key in this regard. in march we will have our first exercise of what is called the european semester. it must not be a bureaucratic process but a real occasion to have an in-depth discussion on the state of play of our economy and the actions to be taken. colleagues, we know of course that we have to strengthen and deepen economic coordination and convergence inside the euro zone. we will work as much as possible in a comprehensive framework and i am convinced we will find the necessary consensus.
president of the commission. − mr president, last year the european union faced a series of stern tests and december’s european council has shown just how determined we are to take whatever decisions are necessary to defend our achievements. in particular, by agreeing to establish a european stability mechanism and to make the linked treaty change, we have demonstrated our total commitment to supporting the euro area and the member states that use it for the benefit of the entire eu. the commission will adopt its formal opinion on the text of the treaty change before the spring european council. we will certainly play our part in explaining to europe’s citizens why this limited change deserves support. this agreement allows us to step up a gear and the commission will work closely with finance ministers to iron out details of the permanent stability mechanism before the spring european council. although this will be an intergovernmental mechanism, which was the only option the member states could consider, it is important that it is set up in a manner fully consistent with the treaty and that it reinforces our stability rules, in accordance with the principles and instruments of budgetary surveillance. these decisions are linked to the wider range of measures we are taking as part of our approach to dealing with both the economic crisis and its consequences and the need to generate growth with jobs. the european council has recognised that. the heads of state and government of the euro area and the european institutions in particular have also made it clear that they stand ready to do whatever is required to ensure the stability of the euro area as a whole. in particular, the heads called for determined action in ensuring the availability of adequate financial support through the european financial stability facility pending the entry into force of the permanent mechanism. these were the conclusions of the last european council. the european council also called for accelerated adoption by june of the commission’s economic governance proposals from last september. it recognised the important role the europe 2020 strategy will also have in returning europe to sustainable growth. the european union semester, which we launched last week with the annual growth survey, ties all these trends together. i believe it breaks new ground, improving decisively the way in which we manage and coordinate our interdependent economies in the european union. it is bringing in genuine european economic governance. this is our new economic governance at work – governance that should be the comprehensive response to the crisis. the commission has signalled this very clearly in the annual growth survey. let me just concentrate on that because i think, based also on the very important conclusions of the december european council, it is now more important than ever to look at the next steps. i believe a new reality is emerging. the politics of economic governance and economic coordination have changed and this is not just because the so-called federalists wanted it. the markets want it. our international partners want it. it is a matter of simple common sense and we are delivering it and will continue to deliver it. the new european semester combines tighter fiscal rules by reinforcing the stability and growth pact with effective economic coordination. it offers ex-ante coordination, which means we discuss each other’s policies, both economic and fiscal, before they are adopted. we are no longer looking back to introduce corrections, but are looking ahead to give guidance. this ex-ante approach is at the heart of what makes this a historic step for the european union. effectively we are introducing a genuine european dimension into national budgetary and economic policy-making. from now on, we will be helping to shape policies upfront rather than assessing and trying to correct them afterwards. the final decisions on national budgets will, of course, be taken by national parliaments. that is right and proper, but this new form of economic governance simply reflects a rational response to a new reality. when we see the level of interdependence in the euro area and the european union as a whole, a country should be able to take decisions knowing what its neighbours intend to do. this sharing of information empowers and strengthens national parliaments. it does not undermine their authority. the annual growth survey launches this process and its key messages are clear: bring back stability, do not delay structural reforms any longer, and speed up growth-enhancing measures. first, we need to re-establish stability by consolidating public finances. unless we balance the books we will not restore confidence in europe’s economies. if we do not restore confidence we will risk economic stagnation and all the negative social consequences that flow from that, especially for employment. but we have to approach this in a sober and well thought-out way. fiscal consolidation does not mean reducing debt by taking a slash-and-burn approach to spending. it is more than anything a matter of prioritising and some areas – innovation, education, new forms of energy – are good candidates for such priority treatment. the second key message from the annual growth survey is to push forward with structural reforms so that we can create new job opportunities. the choice is a simple one: do we want jobless growth or growth with jobs? if the latter, then there are a few things we are going to have to do. we need to urge member states to focus this year on labour market reform so that we can remove obstacles to higher employment levels. we need to help people get back to work or find new jobs by making work more attractive. we need to reform pension systems and make sure that the unemployed are not left worse-off when they find work. let me be quite clear: structural reform does not mean reducing our level of social protection, but it does mean bringing in those who are currently excluded from the labour market, especially our young people. levels of youth unemployment in some member states, even in good times, are a scandal. anyone who truly cares about a social europe knows this cannot continue. in the face of increased international competition, we can only sustain our social market economy if we adapt. the third key message in the annual growth survey is to frontload and speed up measures that are growth-enhancing. our europe 2020 programme is central to this. we must focus on measures that have clear economic benefits in the short to medium term and which lend themselves to relatively fast adoption. that means investing in areas that derive growth, unleashing the full potential of our single market, increasing investment in energy, transport and it infrastructure – in part through innovative financing, including, we believe, the european union project bonds – and continuing to press for a conclusion of the doha round, while pushing forward free trade agreements with key partners. all of this needs to be reflected in the next multiannual financial framework proposal. europe’s next budget must be a growth-enhancing budget. ladies and gentlemen, our economies are starting to move in the right direction. the recovery has taken hold and is currently progressing in the real economy. this year we should see gdp growth at around 1.5%, rising to 2% of gdp in 2012. europe’s manufacturing sector has improved markedly in recent months. we should also see a steady improvement in employment prospects and we are starting to see public deficits decline, thanks primarily to the consolidation measures already taken, supported in some cases by a resumption of growth. in the european union the government deficit is expected to decline from 6.8% this year to 4.2% of gdp in 2012 on average. but to breathe a sigh of relief and slip back into bad habits would be a grave error. the world has changed. we cannot return to the old ways of doing things. if we do not act now, in the face of the biggest crisis since the beginning of european integration, when will member states be ready to take real steps for economic policies that are consistent with the goals they have themselves set? if it is not us at european level who will encourage them to take those decisions, who will do it? only by sorting out our debt and stabilising finances can we move from crisis management to fostering growth – not any kind of growth of course, but sustainable, inclusive growth. that means structural reforms, many of which we have been advocating for several years – reforms that challenge all structures but do so to reduce prices and increase opportunities for new jobs and innovative ways of doing things. i really believe we have a responsibility towards our citizens to choose the path of growth with jobs. the annual growth survey points the way. so let us now commit seriously to proper economic policy coordination and real common european economic governance for all our citizens. thank you for your attention. madam president, i also wanted to vote on the report by my colleague, mrs françoise grossetête, on the directive on access to crossborder health care. i am delighted with the progress made by this text on patient mobility in europe. after many years of uncertainty, including legal uncertainty, and a great deal of work by the european parliament, this text simplifies, clarifies and codifies the conditions under which european citizens can receive care in a european state other than their state of residence, both in terms of access and reimbursement. i am thinking in particular of all the patients with rare diseases who will finally have access to specific treatments appropriate to their situation. i would like to stress that this directive is a concrete european achievement which is in the direction of a people's europe, which grants new rights to european citizens and, in this sense, it is a decisive and essential step for the mobility of citizens within the union.
in writing. more and more people are seeking medical treatment in another european country than their own, but often in complete uncertainty about their rights in this area; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's health system is not undermined by the fact that the health system is not in a position to provide the necessary health care. at this first plenary session of 2011, we adopted a directive clarifying the rights of european patients who choose to seek treatment abroad. the text, which was adopted by a large majority, provides that patients will be able to be reimbursed for care received in another member state. this is good news for all patients who are on long waiting lists and who are having difficulty getting treatment in their own state. encouraging mobility to improve the treatment of european patients is our aim! cooperation on rare diseases will also be strengthened to improve the treatment of patients requiring highly specialised care.
in writing. it is a strong signal that we are sending to our fellow citizens by proposing a system where the needs of patients will be given priority. the european parliament remained united and firm on this real recognition of the needs of patients in europe, which represents a first step towards strengthening their rights to access safe and good quality healthcare in europe. the new rules specify that eu citizens will be able to be reimbursed for care received in another member state, to the extent that the type of treatment and the costs would normally have been covered in their own country. the authorities may require patients to seek prior authorisation for treatments requiring overnight hospital stays or specialised health care and any refusal must be clearly justified. the use of foreign care could particularly benefit patients on long waiting lists or those unable to find specialist care. we must now ensure that the implementation of this directive is well controlled and that it delivers concrete results in health care for patients in europe.

in writing. i did not vote for this resolution on serbia's european integration process. not because of the process itself but because of the ambiguity of the text on the kosovo problem. the joint resolution between the european union and serbia, adopted by the un general assembly, is mentioned, but at no point is it stated that it cannot be considered as an official recognition of kosovo's independence by serbia, or by the eu member states which have not done so. nor is there any mention of the very worrying report of the council of europe on the trafficking of organs from serbian prisoners by the kla, which implicates the current kosovo prime minister, while the bringing of the last two serbian fugitives before the international criminal court is a prerequisite for serbia's accession to europe. as in the various wars that marked the break-up of the former yugoslavia, the evil is considered to be on one side only, repentance is required on one side only. in the long run, this becomes painful, even if the serbian government, blinded by the mirror to the european union's alouettes, seems to be bending to it in the hope of joining it.
in writing. i am voting against this text out of solidarity with the serbian citizens. add to the social bloodletting of the austerity plans imposed by the imf since january 2009 the obligation to meet the copenhagen economic criteria is a social crime which i refuse to subscribe to. the text also contains numerous infringements of the sovereign right of the serbian state to refuse to deal with the representatives of the separatist province of kosovo.
in writing. this eu-serbia stabilisation and association agreement, like all similar agreements, condemns the people to misery in the name of a rapid transition to a market economy and the establishment of a free trade area within the next five years. the european union is unworthy of the citizens of the countries that make up it and of those countries that want to join it. i am voting against this report in solidarity with the citizens of the republic of serbia.
in writing. nearly 10 million europeans suffer from mental disorders, including alzheimer's disease. european responses remain weak and the situation of patients, their families and carers is highly imbalanced across europe: at present, only seven eu countries have national strategies in place. the european parliament therefore urges the member states to develop specific programmes and strategies at national level to combat this disease and its effects. these strategies will need to address the social and health consequences, as well as the services and support needed for patients and their families. at the european union level too, efforts to promote early diagnosis and preventive health services and research must be a health priority. the establishment of a programme of public and private research, development and investment must therefore be encouraged at community level. the speed with which we can slow down the progression of alzheimer's disease, perhaps even eradicate it, will profoundly change the number of people who are addicted and help older people to enjoy their lives to the fullest for as long as possible.
in writing. in europe, it is estimated that nearly 10 million people suffer from dementia, the majority of whom have alzheimer's disease. this figure is expected to double almost every 20 years. one in four people over 65 could be affected by 2020. in france, there are 160,000 new cases a year. it can be said that all europeans will face, directly or indirectly, the problems of alzheimer's disease and other dementias at some point in their lives. i therefore fully supported this own-initiative report which calls on the european commission to make the fight against alzheimer's disease one of the priorities for european action in the field of health. it is essential that people with alzheimer's disease have access to appropriate care; and above all, more european cooperation is needed, both in research (within the next research framework programme), prevention, diagnosis (with common criteria and protocols, etc.) and treatment. we also call for the creation of a european year of mental health, complementary to the world alzheimer's day, which i hope will raise awareness of this issue.
in writing. as president of the european alliance to fight alzheimer's disease, i can only welcome the measures advocated by this european initiative to improve epidemiological knowledge of the disease and to coordinate ongoing research. joint research activities have been possible thanks to european support and i hope they will bear fruit. until then, it is essential to put prevention at the heart of any strategy and to direct efforts towards as early a diagnosis as possible as the report does. all member states must mobilise without further delay, including through prevention campaigns around an ambitious european plan to combat the disease. the behavioural or personality changes resulting from the disease also place the affected person in a situation of gradually increasing dependence on others. not only the sick suffer from the disease, but their families and carers also suffer. i would also like to pay tribute to alzheimer europe, which, in conjunction with the national associations for the fight against the disease, plays a vital role in helping patients and their families.
in writing. i have given my full support to this own-initiative report which aims to encourage the european commission to place alzheimer's disease at the top of the priorities for action in health. we must not only promote early diagnosis, develop ways of detecting the symptoms of this disease at an early stage, and focus research efforts on neurodegenerative diseases, but above all seek to improve the daily lives of patients and their families, because this aspect is still too often ignored by public policies. finally, special attention must also be paid to women, who are twice as likely as men to be affected by this difficult disease.
in writing. every 24 seconds, a new patient with a neurodegenerative disease is diagnosed in the eu. nearly one in 20 people over 65 and one in five over 80 suffer from it. alzheimer's disease is responsible for more than half of these cases. in total, this represents more than eight million europeans aged 30 to 99, a figure which scientists believe could double every 20 years in the future. the european union must take action to cope with the increase in the number of people suffering from these diseases in the coming decades. i supported the european parliament's resolution calling on the member states to take measures to help slow down the progression of the disease in people with the disease - for example, to promote healthy lifestyles, to ensure that medicines are available to all patients, to create specialised centres and to set up satisfactory medical facilities throughout their territory, and to develop a strategic action plan for research in this field.
in writing. the situation in haiti remains very worrying. the efforts of the many humanitarian workers - whose courageous commitment is to be commended - are being hampered by the inability of the government to mitigate the risks of civil war that threaten the island. we must demand full implementation of the european consensus on humanitarian aid (for concerted and coordinated action to improve the collective response to humanitarian crises) and recall that the commitments made at the international donors' conference on 31 march, in particular for the reconstruction of haiti, must be translated into action and not remain at the stage of mere declarations.
in writing. i abstained in the vote on the compromise resolution between the political groups of the european parliament on haiti. because this resolution (although correct in substance) does not propose any lasting solution to enable haiti to get out of the crisis. nor does it ask enough questions about the actual payment of the aid promised by the european union. haitians need real development support, which must be prioritized through the international deployment of btp teams and adapted equipment to actively participate in the urgent reconstruction of public and private buildings in the country, starting with the poorest neighborhoods, cities and communities. the haitian people also need real medical support in order to contain the cholera epidemic as quickly as possible and to eradicate it in a second stage. many doctors, medicines and support structures must be deployed urgently.
in writing. for several months, the lithuanian parliament has been passing a series of laws to ban or punish any reference to homosexuality or bisexuality in public. a draft law currently under debate aims to amend the code of administrative offences to punish "public promotion of homosexual relations" with fines of up to €2,900. this legislation is in total violation of the charter of fundamental rights and the european treaties which commit the european union and its member states to defend freedom of expression, fundamental freedoms, and to provide european-wide instruments to combat discrimination and human rights violations. we are asking for the withdrawal of this law, the inclusion of respect for sexual orientation in the list of protected principles in its law on education, the right of minors to have free access to information on sexual orientation and the clarification of the prohibition in the law on advertising. it is not the first time that a member state, under the guise of the principle of non-interference, has impeded the rights and freedoms of european citizens in matters of sexual orientation and in fact encouraged discrimination. this homophobic misdirection must stop!
in writing. lithuania is trying to control proselytism in favour of certain sexual orientations of minorities, probably and rightly preferring to promote the family, consisting of a father, a mother and their children, the basic unit of any society. some see this as an intolerable violation of human rights and a clear discrimination. but as the epp resolution rightly points out, the legislative process in lithuania, which is far from complete, is being examined by the competent supervisory authorities in the light of lithuania's constitutional and international commitments. the text also appropriately recalls, and i quote, 'the right of every democracy to amend and adopt national laws and regulations without interference in the debates of national parliaments'. the very fact of debating and tabling texts here is an interference and a violation of the rights of lithuania and lithuanian citizens. this is intolerable. and because the subjects are linked, i take this opportunity, as a french citizen, to express my most solemn concern about the action brought before the french constitutional court, in the name of non-discrimination, against the articles of the civil code which naturally enshrine marriage as the union of a man and a woman.
in writing. i welcome the european parliament's position that lithuania should reject a bill imposing fines for 'promoting homosexual relations in public places'. it should be recalled that homophobia has no place in europe and that the charter of fundamental rights, in its article 21, clearly prohibits any discrimination based on various grounds, including sexual orientation. the council still opposes the introduction of a horizontal anti-discrimination directive to ensure equal protection against all forms of discrimination. it is time to act to prevent such laws being tried everywhere in europe, which are far from the values we are defending here.
in writing. i would like to recall first of all that the fight against all forms of discrimination, in particular those based on sexual orientation, is a cardinal principle of the european union. we now have a substantial body of legislation at european level in this area, which makes it possible for this principle to be fully effective in all our member states. the fight against homophobia is a fight we must wage head-on in our own house and in our national parliaments. it is also necessary to emphasize that the text we are considering today is, at this stage, only a bill tabled by some lithuanian parliamentarians. in addition, this amendment, which seeks to sanction the public promotion of homosexual relations, has been openly criticised by the lithuanian president and her government. so we should not be quick to condemn any country or government. i therefore call on our lithuanian colleagues to ensure that our community legislation is strictly respected, in particular article 21 of the charter of fundamental rights, which prohibits discrimination of any kind.

in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution on the violation of freedom of expression and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in lithuania. interparliamentary dialogue (between the european parliament and national parliaments) has become a key component of the european union since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. moreover, the european union is founded on inalienable values, including the fight against all forms of discrimination, which i will strive to defend throughout my mandate.

in writing. if there had been an electronic vote on the 2009 competition policy report, i would have abstained. there were indeed good things in this report (an assessment of competition policy, consumer rights, innovation and an increased role for smes), but i deplore the general angle from which it was drafted: a kind of suspicion towards state aid - which is supposed to be contrary to competition policy a priori - and a way of advocating the early liberalisation of certain sectors of the economy, notably the railway sector, which seems inappropriate to me. we must change this perspective and put citizens back at the heart of the problem. we see that, particularly in the case of public services, the rules on state aid are not suited to the tasks of a public service and deserve to be reconsidered with the needs of citizens and social cohesion in mind.
in writing. the report is an ode to free and undistorted competition, which it presents as the sure-fire remedy for the financial crisis. it's the opposite. competition is the evil, not the cure. this document is an absurd creed. i vote against it.
in writing. it is estimated that one fifth of the world's remaining undiscovered hydrocarbon resources are in the arctic. this region is also a very important route for global shipping. the availability and security of these communication channels is therefore of crucial importance. even if the union does not have a coastline on this sea, it is clear that arctic affairs are of the greatest interest to europeans. that is why i voted in favour of this resolution which calls for a strategy for the far north. the union must play its role as a world power by asserting both its interests in the region and the need for good international governance of natural resources and the ecological challenges that will not be lacking. on this occasion, explicit reference was made to the role that iceland's accession can play in this area.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on a sustainable european policy in the far north, which stresses the need for dialogue with arctic communities in order to gain a better understanding of the living conditions and culture of indigenous communities. this is a vital point, which is repeated many times throughout the text. the interests of the european union must take into account the interests of indigenous peoples in protecting and developing the arctic region. we call for specific measures to preserve the culture, language and customs of indigenous peoples, which requires regular dialogue between representatives of indigenous peoples and the eu institutions. we ask that the european commission guarantee the interests of indigenous peoples when negotiating trade agreements. i therefore deplore the european regulation on the ban on seal products, which is contrary to the interests of the arctic communities in terms of sustainable resource management and culture and customs. this regulation, which is rightly contested by canada and norway, is contrary to the interests of the european union in the arctic region and should, in my view, be withdrawn.
in writing. the text supports the sustainable exploitation of the arctic but relieves oil and gas companies of any responsibility in this area. he dismisses environmentalists' comments on the ongoing plundering of this region crucial to the survival of the human species. worse still, it is not at all planning to limit investment in the exploitation of the fossil resources of the far north in favour of research into renewable energies. this report validates the ecological crime. i vote against it.
in writing. for almost 50 years, the european union has brought peace and stability to the peoples of western europe. however, it should not be forgotten that serious unrest continues to trouble neighbouring countries. the union must take account of these realities and give new impetus to its strategy for the black sea region. this resolution provides that answer, and i have therefore voted in favour of it. it creates a new budget line, which will give priority to financing small-scale development projects and cross-border cooperation, and strengthens human resources. an early warning system will prevent conflict and build confidence in the region by preventing any escalation of violence. the resolution also draws attention to the prolonged stationing of the russian black sea fleet in crimea and the concerns it raises.
in writing. the european union's black sea strategy is entirely devoted to the development of the nabucco pipeline and the establishment of a free trade area ensuring its energy security and hegemony over the region. the fight against the ecological disaster in progress is being put on the back burner, as are the social and economic interests of the peoples of the region. this is an imperialist manifesto. it uses the arguments of the propaganda of the adventurous government of georgia, whose undemocratic practices are not mentioned. propaganda and threats. it's a provocative piece. i vote against it.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i would like to thank the commissioner and the honourable members – my dear ex-colleagues – for giving me the opportunity to comment, on behalf of the council, on the appointment process of the chairs and executive directors of the new european supervisory authorities – the esas – and on the principles that should guide the performance of their duties. the esa regulations, which we adopted less than three months ago, give no specific role to the council in the appointments of the chair and executive director of each esa, which are made by the respective board of supervisors. hence, in accordance with the esa regulations, the chairperson of each esa is appointed by the board of supervisors. furthermore, the esa regulations give a crucial role to the european parliament, which has been granted the possibility of objecting to the appointment of those senior executives and of removing a chairperson from office following a decision of the board of supervisors. where, then, does the council stand in this scenario? well, the council, as co-legislator, has agreed with parliament to insert in these regulations provisions that aim to ensure that members of the board of supervisors – the management board – the chairperson and the executive director of each esa are protected by, and bound to, strict independence so as to act solely in the interests of the union. i will not quote in full the provisions of those regulations, and more particularly articles 42, 46, 49 and 52, but their spirit is clear. this is that neither the voting members of the boards, nor the chairperson or executive director, shall seek or take instructions from eu institutions or bodies, member state governments or any public or private body, and that these, in turn, shall not seek to influence the chair or the executive director in the performance of their tasks. the esa regulations are subject to the staff regulations adopted by the eu institutions. they also contain a number of key provisions that aim to ensure that the chair and executive director of each authority are selected in the most objective way, on the strict basis of the criteria set out in articles 48 and 51 of the regulations. apart from the managerial experience specific to the executive director’s profile, i note that both those articles list as criteria ‘merit, skills, knowledge of financial institutions and markets, and experience relevant to financial supervision and regulation’. as far as financing is concerned, the council placed high ambitions on the esas when it adopted the regulations, and i am sure that was also the case with parliament. it now falls to both institutions, as budgetary authorities, to ensure that those ambitions are translated into the appropriate means each year, on the basis of the commission’s budgetary proposal. the presidency also attaches great importance to all member states fulfilling their obligations towards the new authorities. for the council, as co-legislator, it is essential that all the provisions of the regulations are implemented completely and faithfully. we expect the european commission, as the guardian of the treaties, to ensure that this is indeed the case. as the honourable members will be aware, the commission is also entrusted, in recital 55 of the regulations, with the responsibility of drawing up a shortlist of candidates to steer the process of selecting the first chairperson of each authority. parliament and the council agreed to this starting procedure when adopting the regulations. i hope that the chairpersons will now be able to start their work. it is of primary importance for the new agencies to be up and running as soon as possible. they are an essential part of the eu’s response to the challenges posed by the financial crisis. we cannot afford to wait, and i am sure i can count on the full support of parliament to ensure the smooth establishment and running of the new agencies. as a result of the good cooperation between parliament and the council, the eu has a brand new supervisory authority structure. it is our common responsibility to ensure that esas get down to business as soon as possible. as the representative of a parliament-friendly presidency, i am fully commited to working in maximum harmony with the european parliament, and i also hope to be able to work with a parliament that is a faithful partner.
member of the commission. - mr president, madam minister győri, ladies and gentlemen, since 1 january the european union has had a new system of supervision of the financial sector. this system, combined with a thorough reform of the regulation of financial markets and players, will strengthen financial stability in the union and, i believe, will provide more opportunities and a solid basis for the financial industry, which is extremely important in our countries. i would like to begin by welcoming the major role played once again, over the last few years, by the european parliament in this process. if we have a more effective system of supervision of the financial sector today, if we are drawing the lessons of the crisis on this and other subjects, we owe it in large measure to the european parliament. we are now approaching the final stages of the establishment of this new architecture of the three european supervisory authorities, with the appointment of their chairs and executive directors in the coming days. these appointment procedures, ladies and gentlemen, have been conducted in full transparency, in strict compliance with the regulations which created the authorities and with the other rules applicable to the appointment of the heads of the regulatory agencies of the union. approximately 275 applications were received for the six posts i have just mentioned. they've all been carefully, objectively examined. the roles assigned to the various stakeholders, the parliament, the committee of supervisors, the commission itself, have also been meticulously respected. in future we will continue to ensure that the process is transparent, properly planned, in order to enable the econ committee of your parliament to play its very important role to the best of its ability. your parliament has made very high demands of these authorities, and i think it is right. he's making demands that i can understand. like parliament, the commission considers that the presidents and executive directors of these authorities should be chosen on the basis of their merits, experience, independence, european commitment and knowledge of matters relating to the supervision and regulation of financial markets. it is in this spirit, ladies and gentlemen, that the selection procedures which are now under way have been carried out, so far, on the basis of the applications which we have received. moreover, since the parliament and the council decided in article 68 of the regulations establishing these authorities that the presidents and executive directors were to be subject to the rules applicable to the staff of the institutions of the union, the commission has ensured that this is the case and that, on this and other subjects, the regulation is respected. you have expressed, ladies and gentlemen, concern about the salaries and the maximum age of the heads of these authorities. we have explored all avenues to achieve maximum flexibility on these points and this issue may, if necessary, be further considered when the review of the functioning of the authorities is planned for the end of 2013. i also agree with parliament's desire to ensure the best possible gender balance in the leadership of these authorities. in the pre-selection procedure, the commission rigorously applied this principle of equal opportunities from in writing. whether in economic or ecological terms, waste management has become a major issue in our consumer society. this plenary session devotes a great deal of attention to the recycling of waste in europe: with the directive on electrical and electronic waste and the resolution on waste management in campania, we have decided on a subject which is both technical and political. it will not surprise anyone to hear that we are producing more electrical and electronic waste every year. the products concerned are all those which we use in our daily lives (telephones, televisions, computers, etc.). only a third of the 9 million tonnes of such waste produced each year is currently recycled. the aim of this directive is to improve this rate, to put an end to waste, but it is also a question of strengthening the responsibility of producers. we are asking the member states to ensure that producers finance the collection and treatment of products to be recycled. consumers, who are already heavily involved in waste management, must be accompanied and assisted in this task by retailers and sellers of products.

in writing. the bolkestein directive was delayed because member states took too long to transpose it and applied it poorly. it is true that in france it has only been partially transposed into national law. and for good reason! to avoid a public debate, and thus a new wave of protests, mr sarkozy's government deliberately decided not to use a framework law but to introduce the principles of the directive in all relevant texts. in fact, there is only one principle: total and absolute freedom of establishment and provision of services! the fragmentation of the legislative changes has facilitated the opacity of the process. the scope of the text is still unclear: some social services, which are supposed to be excluded, are in fact covered by the directive. those who are actually excluded today are only suspended: every three years the commission can propose to eliminate the exemptions. and as for the most scandalous clause in the text, the principle of the country of origin, although it has been formally abolished, it is being reintroduced through the possibilities opened up by the directive on the posting of workers and the regulation on the law applicable to contractual obligations.
in writing. the services directive, adopted in 2006 and scheduled for transposition into national law by 28 december 2009, continues to raise questions in the member states and in the local authorities directly concerned by it. the own-initiative report by mrs e. gebhardt, which provides an initial assessment of its implementation, thus points out some of these difficulties, in particular the uncertainty concerning social services and services of general economic interest (what definition? which areas are concerned?), and the lack of transparency of the transposition process in some member states. moreover, it is clear that france is characterized by a problematic opacity and rigidity in the implementation of this directive, with a proliferation of decrees and implementing laws and a restrictive interpretation of the exemptions provided for in the directive, which raises uncertainty about the future of certain services, such as those for early childhood care and for disabled people. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the public authorities.
