in writing. parliament has just extended the generalised system of preferences (gsp) for developing countries for the period from 1 january 2012 to 31 december 2013. the general review of the gsp is due to take place this year and will have to take into account the concerns expressed in the committee on international trade. we are asking for more transparency and genuine collaboration in the negotiations for the allocation of the gsp to a country. commissioner de gucht has committed himself to closely involving the european parliament in the decision-making process. so he'll have to keep his promises.
in writing. the european and american aviation markets account for more than half of the world's air traffic. in the current climate warming context, the european union and the united states therefore needed to work together to reduce the environmental impact of international aviation. that is why i voted in favour of this agreement, in which both parties commit to environmental and social standards, including reducing noise emissions, reducing the impact of air transport emissions on air quality and developing sustainable alternative fuels. the two parties also commit themselves, for the first time, to guaranteeing the social rights of airline employees.
in writing. in the field of air transport, only bilateral agreements existed between eu member states and canada. however, as the european union and canada have long-standing economic and political relations, it became necessary for both parties to conclude an agreement on air transport. that is why i voted in favour of this agreement, which provides for the progressive introduction of traffic rights, the possibility of investment and cooperation in several areas (safety, including the establishment of a single control system, social issues, consumer interests and the environment). the agreement also provides for the abolition of all existing restrictions on routes, prices and numbers of flights between the european union and canada. this is therefore an ambitious and essential agreement.
in writing. until now, bilateral air transport agreements between eu member states and third countries could discriminate against certain eu carriers. the new agreement therefore provides for the inclusion of a union designation clause, which covers all carriers in the european union and will replace the traditional designation clauses referring to air carriers of the member states. the aim of the agreement is to avoid discrimination between air carriers in the european union and to prohibit anticompetitive practices. i therefore supported this agreement, which will allow any airline in the european union to operate flights between any member state and vietnam.
in writing. for some 20 years, the european union and the gulf cooperation council have been trying to negotiate a free trade agreement, negotiations which have still not been concluded to date. but in 20 years the context has changed. the gulf cooperation council member states have become the economic engine of the entire middle east-north africa region and are the leading investor in the countries of the european union's southern mediterranean neighbourhood. the potential for cooperation between the european union and the gulf cooperation council member countries therefore goes beyond the commercial framework to areas such as science and education. that is why i voted in favour of this own-initiative report, which is intended to be a call from the european parliament for the formulation of a more ambitious policy towards the gulf cooperation council.
in writing. the persian gulf region is of strategic importance to the european union for many reasons, in particular with regard to energy supply. the european union wishes to strengthen its links with the gulf cooperation council, an organisation of the six richest countries in the region, and the conclusion of a free trade agreement is a central element in this process. i voted in favour of this report, which lays the foundations for future cooperation between the union and the gcc. the project of my colleague dominique baudis, which covered all the issues raised by such a partnership, such as the rights of minorities, women's rights, freedom of conscience and expression, but also the settlement of the israeli-palestinian conflict, or strategic partnership areas such as research, education and fossil and renewable energy, was the subject of a fairly broad consensus among the political groups. however, following recent events in bahrain, the relevance of the report has been questioned. thanks to the good will of everyone, excellent oral compromise amendments were negotiated to bring the report up to date, thus avoiding the need to call into question months of work.
in writing. i supported this motion for a resolution which sends a strong message to our partners in the arabian peninsula. in a context of extreme economic, social and geopolitical tension, it was essential that our assembly reiterate its willingness to revise our cooperation agreements in the light of events in the arab world. it is not a question of renouncing historical ties, but of adapting them to the realities on the ground and to the needs of the peoples, making respect for the values defended by the union a precondition for any deepening of economic and political ties, and making dialogue with civil society a central and indispensable element of the partnership. while progress and reforms are welcome, significant efforts still remain to be made to permanently anchor these countries on the path to democracy, respect for human rights and the guarantee of public freedoms. part of europe's destiny is at stake in the near and middle east, and the whole point of the union's association agreements with these countries is to find a middle way, a fair one for all, between pursuing economic and trade relations and promoting its fundamental values.

in writing. the european union, the symbol of human rights throughout the world, must ensure fair treatment of third-country nationals residing in its territory and establish an integration policy towards them. the approximation of the national laws of the member states on the conditions of admission and residence of such nationals was therefore necessary. that is why i voted in favour of this text, which should help to simplify admission procedures, to combat unfair competition to the detriment of european workers and to introduce better controls to combat illegal immigration and undeclared work.
in writing. the creation of a single permit for third-country nationals wishing to reside and work in a member state has been discussed for years! the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's social policy is not distorted by the introduction of new forms of discrimination, such as the right to strike, the right to free movement of workers, the right to social security, the right to health and the right to social security. despite the improvements since december, there is still concern about social inequality among thirdcountry nationals. the european right, therefore, by voting in favour of the proposal for a 'single permit' for third country nationals, is voting in favour of an immigration policy which is both discriminatory and restrictive. the text as it stands does not allow equal treatment of all workers with regard to working conditions and social rights. it creates different categories of workers, depending on nationality, depending on the type of contract, which is simply unacceptable! we cannot compromise on equal treatment! yes to a common immigration policy; yes to a genuine single european permit; yes to a common european asylum system; yes to a common european asylum system; yes to a common european asylum system; yes to a common european asylum system; yes to a common european asylum system; yes to a common european asylum system. but we do not want a policy which is restrictive and therefore discriminatory!
in writing. the european parliament voted in principle to create a single work and residence permit for third-country nationals in a member state. this procedure provides for a set of common rights for these workers, in particular concerning working conditions (working time, holidays, etc.). the text also lays down the principle of reimbursement of pension contributions already paid by workers leaving the european union, since they will be unable to claim their pension rights in any event. this text is problematic, however, because it reinforces the principle of the 'country of origin' for certain categories of workers, a principle which had been opposed by the european left at the time of the famous bolkestein directive. this creates a kind of two-tier labour market according to the origin of the workers and is a form of social dumping. this is a contradiction: do we really want to protect the european social model and should it exclude non-european workers, or should it have a universalist aim and stop discriminating against workers by giving them different rights? the text does not yet answer this fundamental question, and that is why i have decided to abstain on this text.
in writing. the creation of a single permit for third-country nationals wishing to reside and work in a member state has been discussed for years! it was a laudable initiative, but the text as it stands contradicts the stated objectives: it is both discriminatory, since the basic principle of equal treatment for all is not respected, and restrictive, since several categories of workers are excluded. in december, meps rejected the text for the first time. despite the improvements achieved, there is still concern about inequality amongst third country nationals. the text as it stands does not allow equal treatment of all workers with regard to working conditions and social rights. it creates different categories of workers, depending on nationality, depending on the type of contract, which is not acceptable. we therefore voted against the final proposal. we remain in favour of a genuine single european licence, but we do not want a policy which is restrictive and therefore discriminatory.
in writing. after a first rejection in plenary, the european right went astray in procedural maneuvers and then today contributed shamefully to the recognition of a two-speed labour market according to the origin of workers, creating social dumping and thus a downward pressure on the level of protection of european workers, which is unacceptable. i therefore voted against this report, which is nothing but dynamite against the european social model. this text introduces exclusions and unequal treatment in terms of social security, pensions and access to employment and training for legal immigrants, which is contrary to my values.
in writing. for the past 20 years or so, the european union has been completing the internal market envisaged by its founding fathers. the establishment of the european economic area has led to the ever-increasing integration of a vast area of economic exchange. however, this area still suffers from the unequal treatment of workers from a member state and those from a third country. this difference in treatment is a double problem. it is both a disadvantage for migrant workers, who do not benefit from the high standards which are usually imposed by the social rights of the member states, and a disadvantage for european workers, who, faced with unfair competition, suffer from social dumping. the "single permit" resolution by véronique mathieu specifically targets the rights of migrant workers. it simplifies procedures by establishing a single residence and work permit and confers on foreign workers rights and duties comparable to those of european workers. the full completion of the internal market is a powerful lever for europe to return to growth, which is why i supported this text.
in writing. the adoption of this report is a significant step forward in protecting the rights of third-country workers in the eu by granting them a single residence and work permit. this illustrates the union's desire to increase its attractiveness on the international scene by facilitating access to the european labour market on conditions. i welcome the fact that the procedure for obtaining such a permit is being simplified by means of a one-stop shop, which will make it easier for foreign workers to get around. the creation of a single working document represents a significant step forward in the control and regulation of migration flows by member states and facilitates the control of legal immigration. in this text, our assembly affirms that a controlled and supervised immigration of workers is beneficial to all. the establishment of a common legislative framework for european and foreign workers protects our citizens against any form of unfair competition on the labour market. i voted in favour of this resolution because i support the idea of a europe which protects its workers, while remaining faithful to the principle of free movement of persons, which is a foundation of the european construction.

in writing. i voted in favour of the content of the report on consumer rights. the text renews four existing directives into one, with a view to simplifying and improving consumer protection rules. the added value of the european union must be achieved through a clear benefit for consumers, in particular by facilitating cross-border online transactions. the proposal for a directive thus seeks to address the problems raised by the different consumer protection rules in different countries. in concrete terms, the text proposes a standard withdrawal form for distance contracts and off-premises contracts. the duration of the right of withdrawal is harmonised to 14 days. the rules contained in the text would also strengthen consumer rights in relation to information and delivery.

i'm the reporter. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, a first step will be taken this week in the revision of the procedures directive. our assembly will have to decide on wednesday on the commission's revised proposal on common procedures for granting and withdrawing refugee status. this opinion of the european parliament is essential in the dialogue which will continue with the council in the coming months on a matter which, i believe, is the cornerstone of the asylum package and on which - i regret it - the council is still holding discussions. it will serve as a basis for a new version of this directive which, i hope, will enable us to meet the 2012 deadline as the horizon to be reached for the implementation of common rules on asylum. the vote on the report comes as unhcr last week published a study of the 44 industrialised countries. it shows how, contrary to popular belief, the number of asylum seekers in rich countries has decreased by 40% in ten years and by 5% in one year. such information raises the question of what the root causes of this observation are. is it the effects of the decline in departure factors or the tightening of immigration controls in some countries? what the report also shows is that developing countries now bear the largest share of the responsibility for asylum, although they do not necessarily have all the means to do so. europe must therefore take its fair share and set clear rules for this. this brings me back to the issue of asylum procedures, to recall the main issues. the current directive, often described as a catalogue of national worst practices, has two major drawbacks. it does not sufficiently protect the rights of applicants, while at the same time creating very wide disparities in treatment in the member states. there are still major differences between the different asylum systems in europe. to take just two examples, the percentage of positive first instance decisions in the member states ranged from 65% in 2009 to less than 1%. the time limit for appealing against a negative decision at first instance varied from two to thirty days. there are therefore differences between member states, whether in the grounds for accelerated procedures, access to individual interviews or effective redress. such disparities are incompatible with a common asylum system which should offer equivalent protection throughout the union. they are also contrary to one of the reasons for the establishment of the dublin ii regulation, which presupposes that the asylum systems of the member states are equivalent. legislative harmonisation is therefore essential to ensure fair, accessible, secure and efficient procedures. because i think they are incorrect, i would like to respond once again to some of the assertions made by the critics of this text, who say that in the end this directive is almost reduced to cost increases and the development of abuses. these procedural changes may, however, entail costs in the short term. but a little lucidity would make it clear that it is rather the misuse of procedures which are inadequate in terms of quality and safety that is currently costing member states dearly. two indicators will serve as validation: the very large number of appeals and the length of the procedures thus generated. i would also like to see a break with the manichean view of asylum, which wants to see only abuse. in a context where immigration issues are being exploited, defending asylum as a fundamental right is an obligation. and if the situation in the arab world means anything to the most reticent parliamentarians, it will mean something about the european union's responsibility to provide adequate protection for victims of persecution. i therefore support the commission's approach to improving first instance procedures, front-loading, because good decision-making at first instance will benefit victims of persecution as much as it will enable the competent authorities to take sound decisions, improve the reasoning behind negative decisions and thus reduce the risk of their being overturned by the appeal bodies, better identify cases of unfounded or abusive applications and reduce the reception costs of member states, while supporting their efforts to get the really rejected applicants to leave the territory. finally, a few words on a number of key points which will hopefully allow this report to move forward now. firstly, the right to free legal aid at first instance is, in my view, an essential guarantee for improving the quality of decisions. secondly, better consideration of vulnerable applicants, a category of people on which the current directive is completely silent. the third challenge is that of more ambitious time limits for appeals, which reinforce the right to effective appeals; greater guarantees in the case of accelerated procedures, in particular a reduction in the grounds for them or the setting of reasonable time limits. and on the concepts of safe countries, we are calling for the adoption of a common european list in codecision, as the court of justice recommended in 2008. in conclusion, the final adoption of this report should be a strong signal from parliament to the council and the commission. the red lines of parliament are, in my view, set and the cursor is set on the side of seeking an upward harmonisation of protection standards, which we must welcome, ladies and gentlemen. the rapporteur. - madam president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank all the parties with whom i have had the opportunity to discuss this matter. all contributions have been useful in the preparation of this report and thanks to the cooperation of all the political groups, of which i thank in particular the fictitious rapporteurs, we have today on the table a coherent text with a strong message. we are indeed at a turning point in european investment policy, at a time when we must seize the new competence conferred on us by the lisbon treaty to meet a double challenge. the first is to give european companies the tools they need to make quality and secure investments abroad, with a legal framework that provides long-term support. europe must also strengthen its position as the world's leading recipient of foreign direct investment and be able to control it in order to promote sustainable development and quality job creation. by voting for this report, the first official expression of our institution since the implementation of the lisbon treaty, parliament is taking its place as the new co-legislator on trade regulation and expressing its priorities at a time when the first negotiations on investment protection are about to be launched. this expression is essential because it is intended to convey the concerns of the citizens, whose interest in commercial matters is growing and whom we must accompany. today, in a world where conflicts are also played out at the commercial level, the protection of our companies investing abroad must be a priority. international agreements have been created to protect investors from unjustified and unjust expropriations, from disguised legislation aimed only at eliminating them from this or that market. and that first calling must be maintained. while europe is one of the most open markets in the world, a balance needs to be restored with our main partners so that european companies benefit from a level playing field. this is what this report proposes, insisting on the need to include in future agreements standards of non-discrimination, fair and equitable treatment and protection against direct and indirect expropriation. however, these standards must be defined in such a way as to avoid any misinterpretation. some companies have used the vague wording of the earlier generations of investment agreements to defend their interests beyond what was legitimate, for example by attacking new social or environmental legislation that harms their interests. before international arbitrators and without transparency or appeal, they demanded substantial compensation, considering that these laws amounted to indirect expropriations. europe, which will receive more and more investment in the future, especially from emerging countries, must guard against such deviations. this is the sense of the reforms undertaken by the united states and canada, two countries whose governments or communities have suffered several setbacks in international arbitration cases and have thoroughly revised their investment agreement model. by proposing new definitions of protection standards, the report strikes the right balance between the protection of investors' rights and the right of public authorities to regulate. this also means that specific clauses should be included in all future agreements specifying the possibility for the public authorities to legislate and regulate in the areas of state security, the environment, public health, workers' and consumers' rights, industrial policy and cultural diversity. finally, increased investor protection must be accompanied by more responsible behaviour, particularly in developing countries, whose social and environmental legislation is less restrictive. the report therefore stresses that social and environmental clauses must be incorporated into all free trade agreements signed by the union. in addition, we must move beyond blaming and shaming and incorporate into all future agreements a set of clear rules that companies will have to respect in terms of corporate social responsibility on the basis of guidelines set by the oecd. if this is really a question of drawing up the outlines of a new european investment policy, i would urge that it should be exemplary, that it should promote sustainable investment, respect for the environment and promote quality working conditions in europe and in third countries. the report must therefore, by virtue of the vote on wednesday, be a reference point for all future negotiations by the commission.
in writing. the extension of the eu's competence to foreign direct investment by the lisbon treaty finally makes it possible to envisage a genuine european policy in this area. at the stage of the development of this policy, the priority is to ensure the greatest possible security for both investments and investors. the transition from national to european competence should not, therefore, in any way affect the proper implementation of the approximately 1200 agreements in force between member states and third countries. for the same reasons of legal certainty and predictability, the eu must now develop an effective, transparent and accessible dispute settlement mechanism for all investors, including the most modest (e.g. smes). the mechanisms in the most recent bilateral trade agreements provide a good basis, but only for disputes between a state and the eu. provisions should be made for the eventuality of a dispute between the eu and a company. finally, the eu must seize this opportunity to go further: it must include in future agreements clauses facilitating the establishment of investors in these countries, but also basic provisions on social and environmental standards.
president of the european council. − mr president, president of the european commission, honourable members, within the space of 49 days, i have chaired 3 meetings of the european council and a summit of heads of state and government of the eurozone. these facts illustrate the great and urgent challenges our union is facing, both on the economic and on the diplomatic front. it also neatly illustrates that meetings of the european council are not just an event: they are part of a process. indeed, in the meeting on which i am reporting today – that of 24 and 25 march – we duly approved a significant set of economic measures that have been prepared and discussed over the last year, we stepped up our action with regard to ongoing events in libya and we initiated our response to the catastrophic events in japan. allow me to take each of those issues in turn. on economic issues, we took forward a comprehensive package of measures. under the impulse of earlier meetings, including the informal eurozone summit of 11 march, we were able to bring together almost all the strengths of this endeavour. of course, approving measures and procedures to deal with the crisis does not in itself take you immediately out of the crisis. this will require perseverance and sustained effort. i will not repeat all the decisions we took in detail. you will find them in the conclusions. however, let me summarise six key points. number one: we agreed on the treaty amendment needed to give full legal certainty to the permanent stability mechanism. in its resolution of 15 december, parliament called for a light treaty change that provides a legal basis for such a mechanism, rather than resorting to a profound amendment of the treaty. we followed that advice, and i was delighted when parliament endorsed the proposed treaty amendment by such an overwhelming majority on 23 march. i am especially glad that we were able to reassure parliament about some of the concerns that had been raised in this context. i would like to thank the rapporteurs, mr brok and mr gualtieri, for working so closely with me to achieve this result. number two: we reached a detailed agreement on the size, scope and mode of operation for the future stability mechanism and on improving the temporary facility. number three: we endorsed the position of the council on the six legislative proposals on budgetary and macroeconomic surveillance ahead of negotiations with parliament. i know you are working hard on this; indeed, i met your rapporteurs and will be meeting your coordinators this afternoon. all those concerned understand the need to conclude by june. number four: we started the european semester. it is an exercise in which we follow up the implementation of the eu 2020 strategy, the stability and growth pact and macroeconomic surveillance. the european council in june will draw the necessary conclusions. i will personally see to it that this does not sink into the sands of a bureaucratic process. number five: we agreed that credible stress tests for the banks will take place soon. the task is double: the banks must do the test and governments must be ready to deal with the outcome of the tests. number six: we provided for a new quality of economic coordination. we call it the euro plus pact for two reasons: firstly because it is about what eurozone countries want to do more – they share one currency and wish to undertake supplementary efforts on top of existing eu commitments and arrangements; and secondly because it is also open to the others. that is why i am glad that six non-euro countries have already announced that they will join the pact. they are denmark, poland, latvia, lithuania, bulgaria and romania. it remains open for any of the four remaining member states to join later on. let me say once again that the political commitment of the euro plus pact comes on top of all the other measures in the package to improve member states’ economic performance: the stronger stability and growth pact on fiscal surveillance, the new macroeconomic surveillance and implementation of the crucial eu 2020 strategy on structural reforms to achieve economic growth. the commitments in terms of competitiveness, public finances and pensions, employment and so on must be translated into the national reform and stability programmes. they will also be evaluated annually at the highest level. i have a final remark on the economy. some people fear this work is about dismantling the welfare states and social protection. not at all. as i said to the social partners at the tripartite social summit, it is to save these fundamental aspects of the european model. we want to make sure that our economies are competitive enough to create jobs and to sustain the welfare of all our citizens and that is what our work is about. these, then, were the main elements of our global economic package to help us come out of the crisis. as i said, they are the result of a long process, not a single meeting. it was on 25 march 2010 that the european council decided to improve european economic governance, launching the task force that i had the honour to chair. one year later, we are getting new rules, new instruments and more ambitious policies. it was, and remains, an effort of all institutions, including this parliament and all the member states. it was not always easy, not always without drama, but the political will has been unflinching, our sense of direction is clear and significant results are there. not all our problems are over. they are the result of past mistakes and a lack of appropriate instruments both at the european and at the national level. but we now have every chance of dealing with them and not repeating them. i should now like to turn to the situation in libya, which was, of course, something we discussed on 24 and 25 march. we showed common determination. i know that some among you had doubts, but we worked hard to secure concrete results. two weeks previously, at an extraordinary meeting of the european council on 11 march, we had adopted a clear line on libya. without that clear european position, the subsequent actions would not have been possible. we decided that, to safeguard the safety of the civilian population, member states could examine all necessary options, provided that there is a demonstrable need, a clear legal basis and support from the region. those three conditions were quickly met. the clear need was obvious when the regime stepped up the violence against its own people. the legal base was provided when the un security council agreed the landmark resolution on libya a few days after the european council meeting. regional support was immediately forthcoming from the arab league. the actions undertaken by a coalition of european, arab and north american countries implementing the un resolution have helped protect the civilian population of libya. a massive bloodbath has been avoided. thousands of lives have been saved. this is the most important result and deserves the highest attention, more so than the decision-making process. the wood is more important than the trees. we all know that the decision to take military action was not easy. there are, quite naturally, questions and hesitations. that is perfectly normal in issues of war and peace. but any difficulties that we have experienced over that aspect of the libyan crisis should not mask for one moment the full track record of the european union. from the beginning of the crisis, the european union was at the forefront. it was the first to impose sanctions, the first to impose a travel ban on leading figures in the regime, the first to freeze libyan assets and the first to recognise the interim transitional national council as a valid interlocutor, at the request of this parliament. the union also coordinated rescue efforts for eu citizens and has provided, and continues to provide, substantial humanitarian aid. the political objectives we set on 11 march remain unchanged. gaddafi must go. we want a political transition led by the libyans themselves and based on broad-based political dialogue. we stand ready to help a new libya, both economically and in building its new institutions. we are also following the events in the rest of the region closely. knowing that the situation is different in each country, we express our utmost concern at the situation in syria, yemen and bahrain. we strongly condemn the escalation of violence and we support political and social reforms in our southern neighbourhood. we also have to change our policy, and i will be discussing this later today with several meps responsible for this region within parliament’s committee on foreign affairs. on the positive side, we noted the smooth conduct of the constitutional referendum in egypt two weeks ago. allow me to say a few words on côte d’ivoire as well. it was not on the agenda of the most recent european council, but we adopted conclusions in december and have been closely following developments there ever since. first of all, we condemn the violence, particularly violence against civilians, in the strongest possible terms. this must stop on all sides. secondly, the current situation is a clear result of the lack of respect for democracy. democracy is not only about elections, but also respect for the outcome of the elections. the international community was clear about the results of the presidential elections in côte d’ivoire last year. we must be consistent in our position. finally, on japan, turning to the accumulation of tragedies that had hit japan, we as the european council expressed our sympathy and solidarity for the japanese people and our condolences for the thousands of victims. we must not forget them, even while other aspects of the drama in japan are retaining our attention. we are ready as a union to assist in any way we can. in these tragic days, as true friends of japan, we reiterate the strategic importance of the eu-japan relationship. as we know, the effects of the events go beyond japan, and that is why the european union is drawing all the lessons fully. we are paying close attention to the consequences for the global economy and to the nuclear aspects. that is a top priority. we therefore decided that the safety of all of our nuclear plants should be urgently reviewed in the ‘stress tests’ on safety. the commission will report to the european council on the stress tests before the end of the year. it will review existing eu rules on the safety of nuclear installations and propose improvements wherever necessary. in europe, we want the highest standard for nuclear safety, because ensuring the safety of nuclear plants cannot stop at our borders. we encourage and support neighbouring countries to do similar stress tests. a worldwide review of nuclear plants would be best. mr president, honourable members, that concludes my summary of what we agreed at this, the third meeting of the european council this year. much of it paves the way for further work in this parliament, be it through legislative procedures or through parliament’s general right of scrutiny over the common foreign and security policy. i look forward to hearing your views.

mr president of the european council, mr president of the commission, madam president, the outcome of the european council on economic and monetary union is impressive. that's good. but let us understand that this will pose a new and formidable problem, namely the political acceptance of the decisions thus taken, at two levels. first level: between the member states themselves. from the outset, this procedure of the euro pact was based on a purely intergovernmental agreement, initiated by one member state, the largest. once is good. but if the political path is the same for several years in a row, we risk heading towards very high national tensions. already the german chancellor has been booed in the streets of athens and dublin. it is therefore necessary to gradually transform this intergovernmental procedure into a genuinely european procedure, not yet community but european. that is the meaning of the amendments adopted by parliament, and president juncker and you, mr van rompuy, should be congratulated and thanked for adopting them. second level: acceptance by public opinion in each member state. how can the parties which are now in opposition in our countries feel bound by political guidelines on which they have never been consulted? let us look at what happened yesterday in the irish elections, let us look at the electoral debate today in portugal. the only way to give these recommendations a form of political legitimacy is to ensure that national parliaments are involved, from day one, throughout the european semester procedure, whereas the council conclusions only mention parliaments in passing, in the same category as the regions, the social partners or ngos. the stakes are incomparably higher. this is a new dimension of european democracy which the decisions taken invite us to explore. in writing. since 2007, three nuclear power plants in lithuania, slovakia and bulgaria have been decommissioned with substantial eu financial support. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. parliament also demanded that these three decommissioning programmes be the subject of a special report by the court of auditors by the end of the year to find out whether the money spent has actually led to increased security. in the face of budgetary constraints facing each country, parliament will only agree to extend its aid if eu funds have effectively improved the security of energy supply, modernised infrastructure and developed sustainable energy projects. in the wake of the nuclear disaster in japan, the eu is aware of its responsibility and cannot afford to neglect the safety of nuclear installations.
in writing. when lithuania, slovakia and bulgaria joined the european union, a plan was put in place to close and dismantle a number of old power stations that did not meet european standards. by releasing very large amounts of funds - which will amount to eur 2 848 million by the end of 2013 - it has made it possible to close all these plants and partially convert these states to renewable energy. however, a number of commitments seem not to have been respected and there are legitimate questions about the use of the funds committed. that is why i voted for this resolution by the european parliament. the commission also notes that the programme has not yet been fully implemented, although the main cause of the programme was the lack of progress in dismantling, and calls on the commission to improve the implementation of this assistance, for example by producing an annual monitoring report. to this end, it may rely on the court of auditors' ongoing audit. it should also set up a team of coordinators and experts to cover all three projects, which is curiously not yet the case.

in writing. the european globalisation adjustment fund is a controversial mechanism. officially, the fund enables the european union to finance concrete actions to counter the effects of the crisis. it's just a cautery on a wooden leg. however, this mechanism is used only occasionally and in a few cases. in fact, he's funding the layoffs. today the european parliament has gone even further in hypocrisy by allocating part of this fund to unilever, which has just closed its factories in the czech republic and laid off more than 600 people, while its net profits have increased by 4.6 billion, or +26%. i therefore voted against this report which raises a more global problem than the unilever case. how can national and european public authorities, in the face of the employment crisis we are facing, continue to use public money to subsidize multinational companies that lay off employees, while making a profit, and thus privileging their shareholders over their employees?
in writing. dual-use goods are products which can be used for both civilian and military purposes, such as chemicals, technical construction equipment, but also software and other new technologies. it is often difficult to predict the real purpose of exported products, so it is necessary to hold exporters accountable and to oblige them to verify the real purpose of the various products they sell abroad. although several monitoring and information mechanisms already exist, we have asked for greater security in this area. that is why we voted in favour of the amendments calling for exports to be notified in advance, for stricter controls and for more transparency. this will be an additional guarantee to prevent abuses and prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.

in writing. this is an own-initiative report drawn up in the context of the various proposals to be announced by the european commission in 2011 and 2012 on combating violence against women. this is a subject which is particularly close to my heart, as well as to the association "women at the centre", which organized a conference on this subject a few weeks ago in paris. the report proposes a new comprehensive policy approach to combating gender-based violence, including the establishment of a european charter establishing a minimum level of victim support services and a european-wide criminal law instrument. i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. in europe, one in four women will experience physical violence in her lifetime and more than one in ten will be a victim of sexual violence involving force. in the face of such figures, action is urgent. the commission must therefore establish a new european policy framework for combating violence against women. all forms of violence against women (rape, prostitution, sexual violence, etc.) must be criminally prosecuted in all countries of the european union. each member state has a duty to provide these women with free legal aid and reception facilities to enable them to build a new and better life for themselves and their children. this recognition of violence against women as a crime at european level is absolutely necessary.
in writing. the european parliament adopted on tuesday, 5 april 2011, a report on combating violence against women. this text looks at the specific nature of violence against women and girls by men, which is one of the most widespread and pernicious obstacles to equality between women and men. today's report will help to put in place a criminal law instrument in the form of a european union directive to combat gender-based violence. it establishes a european charter, which will guarantee a minimum level of assistance including the right to free legal aid and emergency psychological services. the report also calls for the commission to establish a european observatory on violence against women. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances.
in writing. my group is divided on the subject. i voted in favour of amendment no 19 and recital j on the word 'prostitution' because i believe that prostitution is indeed violence against women.
in writing. violence against women is a reality that tends to be forgotten: between 20 and 25% of european women have been subjected to physical violence (at least once) during their adult life. the european parliament then adopted a report on this issue last week and on the need to establish a policy framework in this area, and i welcome that. our report seeks to encourage all the member states of the european union to consider violence against women as a crime and thus to establish a criminal law instrument to combat such violence. in particular, i voted for the establishment of a mechanism to facilitate access to free legal aid and for the establishment of free emergency psychological services for victims. i also supported the amendments which recognise the 'serious problem of prostitution' and consider that 'violence against women' covers prostitution. finally, i voted to make rape and sexual violence a crime, even within a marriage or other type of intimate relationship.

i'm the reporter. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking my colleagues for their active and constructive participation in the work of the committee on fisheries on this report on transitional technical measures, a report which has given rise to a lively debate, given the importance of technical measures, since they determine the activity of fishermen and the sector, by setting out the means that fishermen can use to catch fish in areas specified by this regulation, with the aim of ensuring the protection of juveniles and the renewal of stocks, an objective shared by all and, in particular, by fishermen. the subject of this report is sensitive and controversial, as evidenced by the difficulties encountered by the commission since 2008 in reaching agreement with the council on the evolution of these measures, when these two institutions were the only ones concerned by the procedure. the technical measures are currently governed by an old regulation, amended by successive transitional measures, which has already been extended until 30 june 2011 following the failure to agree with the council on a new regulatory proposal formulated in 2008 by the commission, which aimed to simplify and clarify existing legislation in order to better apply the rules and take into account the regional characteristics of fisheries. today, as the new deadline looms, the context has changed profoundly. since the lisbon treaty, fisheries have been largely covered by the codecision procedure, with parliament playing an important role as a co-legislator, a role which it intends to play by bringing the views of fishermen and those of community policy-makers closer together. as a port city, i am always struck by the distance, or even the distrust, of the fisheries sector towards the cfp, whereas farmers, for example, clearly feel closer to the cap. the fishing industry is also in crisis. the discomfort is growing. the real challenge is to reconcile the economic balance of the sector, and thus the guarantee of decent incomes for fishermen, on the one hand, with the sustainability and renewal of fish stocks, on the other. finally, the end of the application of the regulation comes at the same time as the start of discussions on the reform of the common fisheries policy, which must be given an ambitious framework, attract the support of fishermen, consumers and citizens, and involve the whole sector in the scientific analyses which determine the level of quotas and thus the level of activity in the sector. this new context requires the commission to draw up a genuine proposal on the development of technical measures, which it seems to have avoided, together with the council, to date. a new proposal will have to ensure that technical measures are adapted to the realities on the ground, in consultation with the professionals in the sector. it will also have to seek consistency between the new regulation and the framework of the next cfp, particularly on the issue of regionalisation of measures, and to work towards a clear division of powers between the commission and the member states, which is an element of understanding and support for this community policy. in view of this context and these challenges, my proposal is to grant the commission's request for an extension until 31 december 2012, without substantial changes to the current technical measures, except for an addition concerning the mesh for wild boar. i am aware, however, that this proposal is a concession to the commission and that the questions and demands for change are strong among the professionals, who are disappointed by the postponement of this major project. i therefore attach to this acceptance a double request, that of assessing the impact of the technical measures currently in force, which is essential for effective adaptation, and the request for genuine consultation with all the stakeholders and, in particular, fishermen, for the preparation of the next regulation. in conclusion, i would draw attention to the fact that this future commission proposal must be made within a reasonable timeframe, for a new regulation applicable on 1 january 2013, the date on which the new cfp will enter into force. it is essential that we work on this new proposal now. it would not be reasonable to extend the period of application of the present regulation by another 18 months. the technical measures on which my report is based are transitional and validated as such.

mr president, commissioner, i think many of my colleagues have mentioned that the story of this single market package is the monti report, and the monti report advocated a great compromise, in a way, between those who advocate more competition and those who advocate more consideration of social, environmental and also fiscal aspects. i think that in this parliament, provided that the texts are not torn up in the votes we will be taking in plenary in a few hours' time, we have succeeded in finding this compromise, including in the fourteen proposals which appear in all three reports. and i know that you are discussing within the commission's college which major lines you will adopt, and we will of course be very attentive to ensuring that the balance found in the european parliament and desired by mario monti is taken up and extended in the 12 lines of work you have mentioned. i would like to stress three points which i consider particularly important, in addition to what emilie turunen said earlier for the green group. the first element concerns competition. the question of the single market is what competition is based on. is competition based on innovation, on products, or is it based on rules, on environmental dumping, on social dumping? i think we have found a balance here in this parliament - and i hope you can bring it to the commission - which is to say yes to more competition through innovation, to more capital investment, but also yes to a social clause, yes to environmental standards which ensure that competition does not lead to regulatory dumping. and it is these two aspects which i believe are fundamental to our compromise. the second point i would like to stress is the tax aspect. when you proposed the consolidated basis for multinationals in your first version of the single market act, it was not an optional proposal, that is to say that all companies had to submit to this consolidated basis. in the proposal which the commission put forward some ten days ago, it is an optional measure, that is to say, instead of building the single market, we are destroying the single market. we're going to add a new regime, we're going to add complexity, we're going to add regulatory arbitrage, instead of doing tax harmonization. the commission's proposal two weeks ago is totally contrary to what we want in the european parliament and to what you proposed. the last point, very quickly, is to emphasize the notion of reciprocity, in exactly the same terms as you did. the single market is 500 million people, it is an economic construct, but it is also a political construct which must allow us to weigh upwards in globalisation.
