in writing. the report by sylvie guillaume is an important step towards the revision of the eu's asylum and protection rules for applicants by 2012. in the face of such terrible tragedies as the recent sinking of a libyan ship off lampedusa, this revision is indispensable. especially when we know that an applicant may have, according to the states, very different chances of obtaining asylum. in this text we ask the european commission to include in the revision proposal the right to free legal assistance at the beginning of the procedure, better consideration of vulnerable applicants such as unaccompanied minors and a framework for the time limits for appeals. the european right, however, regrets the adoption of a reinforcement of accelerated procedures which are based on the idea that asylum seekers are first of all potential fraudsters and limit their rights. but the adoption of the guillaume report is a clear signal to the council and the commission to work towards ensuring that all asylum seekers in europe are afforded decent and fair conditions and procedures.
in writing. international protection is supposed to allow people who are really persecuted in their own countries to seek refuge under better skies. however, as it stands, and even if some amendments have been made to improve it, mrs guillaume's report is a real incentive to abuse this procedure, overburdening the responsible services and depriving those who really need it of a rapid examination of their case. minors, regardless of their age or actual situation, are treated with unwarranted benevolence; the possibilities of using the accelerated procedure to reject manifestly unfounded applications are limited; the suspensive nature of appeals is systematised, requests for review of negative decisions become a matter of law; the necessary cooperation of the applicant for protection is very little required, even when it comes to proving his identity and origin, which is still the minimum for examining his file! applications for international protection cannot and should not be a means of circumventing restrictive measures against unwanted economic migration. it is indecent for this parliament to give a hand to these circumvention schemes by granting exorbitant fees to false asylum seekers.
in writing. the european parliament adopted on wednesday 6 april its report on the so-called 'procedures' directive. this vote is an important step towards the creation of a genuine european asylum policy, which we have been calling for for a long time. the adoption of the directive is also a clear signal that the european union needs a common european asylum system by 2012; the european union is a major player in the world economy, and its role in the world economy is increasingly important, especially as recent events in the southern mediterranean and recent migration flows from north africa have clearly demonstrated the limits of the current european system. it is necessary and urgent to revise these european directives for a credible and effective system. in particular, i am convinced that the provisions on the accelerated procedure or the rejection of manifestly unfounded applications should not apply to unaccompanied minors and applicants with special needs; i therefore voted for the amendments which wanted the opposite. secondly, we were totally against the addition of additional grounds to allow for the accelerated examination of an asylum application, given the risks these provisions pose to asylum seekers and i very much regret that the amendments to this were adopted by a very small majority. finally, as regards the concept of a 'safe third country', i preferred to abstain.
in writing. we need to work more than ever to establish a genuine common european asylum system by 2012, better protecting the rights of applicants and improving the quality of procedures. my report goes in this direction with the inclusion of the right to free legal assistance at the beginning of the procedure, as well as better consideration of vulnerable applicants such as unaccompanied minors and a framework for appeal periods. i regret that the european right has focused on strengthening the fast-track procedures, on the assumption that asylum seekers are almost all potential fraudsters, because this is a completely caricatured view of asylum. i believe that with more robust procedures and decisions and shorter investigation periods, there will be fewer appeals and misuse of power and misuse of power and misuse of power and misuse of power.
in writing. in the framework of the asylum action plan, the european union aims to create a common european asylum system. the free movement of persons within the schengen area now requires us to approach immigration issues in a concerted manner. the report on the granting and withdrawal of international protection reforms the existing system through directive 2005/85/ec. the population pressures now exerted on europe make us look at these matters with increased vigilance. unfortunately, mrs guillaume's report does not take account of these considerations, which is why i and the european people's party are opposed to it. it leaves too many inaccuracies and laxities in the procedures, which risk misusing this historic right. for example, the concept of "family members" is too broad and risks abuse. after six months of proceedings, it will be up to the member state to prove that the asylum seeker is not being persecuted, making the task of the competent authorities much more complicated. restrictions on the use of accelerated procedures will increase these difficulties.
in writing. i voted against the sylvie guillaume report because it provides for criteria for harmonising asylum procedures which are unrealistic in relation to the procedures existing today in our member states. we certainly want a common asylum system, but not at the expense of utopian harmonization. the vote in parliament today clearly shows this unease in our house, half of which rejected this demagogic approach, preferring a more responsible approach advocating the adoption of effective and practical asylum systems.
in writing. all un member states have an obligation to protect refugees and asylum seekers. the eu is allowing itself to flout this right by forcing border states to hold refugees and asylum seekers in camps, awaiting an answer that is all the more uncertain as suspicion is raised, accelerated procedures are maintained and the number of officials in charge of these cases is reduced. i note, however, that this text does bring some not insignificant improvements, such as the end of the absurd concept of 'safe countries of origin', the prohibition of imprisoning minors and the inclusion of persecution on the grounds of sexual orientation.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague and comrade sylvie guillaume on the procedures for granting and withdrawing asylum in europe. this text is a key step towards establishing a common european asylum system by 2012 and thus putting an end to the intolerable situation where, depending on the european country in which he or she is seeking protection, the probability of an asylum seeker being recognised as a refugee varies from 1 to 65%. parliament therefore calls for more justice and efficiency in the handling of asylum procedures. it proposes that each country should apply the same - strengthened - rules for the protection of rights and the modernisation of procedures: free legal assistance from the first day, a framework for the time limits for appeals, specific aid for unaccompanied minors, shortening of the time limits for investigations. so while i regret that the right wing, which has a majority in parliament, has succeeded in getting amendments to the text adopted which cast a general and caricatured suspicion on the sincerity of asylum seekers, i very much welcome the adoption of this report. the ball is now in the court of the member states, which have yet to decide on our proposals.
in writing. i congratulate my portuguese colleague from the gue-ngl, joão ferreira (pcp), whose report was adopted by the european parliament today by a very large majority. this report affirms the importance of fisheries management based on recent and rigorous scientific data on the state of the resources. this is the essential condition for the sustainable development of this activity. some of the amendments tabled by mr ferreira, for example, allowing for an increase in co-financing rates (from 50% to 60%) in the collection, better management and use of scientific data on fisheries resources, were unfortunately not accepted. this report illustrates the contribution that the gue/ngl can nevertheless make to the debates in the european parliament, and i know that we can count on joão ferreira to continue this fight for sustainable fishing that favours small fishermen over the industrialists in the sector.
in writing. i voted for this report because the importance of technical measures is great in that they determine the activity of fishermen and have an impact on the future of fisheries resources. it is in everyone's interest to reconcile the economic balance of the sector, and thus to guarantee fishermen a decent income, with the sustainability and renewal of fish stocks.
in writing. we are at the beginning of the procedure for voting on the 2012 budget. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i consider that the one we are voting on today is balanced and i have therefore supported it. for the first time, it proposes a budget increase of 2.3 per cent below inflation (2.8 per cent). in this period of budgetary austerity, it seems to me that this is indeed necessary. i also fully support the need to explore new funding options to define a long-term budgetary strategy. i am now waiting for the european commission to make proposals to this effect.
in writing. i voted in favour of amendment no 15 to avoid an increase in the salaries and allowances of members of parliament, because we are in a time of crisis.
in writing. i voted in favour of the european parliament's 2012 estimated budget and can only be pleased that it has been kept below inflation, thus sending a message of responsibility to our fellow citizens. in these times of great budgetary restraint, it is important that the european parliament should set an example in its management and make savings where possible. i would like to express my perplexity and reservations about the way in which the house of european history project has been carried out so far. as much as i share the aim of creating a place for the public to learn about the major stages in the construction of europe since the aftermath of the second world war, i am equally surprised by the relative approximation with which the necessary investments and the estimated operating costs are estimated and concerned by the opacity of certain decision-making procedures. i therefore abstained on an amendment tabled by the efd group which called for the outright cancellation of this project and set out the arguments against it. i voted in favour of an amendment by the ppe group which introduces more transparency and accountability in the preparation of this dossier and requires adequate parliamentary scrutiny.
in writing. it was absolutely necessary to take account of the current economic and budgetary difficulties when voting on the fernandez report on the 'forecast state of the ep's budget for 2012'. the initial draft of the report, which envisaged the construction of a house of european history with exorbitant operating costs, was therefore totally contrary to my convictions of budgetary rigor when it comes to public money. it is therefore necessary that all financial guarantees relating to this project be clearly identified before work begins. the european institutions must, especially in the present economic crisis, maintain proper budgetary discipline.
in writing. this resolution concerned the authorisation and refusal of authorisation of certain health claims made on foods and relating to child development and health. i voted against the resolution proposed in plenary because i believe it is essential that specific claims for children between 6 and 12 months can exist and be scientifically validated by efsa (european food safety authority).
in writing. we did not want infant formula to be labelled as containing docosahexaenoic acid (dha), a fatty acid found in breast milk, which is good for babies' eyesight. there is no scientific evidence to support the opinion of the european food safety authority (efsa) on which the european commission based its proposal to authorise the use of this indication on baby food. the precautionary principle had to be applied and therefore the mention had to be withheld. unfortunately, parliament decided by eight votes to accept the commission's proposal. this raises the question of the independence and accuracy of efsa's assessments.
in writing. child products such as infant milk should be able to benefit from claims if these have been scientifically validated by the european food safety authority (efsa) as is the case for dha (docosahexaenoic acid) improving the visual development of infants aged 6 to 12 months. prohibiting any communication, even on recognised scientific effects, would be a brake on research and innovation in this area. it should also be remembered that after 6 months not all women are willing or able to breast-feed and they should be able to benefit from infant formulae with scientifically evaluated health claims. there is no question of the superiority of dha-supplemented formula over breast milk, that is not the point! parliament has today chosen the path of reason by rejecting this resolution which seeks to ban this allegation and to cast a shadow over the work of efsa.
in writing. i voted against the proposed regulation to allow a health claim that dha supplements contribute to the visual development of infants. if a majority of members voted for this rejection, 40 votes were short of the qualified majority needed to validate this rejection. however, regulation no 1924/2006 states that a claim must not be misleading and must be supported by scientific evidence. while generally accepted scientific evidence demonstrates that dha naturally present in breast milk contributes to the visual development of infants, there is currently no scientific consensus on a possible cause and effect relationship between the ingestion of preparations enriched with synthetic dha and better visual development in infants. it seems to me that in the absence of scientific consensus, more research is needed on the possible effects, both beneficial and harmful, of supplemental intake of dha before the use of this acid in infant formulae can be announced as being positive in the european union. the european parliament has today missed the opportunity to ban the future use of this claim, pending more convincing scientific evidence. i'm sorry about that.
in writing. the european parliament today rejected a motion for a resolution by the committee on the environment and public health which called for further research before it could be said that dha could be considered as a substance with beneficial properties for infants. i regret that this resolution was not adopted without all the necessary scientific checks having been carried out. this is despite the fact that the systematic review of data on dha (docosahexaenoic acid) and infant neurodevelopment published by the cochrane library in 2008 shows that feeding full-term babies with dha-enriched milk formula and other long-chain fatty acid analogues has no proven benefit to vision, cognition or physical growth. despite the misgivings of meps on public health issues, the majority of the european parliament de facto authorised the european food safety authority to declare that 'dosahexaenoic acid (dha) intake contributes to normal visual development in infants up to 12 months of age'. the case of the ombudsman, in particular, should, however, lead the european institutions to a minimum of caution.
in writing. parliament wanted to clarify the rules that the eu will have to introduce when negotiating future investment agreements. in addition to investor protection, the commission should include specific clauses in all future agreements specifying the right of the third country and the eu to regulate technological areas related to the country's internal security, the environment, public health, workers' and consumers' rights, industrial policy. this is a strong signal which has just been sent to the council and the commission on the eve of the opening of investment negotiations with countries such as canada, india and, in the near future, china. european investors must behave responsibly abroad, while protecting the eu's right to regulate investments in the public interest.
in writing. since the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the commission has exclusive competence in the signing and negotiation of agreements on foreign direct investment. mr arif's report is paved with good intentions, like hell. he is particularly concerned about the nuisance of sovereign funds, speculation which should not be encouraged, the exclusion of sensitive sectors, social and environmental clauses, respect for the principle of reciprocity or the regulatory powers of the states - all subjects which he wants to put at the centre of future european policy. and i agree with him. specifically on the latter point. under no circumstances should the financial interests of foreign investors, of multinational firms, be allowed to take precedence over the power of states to adopt binding social, environmental and fiscal standards. this is what the mif, the multilateral agreement on investment, which fortunately was never adopted at the wto, proposed. and the commission supported this scoundrel! so it goes without saying that i have no confidence in this institution to defend, respect or enforce the principles set out in the report. giving it today the exclusive power to negotiate bilateral mas on behalf of and in place of the 27 member states is criminal.
in writing. while calling on states and peoples to tighten their belts, the text calls on them to ensure that the interests of foreign private investors are protected. it does not even provide for the obligation to protect public services against any private investment. he has no regard for the common goods of mankind like water. i vote against it.
in writing. i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague and comrade kader arif on the european union's foreign direct investment (fdi) policy. in this text, parliament sets out two requirements which i consider to be of major importance in defining the framework for future international investment protection agreements which bind europe. the first requirement is that all such agreements include clauses obliging european investors to behave responsibly abroad in economic, social and environmental matters. the second requirement is that all such agreements leave the governments of the host countries the possibility to legislate in the general interest. in the past, certain private investment protection clauses have made it possible to treat the adoption of social or environmental legislation by the third country as an indirect expropriation, thus resulting in compensation. we must put an end to this drift. the arif report is a real warning to the council and the commission, which are preparing to open negotiations with india, canada and soon china.
in writing. the lisbon treaty has made the management of foreign direct investment (fdi) an eu competence. i have been keen to support this report which outlines this new policy on international investment and reinforces the eu's position as the world's leading recipient of fdi. the report sends a strong message: europe must be a key player in the investments of tomorrow. the emergence of new economies has upended the balance of power between countries and their capacity to invest. european companies need to position themselves in new markets and the eu must support them in their growth by providing them with legal certainty and by strengthening their integration into the world economy. fdi is an essential part of the activity of european countries. but are they always a lever for growth? i do not think so, because fdi is only effective if it is backed up by adequate policies, which establish clear regulations. the report thus guarantees an economic and legal environment for businesses, especially our smes. as a vehicle for growth and jobs, smes are essential to our economic fabric. we must be careful not to leave them at the mercy of aggressive foreign investors.
in writing. the 'protection of the communities' financial interests' includes the fight against fraud and irregularities. it is important to distinguish between irregularity, the failure to comply with a rule, and fraud, the intentional irregular behaviour which constitutes a criminal offence. the commission report does not fully take up this distinction and largely deals with irregularities without going into the cases of fraud. three sectors, representing about 80% of the eu budget, are singled out: agriculture, cohesion policy and pre-accession funds. the implementation of these policies and the execution of expenditure is the responsibility of the member states, which are responsible for the national tools to combat irregularities and fraud. the commitment of administrations is too heterogeneous and the high rate of unrecovered irregularities for some states is not acceptable. improvements are also expected in public procurement procedures, particularly in terms of ensuring transparency and combating fraud.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on fraud in connection with european spending in the member states. the report criticises the increase in the number and volume of suspected fraud compared to the total number of irregularities detected in certain member states (poland, romania and bulgaria) and calls on the commission, the relevant eu agencies and the member states to take the necessary measures to protect eu funds from corruption and to adopt dissuasive sanctions in the event of corruption and fraud. it seems to be the minimum. the report also criticises france and spain for being "surprised" by the curiously low fraud rate in these countries and asks the commission for information on the ability of these states to detect fraud. the fight against corruption is fundamental. however, it should not obscure the complexity of the procedures. however, real simplification should allow better access to funds, both for local authorities and for the small structures that need them. it would certainly facilitate the management of funds and better parliamentary control.
in writing. i supported the report presented by our colleague marrieta giannakou. the commission is proposing that the european parliament and the council adopt a common position on the proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling, presentation and advertising of foodstuffs for sale to the ultimate consumer. it called on the european commission to make specific proposals in this respect. it also confirms that european funding can only be granted to a european political party if it is represented by at least one member of the european parliament.
in writing. it is a feeling shared by all european citizens - and at this level, whether one is pro-european, as i am, or against the construction of europe, does not change anything - it is becoming urgent to take back european issues. european political parties have a considerable field of action. they must invent new perspectives and give a new lease of life to the democratic instruments of europe. in this sense, it is necessary to relax the conditions for the existence of european political parties in order to free up energy. it is necessary to give a clear status to these new spaces for debate and, finally, to give a real perspective to the missions of the european political parties at the next elections.
in writing. european political parties are nonsense. the 'european political area' that many advocate does not exist. ideas and real political debates can only be expressed within an entity in which citizens share the same values, the same language, the same culture, that is to say the nation. the report states that european political parties must be the place 'where the will of the citizens is expressed'. that's an unrealistic goal. the record abstention rate in each european election should remind us that the supranational level is not that of a fair and effective democracy. the great increase in european subsidies to these parties is a scandal. the growing alienation and disinterest of the citizens is palpable, but the european parliament and, more generally, the european institutions are still determined to create a european political area out of nothing.
in writing. giving european political parties a legal status and personality under european law alone would transform them into a supranational entity above the national laws governing the political parties that comprise them. it is to create an artificial and dogmatic political space of 28 which is only virtual. i am also against the tightening of the rules for the creation of these parties, with a relaxation of the financial conditions to which they are subject in return, and against any link between the recognition of the 'european' quality of a party and its access to public funding. every effort is being made to reduce the size of the club so that the privileged few who would be members can more easily enjoy its financial and political advantages. finally, the right of political parties at european level to participate in referendum campaigns on european issues seems to me to be ambiguous. some of my colleagues have agreed, thinking of possible referendums on turkey's membership of the european union, which will not be held anyway. i thought of an unacceptable interference in referendums on the accession or adoption of the euro by a country, referendums which are a matter for the right of each people, and only of it, to decide for itself. i voted against this report.
in writing. i fully support this report because it is a step in the right direction towards the emergence of a european democracy, based on european parties with a clarified status and legal personality, which has the clear advantage of strengthening their legitimacy in the eyes of citizens who still feel that the eu has too little to do with them. it is also a question of promoting a transparent functioning which i consider to be essential for a genuine democracy. finally, their financing will be more transparent, which will only increase their legitimacy, and i welcome this.
in writing. for the past seven years, the major european political parties have been organised into european parties, grouped together in the groups represented in the european parliament. however, the visibility and activity of these trans-european parties remains severely limited by the preponderance of national memberships. without calling into question these principles, which are essential to the democratic life of the union, we must strive to bring about a european debate on a supranational level, which alone will enable europe to move forward. the report by mrs giannakou is aimed specifically at promoting the establishment of european political parties and has my support. it called on the commission to implement legislation which would create a statute for such bodies, facilitate their funding and allow them to be better integrated into the daily political life of citizens. such regulation would thus provide a privileged space for trans-european interests to emerge, while providing the prudential rules that guarantee an open and transparent debate.
in writing. through representation of political parties at european level, the institutions expect them to feed public opinion on european issues. i voted in favour of the report establishing a common legal and financial status for european political parties, made possible by the treaty of lisbon, which gives the eu legal personality. this status is necessary for convergence in the budget and organisation of political parties at european level and their foundations. foundations affiliated to a political party contribute to debates on policy issues of general interest. the rules on financing are clarified to ensure reliable and transparent information on their financing and operation. one of the important rules is that funding is conditional on the party having at least one mep.

in writing. europe is not just a market; it is also a community of citizens, is a statement we often hear here and there! but what about the reality? few citizens believe in it. that is why we have voted today on the report on a single market for europeans, in response to the single market act presented by the commission last october. alongside reports on business, growth and the governance of the single market, this report addresses the expectations of citizens, consumers and users of public services. the ideas raised included greater transparency of bank charges, but also genuine recognition of professional qualifications and the portability of pension rights. the negotiations have included a reference to the horizontal social clause, which was acquired in the lisbon treaty and now needs to be translated into legislation. finally, the text takes up the concept advocated by commissioner barnier of a 'toolbox' for services of general interest, and in particular social services of general interest, which are now at the heart of the concerns of citizens and service providers in national territories. although it is not a legislative report, it does have the merit of involving citizens in the famous need to complete the single market.
in writing. too often the european union is distant from its citizens, its policies seem distant and the european project lacks meaning in the eyes of europeans. the single market, although it is only the vehicle for all-round liberalisation, deregulating public services, social systems and workers' rights by putting them into fierce competition, is worrying, even though it has and can have many positive practical consequences for consumers and in everyday life for our citizens. with the correia de campos report, the european socialists fought for a better framework for strengthening the single market, and for it to serve the general interest of europeans and not just of companies: consumer law, the protection of workers' rights against social dumping, with the explicit recognition of collective agreements in all the countries of the union, the demand for a recognized framework for public services, access to these services for all... the integration of the single market must now go hand in hand with advances in social europe, which is more necessary than ever as the crisis continues to affect europeans.
in writing. last october, internal market and services commissioner michel barnier presented his 'single market act', a set of 50 proposals to boost growth in the european union. the european parliament was then invited to comment on the various parts of the communication. the second chapter of the act lays the foundations for a reconciliation of europeans with the single market. 'you cannot fall in love with a single market' said jacques delors. but we can still try to make it useful for the citizens. i therefore supported the european parliament's resolution, which welcomes the balance achieved in the articulation between the freedoms of workers and the requirements of the social economy. this chapter thus devotes a large part of its attention to such essential elements for europeans as public services and communications infrastructure, solidarity and employment, and consumer protection. the commission is fully aware that the market cannot be set against europeans but in their service, in the long term as well as in the short term.
in writing. while acknowledging the growing rejection of the single market by europeans, this text reaffirms its central place in the community system. the desire to strengthen social legislation and to take account of the concerns of citizens, although positive, is inapplicable to the principle of the single market in the context of free and undistorted competition. this text is contradictory and false. i vote against it.
in writing. i voted for the correia de campos report, which relates to 19 initiatives on the citizens' dimension of the single market presented in the single market act proposed by commissioner barnier. i supported this report which recalls the importance of putting citizens at the heart of the single market: too often, until now, efforts to complete the famous 'great market' have been concentrated on the single market and its organisation. let us review the exercise in the light of the concerns and rights of citizens, workers and consumers. i call on the commission to endorse the key priorities contained in this resolution. i would like to mention three specific objectives which must be urgently achieved in an attempt to make the single market more attractive to our citizens: - improving mobility (either by recognising professional qualifications or by making pension rights transferable for mobile workers), - extending the regulation on roaming, in particular by proposing a ceiling on retail prices for data roaming, - finally, accessibility to basic banking services and transparency and comparability of banking charges throughout europe.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of three resolutions on the relaunch of the single market, which strengthen governance, the role of business and growth, and the role of citizens in this policy. more than 20 years after the single act was signed, the free movement of people, goods and capital within the european area is the hallmark of the success of an ambitious policy for the benefit of the citizen and growth, from which everyone can derive the benefits on a daily basis. but we could not simply take stock of the situation, because the europeans expect us to make concrete proposals to meet the challenges ahead. by recalling our priorities, we have defined a balanced set of measures which embody a clear political, economic and social model. this particular resolution on a single market for europeans puts the citizen at the heart of the concerns. by promoting mobility and exchanges irrespective of place of origin, age or occupation, this text marks a step towards a european labour market. the social protection measures discussed in the resolution are also essential to regulate this market and support a model of social and solidarity-based economy.
in writing. last october, internal market and services commissioner michel barnier presented his 'single market act', a set of 50 proposals to boost growth in the european union. the european parliament was then invited to comment on the various parts of the communication. the first chapter of the act is devoted to the commission's intentions with regard to the creation of an environment conducive to entrepreneurship. the creation and innovation of new businesses must be encouraged in the context of sustainable development, combining international competitiveness with the protection of smes. this resolution of the european parliament approves and supplements the commitments of the commission, and that is why i supported it. it thus recalls the need to support the real economy more than ever, in particular through an ambitious european industrial policy. with a view to making the single market truly one for smes, the resolution calls for the creation of a european private company statute which would encourage the cross-border creation and operation of these essential elements of the economic fabric of the union.
in writing. the report proposes further liberalisation of the energy sector, the postal sector and a stronger application of the services directive, under the pretext of supporting businesses and boosting growth. in keeping with the neoliberal doctrine, he accuses administrative regulation and the protection of public services of hindering growth. european leaders have not learned the lessons of the 2008 crisis. the bifurcation into another europe is, however, indispensable. i am voting against this text.
in writing. a well-functioning single market is essential to ensure competitiveness, job creation and sustainable growth in europe. that is why i voted in favour of the excellent report by my colleague mr busoi, which sets out a number of priorities for improving the functioning of the single market, accompanied by a number of legislative proposals to achieve this. the creation of the community patent needs to be accelerated, public procurement procedures streamlined and the digital economy further stimulated by increasing business and citizens' trust in online commerce. finally, we should emphasize two key levers for growth which must be activated urgently: - innovation in the long term, accompanied by the ecological transformation of economies: this can be done by the creation of bond loans in the eu, more specifically in the fields of energy, transport and telecommunications; - improving the participation of smes in the single market: by expanding their sources of finance and improving their access to capital markets, by removing tax barriers to their cross-border activities and by revising the public procurement framework to make procedures more flexible and less bureaucratic.
in writing. i supported the report by our colleague silviu busoi, as well as the two reports by sandra kalniete and antonio correia de campos. these three reports were drawn up following the proposal for a single market act published by the european commission. the aim of internal market commissioner michel barnier is to revive the internal market, but above all to bring it closer to the citizen. a goal i fully support. the single market act must be an opportunity to demonstrate to the citizen that european construction and the internal market in particular are for him and not against him. the guarantee of access to basic banking services or, more broadly, the protection of the quality and accessibility of essential services to our citizens, go in this direction.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, nuclear energy is a non-carbon energy, but also a transitional energy based on exhaustible resources. it's also a potentially dangerous energy. the priority, after fukushima, is obviously to decide on the safety of our power stations. these stress tests must be carried out in the most coordinated way possible across the union, and even beyond in our immediate neighbourhood, by independent entities working to the highest standards and with the greatest transparency. secondly, the fight against global warming requires a coherent and ambitious policy. if nuclear power allows us to emit less co2 into the atmosphere to produce the electricity we need, we should not be dependent on it. in countries such as france which produce nuclear energy, reducing it in the mix is a prerequisite for any decision of greater scope. it is a process which implies that we redouble our efforts to save energy, to increase renewable energy sources, which in the medium and long term will be able to cover almost all our consumption. it is a question of safety at the power stations, and it must also be a question of security of supply throughout the european union so that no country is put in difficulty for its economy. finally, true solidarity requires the creation of an energy community.
mr president, on the subject of safety, i can of course only support all the points made by my colleagues on the essential independence of those who will be responsible for carrying out the stress tests and the fact that these rules are set at community level. but make no mistake, we have old power stations, which were designed without regard to the accumulated risks and, therefore, stress tests or not, we will never have absolute safety with the power stations as they exist. we must be fully aware of this. and i do not believe that there is a majority of european citizens today who would be willing to pay the price of a nuclear accident in europe. it is a luxury we cannot afford, we must be fully aware of it. so we have to plan for exit, keeping in mind our economic needs, our employment needs, our industrial capacity and the need not to increase our greenhouse gas emissions. i think we're all aware of that. how can we do that? well, with the great european project which would be the one, in fact, of the nuclear phase-out. claude said 15 years. i think it's very optimistic, it'll probably be a little more. but this is a major project which could mobilise europeans, which could restore confidence in ourselves and in the institutions, because behind fukushima, mr president, there is still an act of distrust of the public authorities and the monitoring bodies. you have to be aware of that.

in writing. the excitement that has gripped some political groups after the fukushima nuclear accident, who hope to gain political benefits from it, is unbearable. i do not recall the communists being so virulent after the chernobyl disaster in 1986. so it's true, there is no "zero risk" in nuclear. there's no such thing as zero risk in life. and we must do everything we can to minimize that risk. but we have no credible alternatives at this time. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of certain substances and preparations is a very good one. nuclear energy or fossil energy: you can choose one or the other; you can't rule out both. neither hydropower nor the current alternative energy sources are capable of ensuring our supplies. the countries that have given up nuclear weapons but not the idea of teaching others to do so are glad that their neighbors, who supply them, have not made the same choice. stop being a hypocrite.
in writing. the parliamentary resolution intended to draw lessons from the nuclear accident in japan contained very positive elements on the safety of power stations, for example advocating 'stress tests' coordinated at european level by independent entities working to the highest standards and with the greatest transparency. like the whole of the french socialist delegation, i also supported the amendments in favour of a deliberate and prepared exit from nuclear energy, taking account of the fight against global warming. this phase-out of nuclear power will have to go hand in hand with increased investment in research and innovation, to reduce energy dependence and increase renewable energy in the energy mix of the eu member states. i voted against the whole proposal, however, because it was merely a juxtaposition of views forming an incoherent proposal. the question of the future of a sector as sensitive as nuclear power requires more than a "done-it-yourself" solution following a catastrophic event such as fukushima. we must now take the time to organise a really constructive debate, addressing all the relevant issues and allowing all views to be expressed.
in writing. i welcome the rejection of this resolution by the european parliament. the lessons we need to learn from post-fukushima are to advocate the introduction of stress tests, to establish new common safety standards in the eu and to guard against all imaginable scenarios. however, the introduction of a moratorium on new nuclear power plants during the period of stress tests in the eu is not acceptable. it will be a brake on the development of the next generation of much safer facilities. the question here is not whether the validity of this energy should be questioned. it is not a question here of succumbing to the idealistic and obscurantist values of those who would like to banish this energy. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the fact that it is not able to meet the needs of the people of europe.
in writing. the fukushima disaster reminds the world that when it comes to nuclear power, there is no zero risk. the danger posed to mankind by nuclear energy is unsustainable. so we need to go beyond improved safety and safety testing. we must prepare a european plan for the withdrawal of nuclear power immediately. getting out of the nuclear plant takes time. not to start planning this exit now is a crime against humanity. i will not support this resolution if the amendments calling for an end to nuclear power are rejected.
in writing. i voted against the resolution on the lessons to be learned from the nuclear accident in japan for nuclear safety in europe because i believe that the question of the future of nuclear energy, which is of paramount importance to our fellow citizens, cannot be decided by our assembly in a few hours on the basis of amendments adopted without a real debate. all the issues must be put on the table, no option must be ruled out, but that is precisely why we need time. the credibility of our assembly and the well-being of our citizens are at stake, who would not understand - and rightly so - that we are committing them to long-term paths which have not been the subject of a calm and exhaustive discussion beforehand, taking into account the different national situations and the constraints of our common fight against climate change. finally, i would like to deplore the fact that, because of extremists on all sides, parliament has not been able to vote in favour of immediate reinforcement of plant safety, even though there was a consensus among us that the maximum of seriousness, transparency and independence in the controls should be ensured.
in writing. the nuclear accident in japan must necessarily lead to a thorough reflection on the power stations in france and europe. it is necessary to carry out stress tests on all nuclear power stations in operation, especially when they are located in areas of seismic activity. i am thinking in particular of the fessenheim power station in the upper rhine. i also believe that an indefinite moratorium on the construction and commissioning of new nuclear reactors is not an economically viable solution and would put many jobs at risk and dangerously weaken our energy production.

in writing. as the author of the resolution on the fourth united nations conference on the least developed countries (ldcs), i believe that it is absolutely necessary for the european parliament to show unwavering commitment to the people of the ldcs. the increase in the number of ldcs (from 25 to 48 since 1971) requires the international community to redouble its efforts to achieve the goal of halving the number of ldcs by 2020. in this context, it is essential to find genuine coherence between policies directly affecting ldcs, including development aid, trade, fisheries, the environment, agriculture, climate change, energy, investment and the financial system, in order to stem poverty and guarantee decent incomes and livelihoods for ldcs.
in writing. i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on the fourth united nations conference on the leastdeveloped countries. in this resolution, parliament reaffirms the principle of consistency between the various union policies in the field of development aid and cooperation. in other words, in the eu's relations with the least developed countries, all areas of intervention - such as trade, fisheries, the environment, agriculture, climate change, energy, investment and the financial system - must be designed to support the development needs of these countries. the resolution also stresses the importance of achieving the target of 0.15% to 0.20% of gni for development aid to the least developed countries, and warns of the negative effects of agricultural land purchases, such as the expropriation of small farmers and the unsustainable use of land and water. the principle of coherence is intended to avoid declarations of good intentions which are never followed up in practice, or sectoral policies which are in conflict with one another. you just have to put it into practice.
in writing. by voting, i wanted to reaffirm my firm commitment to the fight against poverty, its causes and effects. the least developed countries are inexorably left behind in the global economy, creating a vicious circle of suffering for the people. the delays in achieving the millennium development goals are a collective fault which makes coordinated action by the union and the un urgent. the priority projects are well known: food security, access to water and health care, and literacy. the solutions are also important, but i regret that declarations of good intentions are rarely followed by action. however, it is by working for a better distribution of wealth, by supporting these countries on the path to growth and democracy and by fighting against rampant speculation in commodity prices that these extremely vulnerable countries will be able to break out of the vicious circle of poverty. this is a responsibility, but also a security imperative for the union, because poverty is unfortunately often a source of instability.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing industry is not left behind. the particularly difficult situation for them of reductions in fishing quotas and plans to leave the fleet is compounded by the additional difficulty of the soaring cost of oil. although the price has fallen somewhat, it is still fluctuating and for the last two years this situation has been weighing on the daily lives of all our european fishermen, especially in the artisanal and coastal fishing sector. this is a very worrying situation and we want to express our full support to the fishermen. we therefore ask the european commission to raise the ceiling on de minimis aid that can be granted to them to help them cope with this crisis. this is nothing more than a transitional measure, motivated by urgency. in 2007, the commission had already reacted to such a phenomenon and, faced with this new peak, we would like to know, as you have already detailed some of them, the concrete actions it intends to put in place. it is also essential, as mrs fraga estévez has said, to check that the member states are using all the amounts currently provided for in the regulation. at a time when the outlines of the future cfp seem to be becoming clearer, i believe that our fishermen are not resistant to change, quite the contrary. many have told me that they are willing to make efforts, especially in the area of conservation. this is a collective responsibility. this also requires that they are not subject to factors outside their work over which they have no control. a rapid and effective response on your part, madam commissioner, would be a sign that would also help to strengthen the historically delicate links between the commission and the profession.
for the greens/efa group mr president, i must say that i am quite satisfied with commissioner damanaki's answer to this question of the consequences of the increase in oil prices for fishermen. because we are faced with a real question of political coherence in the european union, a serious structural trend, namely the increase in the price of oil because of its scarcity - which we all know here is a permanent feature - we cannot provide a short-term and circumstantial response by increasing subsidies in accordance with the vagaries of the price of oil. it is a question of political logic. the european union must remain firm on the principles and objectives it has set itself, namely the priority of combating global warming and reducing greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels. the point is not to send the opposite signal, not to pursue a contradictory policy. it is not helping the fishermen to perpetuate a doomed energy system which will inevitably do them in turn. instead, they should be allowed to convert their fishing gear and reorient the factors of production towards energy-saving tools. subsidies should be geared to this and not to supporting the economy in the face of oil price fluctuations.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we know that the fishermen of the union are faced with three major difficulties. firstly, the quota system, which is very complex and not shared, has forced them to adopt very restrictive practices. secondly, the lack of training opportunities and the devalorisation of the trade have led to significant recruitment problems. finally, and this is our subject today, the increase in fuel prices makes operating conditions in this crisis sector even more difficult. between 2008 and 2010, fluctuations in fuel prices caused french fishermen to lose between 100 and 200 euros per week in wages, for example, with a constant turnover. as a port city, i strongly support my colleagues in calling on the commission to authorise an increase in the ceilings for de minimis aid. this would reduce the pressure on fishermen to enable them to live with dignity from the income from their activity, without having an impact, contrary to what is also intended, on the renewal of stocks. the future reform of the cfp will have to seek the support of fishermen. it would be a good start to show them that the european union, and especially on this europe day, is aware of their needs, madam commissioner.
mr president, i have just heard two of my colleagues raise the issue of sustainability and the need to subsidize professions because they cannot live. but it's the opposite of what we should be doing. the fishermen only ask for one thing, to be able to live off their work and to be able to take charge of their work. so if oil is a one-time problem, it will be a one-time problem in the future. we need to invest in finding cheaper, less voracious engines. but the reform that is now under way is to kill all the little people, all those who consume less oil, to increase the wealth of the richest. so much so that, reform after reform, there is a permanent decline in the price of fish, whereas in the fisheries it has never been so expensive and, for some fish, it is of such value that the consumer cannot afford it. what is important is not only to reform the quotas but also to reform and examine the practices of the profession which make the small suffer endlessly while the big get richer and richer!

madam president, madam vice-president of the european commission, dear neelie kroes, dear rapporteur, dear colleagues, i would first like to congratulate my friend gunnar hökmark on his excellent report and the openness he has shown throughout this debate. the draft report broadly supports the european commission's proposal, in particular on the need to make available, by 1 january 2013, the 800 megahertz band freed up by the switchover to digital television and the total cessation of analogue television broadcasting. the digitisation of terrestrial television broadcasting makes available a significant amount of frequencies designated in terms of digital dividends. these frequencies have generally recognised qualities of coverage and penetration of buildings, and are known as the golden frequencies. it is in this context that the european commission is proposing a first programme developing the vision for the years 2011 to 2015 of strategic issues for the european union in the field of radio spectrum. i would like to stress two aspects which i consider important, madam commissioner and mr gunnar hökmark. first of all, i think we should take the inventory proposed by article 8; it is preferable to rely on a precise inventory, drawn up by experts, to identify new bands before explicitly mentioning harmonised frequency bands. if the objective of finding more frequencies for wireless broadband communications is to be pursued and encouraged, it is appropriate to rely on this inventory without prejudging its outcome by designating, without prior technical expertise, one or more specific frequency bands. the last point i would like to make is the use of the frequency bands which are currently used for military purposes. it is not disputed that the commission has no competence to study the possibilities of sharing spectrum with military uses. i am therefore opposed to the amendment which amends article 7 (3), which deals with the radio frequency needs of specific union policies and uses civil frequencies for military purposes.
, in writing. i support the principle of helping pakistan to revive its economy after the floods of july 2010. however, i do not think that the commission's proposal is appropriate for a number of reasons. firstly, it is not a quick enough solution: almost a year after the disaster, we have no positive sign of the derogation that the union must obtain from the wto before its proposal can enter into force, we have not completed our legislative work and the negotiations in the council are still to be concluded. secondly, no impact study has been carried out and we do not know the effects of these measures, either on the pakistani economy or on the european economy (in particular the textile and ethanol sectors, which are specifically targeted by the proposal). it is also unclear how pakistan will redistribute export revenues benefiting from these measures so that they actually benefit the flood-affected areas. finally, it should be noted that the proposed measures do not impose any human rights obligations on pakistan. this goes against all the positions adopted recently and must remain exceptional.
the negotiations for a free trade agreement between the european union and india are ambitious, they interest many economic sectors, but they are also a source of concern in europe and india, as i saw last month at the meeting between the trade committee of the two houses of the indian parliament and the european parliament's delegation for relations with india. india is a growing country, a strategic partner - you reminded us. everyone understands the value of developing our exchanges. but we are not starting from scratch, because the union is already india's largest trading partner, the largest investor in india, the largest destination for indian investors, and india is also the largest beneficiary of the gsp. a new, larger trade agreement will therefore have to be alert to new effects on fragile sectors of the indian economy. i am thinking, for example, of agriculture - as our indian colleagues have told us - and the consequences for sectors particularly exposed to competition from the emerging countries in europe, and i am thinking of the automobile. such an agreement must be geared to the development of our societies and employment and not lead to wild liberalization with disastrous consequences. that is why my group wishes to stress a number of points in this negotiation, which must lead to an agreement that contributes to the objectives of sustainable development and poverty eradication, and which must also be accompanied by clear and verifiable commitments, based on cooperation, but with serious social and environmental commitments. i would like to stress a few points in particular. firstly, on agriculture - i have mentioned this - we ask the commission to ensure that no provision of the agreement, either through the liberalisation of agricultural trade or through provisions on intellectual property rights, threatens small-scale indian agriculture. i am thinking of the seed arrangements, for example. second, on generics, india is the largest producer of generics in the developing world. we ask the commission to stop requiring data exclusivity, which all the ngos say is likely to hinder the distribution of generics. thirdly, in the area of services, we ask, on the one hand, that public services not be included in the sectors to be liberalized and, on the other hand, as regards mode 4, that the principle of equal treatment be guaranteed, that is to say, that all forms of social dumping be rejected. finally, thank you, mr president, we believe that the chapter on sustainable development must include binding commitments to respect social and environmental standards, in particular the ilo social standards.
madam president, commissioner, we support the negotiations on this free trade agreement with india, which must be ambitious but which nevertheless still raises some questions. first, the inclusion of a chapter on sustainable development. this free trade agreement is a new generation agreement, so it is only right that it should contain such a chapter. it is not therefore a currency for exchange but a negotiating chapter as such. moreover, while the free trade agreement must take account of the level of development of each party, it cannot ignore such fundamental standards as, for example, the prohibition of child labour. although officially banned in 1986, there are still an estimated 60 million children working in the fields and factories in india today. the commission cannot ignore minimum social standards in these negotiations. to return to the purely commercial negotiations, the question of reciprocity in access to public contracts is not completely settled. i welcome the fact that access to federal indian public procurement is covered by these negotiations, but what about provincial procurement? finally, i have some concerns about the protection of intellectual property rights, in particular - and this has been said many times - that of geographical indications. indian law only protects them at the national level, not at the international level. i understood that the commission had listed 200 indications which it would protect by means of an agreement which would come into force before the free trade agreement. is this still the method envisaged?

in writing. every year, the european parliament adopts a report on the european agencies in the margins of the budgetary discharge debates. and every year, the same report is made of mistakes, shortcomings in recruitment procedures or in the award of public contracts, of too many deferrals or cancellations of appropriations... it is not necessary to find fraud, as in the european economic and social committee, to conclude that there is maladministration. but each time parliament pretends to see progress and grants discharge. worse, he never questions the commission's policy of outsourcing to these agencies, whose aim seems less to be the effective implementation of european union policies than to provide every major city in the union with its own small batch of european institutions. the pressing question of the effectiveness and usefulness of these agencies unfortunately remains unanswered year after year. the few agencies that analyse their performance do so in terms of the procedures and processes imposed on them and not in terms of concrete results. the agencies are useful first of all... to the agencies. that is why we refused to discharge many of them and we abstained on the resolutions that accompanied them.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the 2009 discharge: performance, financial management and control of the agencies. if we want parliament to exercise its discharge authority responsibilities seriously, members must be able to have more complete and detailed information on the budgetary and financial management of the agencies. we see that the responsibilities are shared, but they also seem to be diluted. thus, the european commission, although represented on the boards of directors, reminds us, in relation to cepol's accounting errors, that an agency is "an entity with its own legal personality and full administrative autonomy, including financial autonomy". the board of directors, on the other hand, sometimes delegates management responsibility to the executive director alone. the european parliament ultimately decides whether to grant or refuse discharge to an agency on the basis of the rather succinct reports of the external auditor and depends on the goodwill of the executive director for further information. i think it is imperative that we address this gap in the legislation on the iac reports on agencies and propose a solution to give real power to parliament.

in writing. late payments and defaults are detrimental to businesses and consumers alike. even where a judgment has been given, in practice it is often difficult for creditors to recover debts if no information is available on the debtor's location or assets. this is all the more so where the debtor is domiciled in another member state. currently, the number of cross-border debt recovery is particularly low, and the cost of cross-border debt recovery can be prohibitive and discourage the pursuit of legal action. the time has come to simplify and speed up the recovery procedure. in order to improve the recovery of claims within the european union, and thus better protect consumers and encourage trade between member states, the commission will have to propose new laws on the freezing and transparency of the debtor's assets.

in writing. in the current economic climate, the european parliament must set an example in reducing costs. as part of the cost-saving measures, it was decided that working party meetings would be systematically provided with an interpretation service limited to six languages (english, french, german, polish, spanish and italian), the other languages being available only on request of members. other requirements include rules to limit the long distance travel of parliament's official cars. the resolution also calls for a long-term review of parliament's budget with a view to reducing costs. the vote also gave rise to a new debate on the location of the european parliament's seat. however, this situation refers to historical references and legal texts which cannot be called into question by often erroneous attacks on the costs or damage of the dispersion of the european parliament's premises. the question of strasbourg or brussels does not arise here, since according to the treaties which historically founded our union, strasbourg is the rule and brussels the exception.
in writing. as every year, the european parliament is called upon to give its opinion on the proper implementation of the community budget by the various agencies and institutions responsible for it. the amounts allocated are allocated for a specific purpose, and the purpose of the discharge procedure is to verify ex post facto that this purpose is being met. this is an important prerogative of parliament, which was for example the reason for the resignation of the santer commission in 1999. this year, i refused, with the overwhelming majority of meps, to give the council of ministers discharge for its work in 2009. the institutions whose activities are monitored by parliament, through the committee on budgetary control, of which i am a member, are obliged to cooperate with parliament, in particular by providing it with all the documents necessary to verify the proper use of public funds. it is true that the council's cooperation in this case was quite inadequate. that is why we have decided to postpone the discharge until next autumn, in order to carry out the checks which budgetary transparency requires.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, this will be the first of three contributions that i will make to honourable members this morning, so i want to start by giving you my vision of the issues that face us and also to try and touch upon some of the detail of the issues that honourable members have added to this debate, knowing the importance that you attach to them. let me begin. there are storms blowing across the countries we call our neighbours – arab spring, winds of change, whatever imagery we use. none of us in this house know where it will end and what that end will bring. aspirations are high and expectations too that the revolutions will have been worth the blood that has been spilt, worth the turmoil and fear, worth the economic havoc in a world already grappling with the worst economic problems for decades. the uprisings across north africa and the arab world pose great challenges for europe, but also opportunities we cannot afford to miss. two principles have to underpin what we do. the first is that we in europe know how long and painful the journey towards liberty can be. our own path to 20th century liberal democracy was a very slow one. the european union itself was born in the ashes of conflicts that remind us how terrible life can be when democracy breaks down. add into that the mixed record of europe’s empires and some humility is in order, even as we assert that democracy is the necessary foundation of human progress. second, democracy is of course about votes and elections – but it is also about far more than that. what we have learnt in europe the hard way is that we need deep democracy: respect for the rule of law, freedom of speech, respect for human rights, an independent judiciary and impartial administration. it requires enforceable property rights and free trade unions, and is not just about changing governments but about building the right institutions and the right attitudes. in the long run, surface democracy – democracy that floats on the top with people casting their votes freely on election day and choosing their government – will not survive if deep democracy fails to take root. but there is no certainty – not in the outcome in any country – and no quick fix or short-term solution that will create the world so many people want to see. meanwhile the spectre of religious intolerance casts its shadow – witness the recent events in egypt – finding its excuse in uncertain times to play on fear and to wreak destruction. freedom of religion or belief is a universal human right that must be protected everywhere. we need to condemn all those who seek to use religious belief as a means of oppression, and support those who advocate tolerance, whether in syria, in pakistan, in egypt or elsewhere. europe has choices to make too. when we look at our neighbourhood we have to be ready to rise to challenges that are being asked of us. i can make hundreds of statements – and i do. i deplore, i condemn, i urge, i demand, but we also need to act and that action has to come in different forms. let me mention sanctions. we impose sanctions against regimes that treat the lives of their citizens as worthless, with people killed at the hands of police or security services that they command. sanctions on syria were imposed yesterday – an embargo on arms, an asset freeze and a travel ban for 13 key individuals in the regime, the freezing of our association agreement and of our cooperation with syria. let us be blunt and clear, as i was with the foreign minister of syria yesterday. what is happening in syria is a popular aspiration for democracy and the rule of law – it is not some foreign plot. by failing to see what it is, the regime loses its legitimacy and estranges itself from the people and from the international community. violent oppression and threats inside and outside are tools of an era that is long gone. our concern, in this house and in the european union, is with the people of deraa where the un has been refused access, in baniyas where the crack-down continues, in hama where the tanks have moved in. the syrian people will not bow to tanks. we say to the regime to change course, and to change course now.
