i'm the reporter. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, a priority debate on cohesion policy is rare, and today's debate is extremely important. regional policy, in its long history, has had many successes and in 2009 became the european union's largest spending item, with €350 billion invested in our regions between 2007 and 2013. today, parliament must decide on the future of this policy and define its priorities for the next budgetary and regulatory negotiations for the next financial framework. i had the honour to work on the future of european territorial cooperation - objective iii of cohesion policy - and i would like to thank the fictitious rapporteur and the european commission for their fruitful collaboration. what is territorial cooperation? what's it for? what are the challenges? how important do we want to make it in regional policy? these are the questions we must answer. today, 196 million european citizens live in border areas. these regions reveal, through the disparities they face, the difficulties our countries are having in adapting to the challenge of opening up borders, completing the european common market and globalisation. europe is divided into 27 member states and 271 regions. the european territory is thus divided and fragmented by administrative borders which define different political and legal systems. to paraphrase a french sociologist, the border is a political object that puts distance where there is closeness. the european union, on the other hand, wishes to bring closeness where history has brought distance, misunderstanding and, at times, hatred. the preamble to the 1957 treaty of rome is the guiding principle for our action as elected representatives of the european parliament. the european union aims to bring people closer together. without erasing them or calling into question their legitimacy, objective iii, with €8.5 billion, aims to mitigate the negative impact of borders in the daily lives of our citizens, in order to transform these fracture borders into seamless borders. this is what makes european territorial cooperation the embodiment of european integration and an extraordinary source of competitiveness. what future are we going to give him? the report contains concrete and pragmatic proposals, based on the demands of the field, the many actors encountered and the expectations of citizens. firstly, an explicit reminder of the added value of european territorial cooperation and its potential for gaining competitiveness. a proposal to increase its budget to 7% of the next cohesion policy budget. maintaining the overall architecture and the predominance of the cross-border component in order to meet the local needs of the border communities. the allocation of funds for each cooperation programme is based on harmonised criteria, in order to avoid the calculation of financial returns which is practised in some member states. more strategic programming of the funds in connection with a europe 2020 strategy on a territorial basis. incentives for regional operational programmes to participate in major cross-border or transnational projects, such as the trans-european transport networks. increased coordination between the transnational component and the macro-regional strategies, simplification of implementation by adopting a separate regulation. better use of the european groupings of territorial cooperation, the only purely community instrument of multilevel governance. finally, improving the visibility and readability of territorial cooperation with local administrations and citizens. in conclusion, i would say that territorial cooperation is one of those purely european policies with high added value. it is the simplest, shortest and cheapest way of achieving a living and practical european integration. today, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we have the duty to strengthen the most european objective of cohesion policy.

in writing. while they account for nearly 70% of the population and 4/5 of the union's gdp, urban areas must become highly competitive areas with a dense economic fabric, attractive centres of technological excellence, and be in direct contact with their regional back-base. by supporting the report on the european urban agenda and its future in cohesion policy, i am therefore advocating a new approach to urban policy, based on close cooperation between the actors at the different levels of decision-making (eu, state, urban area, peri-urban...). the almost unanimous inclusion of such ambitions in european cohesion policy by the members of the european parliament is a testament to the importance attached to the project of rebalancing development between territories.
in writing. under the principle of subsidiarity, urban policy is a matter for the member states. however, the development of our territories cannot be complete without a genuine consideration of the urban dimension at european level. indeed, cities play a key role in achieving our objectives in terms of employment, training, energy efficiency and so on. this report successfully demonstrates the added value of european policies, and even more so of cohesion policy, in the development and modernisation of the infrastructure and services of european cities. i therefore welcome the adoption by a large majority of this report, which successfully reconciles national concerns and local needs with the european priorities of the europe 2020 strategy, while respecting the principles of multi-level governance and partnership.
in writing. although i am an elected representative of regions (centre, auvergne, limousin) which do not border other eu member states, i am convinced of the usefulness of crossborder cooperation and, more broadly, territorial cooperation for the development of the european continent and the rapprochement of peoples. i fully support the proposals made by the rapporteur, my colleague marie-thérèse sanchez-schmid, particularly with regard to strengthening the role of the european groupings of territorial cooperation (egtcs) and the financing of this objective.
in writing. objective 3 of cohesion policy aims to bring all european regions closer together, particularly crossborder regions, in economic, social and environmental terms. it is important to strengthen links between these regions, particularly in the energy and transport sectors. at a time when we are experiencing a crisis of the european idea, it is worth recalling the european added value of territorial cooperation. in order to pursue this objective as far as possible, we have therefore asked for a substantial increase in the structural funds devoted to it, in particular to improve transport infrastructure and thus improve the mobility of europeans within and between regions. as a crossborder elected representative, i was particularly attentive to this issue and i am pleased that we have called for closer cooperation between local authorities and with the european institutions. we need to improve the dialogue with them in order to understand the problems better and to face the challenges. finally, since the implementation of territorial cooperation programmes is still too complicated, we called for simplification and stressed the specific nature of the programmes relating to this objective, which are by their nature international.
in writing. i would like to welcome the adoption of this report and to underline the importance of objective 3 'territorial cooperation' in the european union's cohesion policy. our parliament is calling for the share of the structural funds (currently 2.5% to 7%) devoted to this objective to be increased, and i am in favour of this position: objective 3 must be maintained and, above all, developed, in order to continue the integration of the community beyond national borders. as a member of the european parliament representing a constituency fully concerned with crossborder issues, and coming from the only region of france which shares a border with three other european states, i am very much attached to crossborder cooperation issues and projects. these areas of territorial cooperation, especially where cooperation is cross-border, are privileged areas of european cooperation, areas where borders, barriers and obstacles 'exist less'. and by becoming real project areas, these cooperation areas play a key role in strengthening links at local level, between partners from different member states or between citizens, united around common issues. territorial cooperation must be encouraged.
in writing. representing 37.5% of the european population, border regions are a real pillar of integration and bringing european citizens closer together. the success of territorial cooperation is no longer to be demonstrated today. created in 2007 and with a budget of €8.5 billion for the period 2007-2013, this objective, whose resources are divided between cross-border, transnational and interregional components, allows 271 european regions to benefit from significant funding to develop and strengthen common projects and to overcome the various borders (land or sea, administrative, etc.) that affect the daily lives of our citizens. i have no doubt that mrs sanchez-schmidt's report, adopted by a large majority, will have an influence on the work of the european commission in preparing the legislative proposals it will present in september. the report stresses the need to maintain the primacy of the crossborder pillar and to develop incentives to encourage major crossborder or transnational projects such as the trans-european transport networks (tens). these are recommendations with which i fully agree. i would therefore like to congratulate the quality of this report, which has received wide support, beyond the partisan logic.
in writing. all the actors in cohesion policy agree that the parallel existence of several european funds (erdf, esf, cohesion fund, eff, eafrd) does not always allow for an optimal management of the financial resources of the european union. i voted in favour of this report because it offers interesting ways of achieving the essential objective of strengthening the coherence of these systems. supported by the european commission, i am hopeful that this approach will be part of the european commission's future proposals for the regulatory framework for the future cohesion policy (2014-2020).
in writing. as we reflect on and debate the next multiannual financial framework, it was important to recall that cohesion policy remains an indispensable lever for growth and that the budget devoted to it should not be reduced. one of the ways to improve is to improve the coherence between the different instruments and policies, in particular with regard to the europe 2020 strategy, in order to achieve better synergy between the different funds and thus make it possible to conduct a more results-oriented regional development policy. the multiplicity of funds reduces their visibility and thus their knowledge by citizens and interested parties and may also lead to duplication or inconsistencies and thus reduce the overall scope of the policy. in this report we have therefore called for three main objectives to be pursued: the creation of multi-fund programmes, the improvement of technical assistance and the creation of a european guide. improving synergies will thus increase the european added value of cohesion policy for local and regional partners across the european union and may therefore increase the benefits for citizens.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of this report, which sets out ideas for strengthening synergies between policies with a territorial impact, on the one hand, and between funds, on the other, through cross-financing and multi-regional programmes, in particular. but i regret that the involvement of local and regional authorities in the decision-making process is not seen as a priority. improving governance by supporting decentralised authorities in their management capacities is a response to the absorption, efficiency and simplification needs that are desired in the implementation of cohesion policy.

in writing. i believe that this report is a definite step forward for a strong and sustainable cap, which is why i voted in favour of it. our message is clear and centred on three priorities: to provide food access for all european citizens; to encourage farmers to change their working methods by focusing on biodiversity issues; to manage water and soil pollution problems; and to recover waste; finally, we must defend the employment of farmers while limiting the impact on the territories. all this requires a better distribution of direct aid, a different regulation of markets and a priority which must be given to sustainable development. i am advocating a fairer cap here, so that it can provide support to the people and sectors that need it most.
in writing. i supported my colleague albert dess' report on the future of the cap after 2013. the european parliament has once again shown its determination to maintain a strong and ambitious cap with a high level of funding. the cap is designed to support our farmers' vocation and to meet the great challenges of producing food to feed our 500 million citizens and contributing to feeding the rest of the world. since the last cap reforms, the issues have changed: increasing global food demand, internationalisation of agricultural trade and price volatility, climate change, energy crisis, the scarcity of available natural resources or questions from our citizens about the role and purpose of the cap... these are all issues that must be part of the cap after 2013 and must be taken into account in its reform. i also welcome the european parliament's willingness to help small farmers and young farmers, particularly when they are setting up. finally, it is important that the cap ensures better incomes for farmers, which have been steadily declining in recent decades, now amounting to only half the incomes of urban households.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the common agricultural policy after 2013, so that the cap budget is maintained at its current level until 2020. i also want farmers to be rewarded for their work on biodiversity. we want the protection of biodiversity to be a priority for the european union, across its various areas of competence. most farmers are aware of this issue and choose environmentally friendly production methods. the contribution of agriculture to environmental protection should therefore be recognised and included in the objectives of the cap post-2013. i support the commission's proposals for an eu-funded incentive scheme to support farmers who are moving towards sustainable development.
in writing. the text proposes several interesting advances, such as the liberalisation of fossil energy, support for short supply chains, strengthening the bargaining power of producers and the establishment of a global alert system and coordinated action for agricultural stocks. unfortunately, it does not include any of these advances. it does not call into question the abolition of milk quotas or the dismantling of the mechanisms for protecting agricultural markets. i am voting against this text.
in writing. although the idea of setting up a cap on direct payments according to the size of farms seems to be a good one, i am convinced that this would simply result in the implementation of technical arrangements for farms that would exceed the authorised limit in order to continue receiving european aid. i am, however, in favour of the introduction of another system to provide more support for small farms, for example by introducing a certain degressivity of direct payments according to the size of the farms. that is the meaning of my vote on amendments nos 10, 11 and 25. i also welcome the fact that parliament is calling on the commission in this report to consider proposing the maintenance of planting rights in the wine sector, including beyond 2015. for the many wine producers in the south-west of france, this is very important, and my vote was of course in that direction. finally, on the question of the regulation of the milk market, the final text seems to me to be very balanced. i therefore support it.
in writing. the common agricultural policy is one of the oldest at community level. it must be adapted to meet new needs and new expectations, but it must not disappear. it is a policy which has proved its worth and which i am determined to support, as are many of my colleagues and citizens. this report, which i supported in plenary, shows clearly the changes in the agricultural world which are such a challenge for the future. these are demographic developments such as the ageing of the farming population or the difficulties young farmers have in establishing a farm. these are also new concerns, for example the need to combat the volatility of agricultural prices in order to ensure better food security, or the need to take account of environmental protection. the solution to all these challenges can only be found at european level. this is precisely what this report calls for: the common agricultural policy must remain a genuine community policy, but its operation must be reviewed to make it more efficient and fairer.

for the greens/efa group mr president, i would first of all like to thank the rapporteur, werner langen, for the quality of the atmosphere he created in the discussions we were able to have, which resulted in a text with very broad consensus in parliament, but an ambitious and responsible text. i would also like to stress two points which were the subject of proposals made by us, the green group, and which were subsequently taken up by all the political groups which supported this text. the first concerns the harmonisation by esma of rules on competition between clearing houses at collateral level. we know that one of the great dangers of this text is to concentrate risk in clearing houses where it was previously dispersed, but to concentrate risk in clearing houses which compete with each other and which compete with each other by reducing the level of security of the system. nothing in the commission's original proposal was intended to ensure that clearing houses did not compete with each other on the level of security, one of the important criteria of which is the level of collateral. the second point i wanted to stress is that we have proposed enlargement in the text of parliament. we have exceeded the threshold set by the commission which limited the transmission of information, the reporting of information on trading, since one hundred per cent of derivatives will not be traded in clearing houses, so we have provided for all information, whether it is otc trading or trading in clearing houses, to be transmitted to the supervisor so that he has a comprehensive view of the risks. i hope that the council will be able to take account of this important development in parliament's text.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, this report concerns short selling and the regulation of cds, these debt insurance products against default, and in particular the default of the states. this text has its origins in the greek crisis in the spring of 2010, when, following movements in the financial markets, a political request was sent to commissioner barnier and the european commission to create a european framework for short selling and speculation in sovereign debt. the commission produced this regulation in september and since then we in the committee on economic and monetary affairs adopted our own position in march and the council adopted its own position in may and since then we have been in negotiations, since we have already had five trilogues which have resulted in the formulation of a number of possible compromises. and i would like to thank, even though they are not here, the representatives of the hungarian presidency who took part in these trilogues and helped to move the matter forward. but after these four or five negotiating meetings, we, together with the shadow rapporteurs who voted for this text by a majority in the committee on economic and monetary affairs - the socialist group, the epp group and the greens, which i represent - have decided to vote in plenary on this text in july, but without a legislative proposal, to send two messages. the first message is that we want to continue negotiations with the council because it has been almost a year since this text was tabled by the commission and, as in other matters, parliament wants to be responsible but ambitious. we want these texts, we want the rules to change on the financial markets and all too often we have to wait for a council which obviously takes much longer than we do to take its decisions. so we want to continue the negotiations, which means that we will not vote on the legislative proposal tomorrow. on the other hand, we also want to send three messages on the substance to reaffirm the positions adopted in the committee on economic and monetary affairs and which will become tomorrow - by a very large majority, i think - the positions of the european parliament. the first is the role of esma. we have strengthened the role of esma in our version and you, commissioner, have repeatedly stressed the importance of this institution in ensuring the consistency of the rules of the single market for financial services. and i have to say that the position that has been adopted in the council - to have a red line which is an absolute red line for us, to create a right of veto for states on european regulatory issues concerning sovereign debts - is totally unacceptable. the second point i wanted to make is that we want a simple rule in parliament, that is, when you sell a security, whether it is a share or a bond, you must be sure you know where to find it, there must be an agreement with someone who will lend it to you. this is called the "hard lease rule", in technical terms. that is the position of parliament, and i think it is a common sense position. the last point i would like to stress, which is obviously key in the discussions we are having, is the ban on naked cds. that is a very majority position in the european parliament. we do not understand why, in financial matters, it is possible to hedge against a risk through a cds when one does not hold that risk, that is to say, one does not hold the bond of the country which issued that financial security. it's nonsense, it's an open door to speculation. in conclusion, i would say that the current debate on greece is justifying us, because part of the arguments put forward to limit greek restructuring is to say 'yes, but some have speculated. the rapporteur. - mr president, you are right, this is an important text because our citizens attach great importance to it. first of all, i would like to thank very warmly the fictitious rapporteurs who have helped me enormously in the preparation of this report. the commission proposal aims to enable member states who so wish to prohibit the cultivation of all or part of gmos on their territory. the original proposal did not set out any kind of grounds for doing so, which has given rise to a number of legal criticisms. my aim was therefore to define common rules at european level to govern the opt-out process. a little subsidiarity is necessary, but it must be framed in such a way as not to unravel the community policies which we are having such difficulty in putting in place. but it is also a question of responding to the wishes of the states, the many regions in europe and the citizens, even more numerous, who do not want the cultivation of gmos to develop on their own territory. we have therefore established three categories of grounds which could lead to a ban on the cultivation of gmos. first, a first reason on which all the groups agree: environmental reasons complementary to those assessed at european level. they are complementary because they address local or systemic aspects of the use of gmos in a given agronomic context. for example, weed resistance to pesticides used with gmos. the second category of reasons is the socioeconomic impacts. should not the cost of contamination or the measures to be taken to control it, for conventional and organic farmers, be known and taken into account? finally, there are reasons related to land use and land use planning. while fully aware of the importance of giving full effect to the decision voted by the environment council in december 2008 calling for better expertise from efsa in the field of gmos, we want to maintain centralised management but leave room for manoeuvre to the member states. this implies, of course, that efsa needs to improve its work in managing conflicts of interest within the gmo panel and in risk assessment. secondly, we propose a change in the legal basis from article 114 to article 192, to ensure that the measures taken by the individual member states are effective. the aim is not to involve the states in decisions which they would not be able to defend in court if brought by the producers of gmos. finally, we believe it is essential to make it compulsory to draw up measures on coexistence. the last thing a country wants to do is to allow the cultivation of gmos, and that is to take the necessary measures to protect the other sectors. a satisfactory text was voted by the committee on the environment, but it was necessary to reach compromise solutions to allow the vote in plenary. i very much regret the position of the epp group and its rapporteur, because we were, in fact, very close to each other and we were unable to find a compromise solution. the amendments tabled on behalf of my group - the alde group - are compromise amendments which i hope will be supported by all the groups, and even by a large part of the epp. these amendments seem to me to be the right balance between the need to respond to the wishes of the europeans and the commission and the need to maintain a centralised system without, in effect, dismantling the internal market. but the main thing is to give the states, regions and citizens who wish to do so the opportunity to act in the way they wish. we talked a lot about democracy this morning. the text proposed here is also in line with european democracy. we cannot pretend that we do not know what our fellow citizens want. we must do so with the rule of law, taking into account the needs of the economy, health and the environment, and democratic demand is a fundamental imperative for all of us in the european parliament.

member of the commission. − mr president, let me thank the parliament once again for its active and efficient handling of this proposal. let me start by reacting to some of the comments that were made during this debate. first of all, i do not share mr häusling’s assessment on the competence of efsa to decide on gmos. i believe that we have the competence, but naturally the processes need to be strengthened and are always susceptible to being strengthened. this is, as you all know, what we are doing now. on the other hand, we have to understand that efsa’s decisions are not instructions or edicts requiring member states to cultivate gmos. they are statements on safety from the health and environmental perspective. therefore we need other processes when it comes to cultivation. on these processes again, i would like to comment on what ms grossetête said, with which i totally disagree. ms grossetête said that the commission, through this proposal, is avoiding its responsibility and passing it on to member states. i would suggest that it is completely the opposite. cultivation comes at the tail end of a process which starts from the authorisation phase. at this authorisation phase, where member states have total competence to decide on whether to authorise gmos or not, member states are on record that they have never decided one way or the other, thus passing the responsibility from them to the commission. at the same time we have countries who are opposing this proposal who are today prohibiting cultivation in their own territories through safeguard clauses which are illegal under the european directive. it needs to be said that, every time the commission tries to take action against these safeguard clauses, it is always blocked by the council. i think it is time that we stopped this situation. i would also like to look at some positive elements of these proposals. i believe that having this provision implemented would put more pressure on the biotech industry to persuade consumers and their representatives about the benefits of their products, and to ensure that risks are reduced and benefits are increased. the objective of responsible innovation which we are pushing is not an economic benefit but it is a citizens’ benefit. may i remind you that the proposal addresses the long-standing demands of some member states for more subsidiarity on gmo cultivation. the swift work of parliament gave us additional impetus to work hard with the hungarian presidency towards a compromise proposal which could have been the starting point for discussions and a possible agreement. unfortunately, despite the substantive progress achieved under the hungarian presidency, it was not possible to open discussions with parliament before today’s vote. whilst many member states continue to emphasise the importance of the commission’s proposals, others keep asking for extra time and further clarifications. we must double our efforts to find the necessary common ground, thus accommodating those who want to cultivate gmos and those who may wish to restrict or prohibit cultivation. i remain committed to working with parliament and the council on the clarification and possible improvement of the proposal, to reach an agreement as soon as possible.

in writing. short selling is when a natural or legal person sells a security that is not owned by him with the intention of buying back an identical security later. this is a common practice in most financial markets and has been regulated in many countries following the financial crisis, but in europe in a very disparate way as the eu did not have a legislative framework adapted to short selling. this proposal for a regulation is therefore intended to fill this gap. today negotiations are under way on this matter with the council, led by our rapporteur pascal canfin, whom i support, on behalf of parliament. i therefore voted in favour of this report and i hope that the negotiations with the council will be concluded quickly.

in writing. europe must learn from the greek crisis and bring the financial and banking markets out of the dark. the use and promotion of financial products which enrich only speculators must be denounced. it is also necessary to prohibit "naked sovereign debt" cdss, i.e. the possibility of buying an insurance policy without holding a government bond (greek for example), and thus speculating on the bankruptcy of the country without being exposed to risk. this would eliminate the most speculative trades, which increase market volatility and have put greece, ireland and portugal in untenable positions. this is a strong message to the council as negotiations with the 27 will resume after the summer, with the aim of reaching an agreement in early autumn, before legislating on financial instruments.
in writing. this report has two merits. it called on the national authorities to be given the right to restrict short selling in their territory. he demands fines large enough to prevent short sellers who are unable to pay their debts from making a profit on their sales. it is therefore unfortunate that this text does not at any time refer to the harmful logic of short selling and so-called cds contracts. the poor guarantees requested by the commission are not reinforced here. and once again, all powers are given to the commission. i shall abstain on the two acceptable proposals contained in this report.
in writing. the investor compensation schemes directive 1997 allows clients who have received services from an investment company to be compensated in certain circumstances where the company is unable to return money or financial instruments held on behalf of the client. however, this directive leaves a large margin of manoeuvre to the member states. the present proposal therefore aims to improve the functioning of these compensation schemes, to clarify their scope and to take account of the financial crisis and the regulatory measures adopted by the eu in the wake of it. i support the guidelines of this report and those adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs.
in writing. the text proposes to raise the minimum level of investor compensation to eur 100 000 across europe. the unilateral decision to abolish the ceiling for compensation for the latter, which was never lower than 90%, is not affected. in this europe, the risks are borne by the citizens. i vote against it.
in writing. the european commission proposed to give member states the right to ban gmos on any grounds other than health or environmental grounds, which would be assessed exclusively by the european food safety authority. the european parliament, which is committed to ensuring a stronger legal basis for international trade rules, insisted that member states should be able to invoke additional environmental grounds. i think that all member states must take measures to prevent contamination of gmos in conventional or organic farming and ensure that those responsible for such incidents are held financially responsible. that is why i voted for this balanced report, which will allow, if the council succeeds in reaching a common position, those states and regions which so wish not to cultivate gmos.
in writing. the issue of cultivating genetically modified organisms (gmos) regularly arouses passion, unfortunately sometimes without sufficient reason. in my vote i asked that decisions on authorizing or prohibiting the cultivation of gmos should be taken as far as possible at european level in order not to break up the internal market and not to create distortions of competition between european farmers. indeed, if the cultivation of a specific gmo is bad for sweden, it is also bad for france! it therefore seems to me essential to strengthen the role of the european food safety authority (efsa) in order to ensure optimum food and environmental safety throughout the continent. however, i recognize that certain criteria such as public policy, which is recognised in the wto and therefore legally applicable, must be able to be used by member states to restrict or prohibit, on a case-by-case basis, the cultivation of certain gmos which pose particular difficulties in certain member states.
in writing. to say that gmos are controversial in europe is an understatement! while several member states, including france, are using their safeguard clauses to refuse certain gmos, the states have very little room for manoeuvre at the moment and, in the absence of unanimity or even a majority, decisions are regularly blocked in the council. the idea of this directive is therefore to re-introduce a degree of freedom for the member states: they will be able to restrict or ban the cultivation of gmos on their territory. we have adopted mrs le page's report by a very large majority, the result of long negotiations, which i believe is a balanced compromise. the report therefore seeks to strike a balance between the eu's authorisation system and the freedom of states to respond to their specific national or local problems. but it must be stressed that the states will not be able to do as they please either: a list of reasons has been drawn up; it will serve as a basis for justifying the restriction or prohibition of the cultivation of gmos. these include environmental, socioeconomic impacts, land use and land use planning.
in writing. whether or not gmos are grown should remain the responsibility of the member states. this is the message which parliament has just reiterated to the council and the commission. the diversity of ecosystems and agricultural practices in europe, as well as the lack of reliable data on local impacts, resistance to pesticides, the preservation of biodiversity, the risks of contamination of traditional or organic crops that can practically not be controlled are sufficient justifications for member states to legitimately prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. at a time when we are experiencing health crises in succession, it is our duty to ensure that all our citizens have a quality diet.
in writing. within the european union, the debate on whether or not to allow the cultivation of gmos has been raging for many years. with the adoption of this report by a large majority, we wanted to bring more clarity to this debate. the member states will now be able to choose what they want to do with gmos. they will be able to restrict or ban the crop more easily than they can at present. the member states will be able to invoke environmental reasons such as the preservation of biodiversity, the lack of data or resistance to pesticides. in short, i voted for this text because it provides a clearer framework for what is and is not acceptable in relation to the cultivation of gmos in the european union. we have sent a strong message to the council to translate these aspirations.
in writing. i supported the lepage report as amended, which aims to strengthen the rules at eu level so that states that do not want to use gm seeds can have clear and concrete arguments for doing so. i agree with the analysis that the commission's original proposal was rather vague, suggesting that gmos could be refused on purely ethical grounds but not on environmental or health grounds, which was not satisfactory. the aim is to send a message to the member states that they should finally take up their responsibilities in this area and to give the commission a guideline to take account of these elements in the new revised text it intends to present in 2012.
in writing. i voted in favour of the legislative resolution giving eu member states the possibility to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of gmos in all or part of their territory. it is a good compromise between a straightforward ban on them, which is difficult to obtain, and an authorization which would prevent states wishing to apply the precautionary principle from doing so. the text voted on tuesday therefore allows member states to be free to choose and, if they wish, to prohibit the cultivation of genetically modified organisms for reasons other than health or the environment. the european parliament has amended the commission's proposal by asking member states to strengthen measures to prevent contamination of gmos in conventional or organic farming and to ensure that those responsible for such incidents are held financially responsible.
in writing. the report has the merit of allowing member states to ban the cultivation of gmos on their territory and to request labelling as 'gmo-free'. but that's not enough. i call for a european moratorium on gmos until it is proven that they are safe. the free movement of the gmo products endorsed by this text should be able to be prohibited by each member state if it so wishes.
in writing. i voted against the lepage report on the possibility for member states to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory. the question of whether or not to allow the cultivation of gmos on national territory is of extreme importance for french and european agriculture. it must be the subject of deep scientific and environmental reflection and must not be subject to demagogic and unrealistic considerations. in my view, authorization to prohibit or not to prohibit the cultivation of gmos can only be granted following an independent expertise based solely on objective health and environmental grounds and in full respect of the precautionary principle. moreover, this decision must also be taken at community level under the aegis of the european food safety authority: the criteria must be the same for all member states in order to guarantee the conditions for healthy and balanced economic competition.
in writing. − in my work as both the latvian minister of the environment and the chairman of the foreign affairs committee of the saeima, i have always advocated latvia as a country free of genetically modified organisms. this is the issue that most directly affects the health of each citizen, but there is a lack of research on the effects of gmos on human health. in my view, therefore, their use should be limited as much as possible, because if gmos are allowed to be used, for example, as seed material, there will be no return route and the soil will be contaminated. that is why today i supported the corinne lepage report, which gives the member states of the european union the possibility to restrict or prohibit the cultivation of genetically modified organisms on their territory, by voting for amendments that are in the interests of the european and latvian people and that have also been advocated by greenpeace and friends of the earth in latvia.
in writing. i voted in favour of mrs lepage's report and therefore of the possibility for member states to prohibit the cultivation of gmos on their territory through new legal provisions. this report responds to the demand of a large majority of european citizens who are very suspicious of or opposed to gmos and their use in food. the risks to biodiversity, the diversity of cultivation methods, the economic impact on conventional and organic farming and the low number of studies on the environmental and health impacts of gmos require that member states have such a legal framework to prohibit such cultivation. the vote is a clear signal to the council and the commission to finally improve the guidelines governing the evaluation of gmos in line with the conclusions of the council of december 2008 under the french presidency of the union. it is now up to the commission and the council to take up their responsibilities on gmos and to verify that member states, such as france, will actually support this necessary development of community legislation. the problem of the wto and the need to take environmental and social issues into account at this level will remain unresolved.

in writing. while the european commission, the committee of the regions and the parliamentary committee on regional development had already expressed their support for the creation of a new category of intermediate regions under the 2014-2020 cohesion policy, the vote on this report was a crucial new step towards this eventual creation. i voted in favour of this new category of regions and therefore call on the council to take this matter forward. the creation of a new category for regions whose gdp is between 75 and 90% of community gdp would enable them, with a constant budget, to cope better with the current challenges, particularly in terms of employment, competitiveness and social cohesion, while they are suffering the effects of the economic crisis or are experiencing structural difficulties that are holding back their development. some 50 regions would then be affected, including 11 regions in france alone. another important point in the report is the recommendation that controls and procedures be simplified in order to improve the efficiency of community funds and reduce the administrative burdens which often prevent small businesses and organisations from benefiting from these funds.
in writing. on 5 july 2011, i voted on the fifth report on cohesion and the cohesion policy strategy after 2013 to send a strong signal to the european commission on the priorities for regional policy after 2013. this fifth cycle aims to reduce the inequalities of development and wealth which persist in the union. these inequalities are glaring. my vote on this report will allow the european parliament to assert its key role in ensuring the future competitiveness of the eu. with this vote we propose to concentrate european efforts on financing border areas, which are lagging behind in the development of transeuropean networks (transport, energy, communication), whereas they are the points of articulation of the european territory. i particularly supported the creation of a 'middle-range category', i.e. a new level of funding for regions with an average gdp between 75% and 90% of european gdp, to finance social and economic projects and improve the living conditions of citizens. i therefore voted for greater convergence and solidarity between the regions of europe and for a return to economic growth.

in writing. intermediate regions and strengthening the territorial cooperation objective: two essential elements of this report which i fully support in the context of the development of cohesion policy for the next budgetary period. i therefore voted strongly in favour of paragraph 34 on intermediate regions, which calls for the creation of a new category of regions with a gdp per capita between 75% and 90% of the community average, for greater fairness and equity in the distribution of european funds and between regions. some 50 regions would be affected, including 11 french regions, including lorraine! another key point is the strengthening of the territorial cooperation objective. territorial cooperation areas are privileged areas of european cooperation and play a key role in strengthening links at local level, between partners from different member states or between citizens, united around common issues; the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. the last element is the necessary simplification of procedures to reduce the administrative burden which often prevents local actors from applying for structural funds, which nevertheless offer many possibilities for our territories and their future.
in writing. i voted in favour of the pieper report on the cohesion policy strategy beyond 2013, a key text among the 5 reports on regional policy, which underlines the importance of regional and local investments co-financed by the union. the most important advance in this report is the creation of intermediate regions, or 'transition regions', which balance the rate of investment between regions lacking infrastructure and those affected by the economic crisis. the commission has now included the term 'transition regions' in its proposal for the financial perspective 2014-2020. i am also pleased that this cohesion policy is in line with the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy, but i regret that the rapporteur's reference to the 'often tense coexistence of majority and minority cultures at the subregional level' has finally been adopted. the pieper report is, in the end, an expression of european solidarity and cooperation at a time of economic crisis when the right-wing governments have only the word 'austerity' on their lips.
in writing. the vote on this report should enable france to benefit from the european structural funds for about 10 additional regions. these funds, which constitute the second expenditure of the union, were hitherto directed solely to the richest and poorest regions of the union, under the cohesion objective for the latter, and the competitiveness objective for the former. this injustice should be remedied by creating a new intermediate category allowing regions whose gdp is between 75% and 90% of the average gdp of the union to also benefit from this financing. it is the fruit of a long battle in which the french members of the epp were in the forefront and which led us to oppose the author of the report very strongly. i voted for this text because i believe that an effective cohesion policy on the part of the union cannot ignore such a large part of its territory.
in writing. i voted in favour of the fifth report on the european policy of economic, social and territorial cohesion after 2013. in view of the importance and positive results of the structural funds for the regions, which enable them to support a large number of small-scale local projects, we want the fund to remain an integral part of cohesion policy. as regards future changes, i have supported in particular the creation of a new category of regions to be added to the current classification. thus, regions with a gdp per capita between 75% and 90% of the community average will constitute a new category of beneficiaries, thus avoiding a difference in treatment between regions in a similar situation.

in writing. cohesion policy is an essential tool for achieving the objectives of the lisbon strategy, and at the same time a real challenge for citizens, as it makes europe tangible and visible in the territories. the ongoing debate on the 'outlines' of cohesion policy after 2013 is therefore of particular importance in the context of the economic, social and institutional crisis we are experiencing. in the context of this debate, the european commission and the committee of the regions supported the creation of an intermediate category between objective 1 and objective 2 for regions whose gdp is between 75% and 90% of the eu average. i was convinced that this would ensure equal treatment of regions with similar levels of economic development and avoid injustices linked to threshold effects, and i supported it when voting on this resolution in plenary. while this would not entail any additional expenditure, merely involving a re-allocation of current funds, several french regions - as well as spanish, belgian, british, german and italian - could thus benefit.
in writing. after long discussions, we are finally able to express a clear position on the future cohesion policy: europe needs an integrated and ambitious cohesion policy, which is simpler and more visible, which strengthens territorial cooperation and which addresses all regions in a fair way. for many months the french epp delegation has been fighting for the creation of an intermediate category for regions between 75% and 90% of community gdp. these regions, which are experiencing development difficulties without being able to benefit from additional funds, risk being left behind if they are not given special attention. a dozen french regions could be affected. we have won the support of this group in parliament today thanks to our fight. i regret, however, the rapporteur's reluctance to create multi-regional operational programmes which are good means of action at the level of territories such as mountains or rivers. finally, i welcome the enthusiasm shown by the report on territorial cooperation, which echoes my proposals for an increase in the budget.

in writing. the eu's policy is to make our partner countries the agents of their own development. hence the notions of partnership, political dialogue and ownership by the partner countries of their development. the so-called "budgetary aid" formula responds to the latter type of relationship. this is the transfer of financial resources from an external funding agency to the partner country's treasury, provided that the partner country respects the agreed payment conditions. at first sight, budget support may seem like a risky undertaking. this is not the case if the necessary precautions are taken to ensure that the funds are used wisely. the fact that the imf has to give its approval to any disbursement limits, even more, the possibilities of abuse. any disbursement requires the appropriate management capacity of the recipient country, which must also have a poverty reduction strategy in place beforehand. the countries concerned are invited to promote their capacity for dialogue with their civil society and parliaments. finally, better control of public finances by recipients of budget support can have a beneficial effect on the ability of their taxation system to generate additional revenue.
in writing. i supported this report on the future of eu budget support to developing countries, which reaffirms the conditions under which this policy of solidarity with the poorest must be implemented in order to eradicate poverty. it is essential to strengthen the accountability of the countries receiving european budget support and their ownership of this aid. this is essential if we are to deal with our partners on an equal footing and ensure that the aid we provide is actually meeting the eu's objectives. all too often, the absorptive capacity of this aid is overestimated, leading to either waste or spillage. i reject the idea that eu financial aid to developing countries, which represents a significant part of the eu budget, should be granted without preconditions and without any monitoring. i therefore support the establishment of effective monitoring and evaluation mechanisms along the whole financing chain. i also stress the need to involve civil society in developing countries closely in this process, because it is the people who must be the real beneficiaries of eu budget support.

in writing. social services of general interest make a very significant contribution to employment they account for 9.6% of jobs in the european union economic activity and quality of life for eu citizens. until now, european legislation on these services has been partial, since it dealt only with aspects of competition law, and variable, since it is subject to different interpretations by the court of justice of the european union and the commission. it is not only necessary to provide a secure and flexible legal framework for these services, but also to approach them from an economic and political point of view. our societies have chosen to have social institutions which protect citizens from the vicissitudes of the market. since there are as many schemes for implementing these services as there are member states of the union, the report adopts a pragmatic approach which is particularly consistent with this broad subject. in defending the model of a social market economy, in which social services of general interest are essential tools, i voted in favour of this report.

in writing. for rules adapted to the specific nature of social services: the european parliament, meeting in plenary, recognised the importance of social services of general interest (ssig) in the context of the current economic and financial crisis. as a vehicle for social cohesion, these services play a key role in cushioning the effects of the crisis. while they remain primarily the responsibility of the member states, they are often confronted with the rules of the internal market and in particular those on state aid. it is because these rules seem inadequate and recognise too little of the specific characteristics of these public services that we must, in a pragmatic way, work on their revision and on strengthening legal certainty. the challenge is to enable public service providers to fully fulfil their mission of general interest! the legal vacuum is filled by the court of justice, which is neither democratic nor a source of security for service providers. the vote we are taking today is a recognition that social services of general interest must be given the conditions which enable them to fulfil their mission fully. we must make accessibility, universality, quality and efficiency of these services a priority!

in writing. i welcome the vote on mr de rossa's report, which recalls that social services of general interest (ssigs) are at the heart of the european social model. we recall that these sgeis are for everyone and that universal access must therefore be guaranteed, particularly as regards social housing. parliament also called on the commission to propose legislation recognising universal access to basic banking services and broadband internet. finally, we ask for clarification of the criteria for distinguishing between economic and non-economic services, which would make it possible to protect social services more effectively. unfortunately, while the urgency of the economic and social situation would have required members to call for a framework legislative instrument on ssigs, as proposed by the greens/efa group in its alternative resolution, my colleagues refused to take this courageous initiative. the horizontal social clause and article 14 of the lisbon treaty guarantee social rights, including the right to access services of general interest. it is high time to prove to the european citizens that social europe is in motion and to give public services the place they deserve in european law.
in writing. the problem with the european union is that the concept of public service is completely foreign to it. there are services which are marketable and can generate profit for the industry and which should be subject to competition, preferably worldwide. potentially all sectors are candidates, although some non-profitable segments can and even should be left to the care of the states and taxpayers. what the hell! corporations are for profit, not solidarity! that's the general philosophy of this text. a few highly sensitive exceptions for the good reputation of the brussels bureaucracy have been made: financing of certain transport, but only to compensate for their public service obligations; social security, even if it is believed that private insurance would do better for their own benefit, and a few others. in this context, mr de rossa's report, although well-intentioned, seems like a desperate attempt to save the furniture. it is primarily up to the states to define public services, services not subject to competition law, according to the needs and traditions of each nation, and to decide on their organisation and financing. the commission must take note of this.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report to underline the essential nature of social services of general interest for our society, but also for our economy. they are the guarantors of social cohesion and of real equality between all citizens. they also ensure greater economic efficiency, because they provide services which the short-term market alone cannot provide. the specific features of the gis must therefore be recognised and therefore they should benefit from a secure legal framework, particularly in the context of austerity measures linked to the economic crisis which may put them in question. the current european texts advocate solidarity and the defence of the service to users, but these are often only words. the report also proposes to move forward, starting with the creation of a high-level multilateral working group with a mandate to identify and find solutions to the problems faced by gis providers and users. it is a step in the right direction and deserves to be welcomed.
in writing. i abstained in the final vote because the right-wing majority of the european parliament has drained some of the substance from the report of the committee on social affairs. the european parliament resolution recognises the specific features of the gis and stresses the persistent legal uncertainty concerning them, their universal nature, their stabilizing function in the face of this crisis, etc. it also called for the creation of a high-level multilateral working group to identify and address the problems faced by gis providers and users. the resolution also calls for an assessment of the liberalization of public services, including networked services, the consequences of which we are constantly measuring for our fellow citizens. the majority of the european parliament has distorted this report by dropping the demand to put an end to the policies of liberalisation of public services. it also deleted the part supporting the revision of the provisions on public procurement and the request for recognition of alternatives to public procurement for the provision of gis, including gis-ss. so this is a setback. the final text calls for us to redouble our efforts to achieve full recognition of gis.
in writing. reducing poverty is the main objective of eu development policy, as defined by the lisbon treaty. the european union is the world's largest provider of aid to poor countries. this aid is fundamental and must have the greatest possible impact! this text, which i support, calls in particular for the provision of this in a predictable manner and for the member states to keep their promises despite the economic crisis we are going through. it also called for eu-funded development projects and policies to be subject to systematic evaluation, without this leading to a purely quantitative or short-term evaluation of the results achieved, and for greater transparency in the use of aid. these two ideas seem to me to be correct, and would make it possible to optimise the aid given to the poor countries. the report also stresses the need to promote industrial and infrastructure development in a sustainable way and to develop technology transfers in order to stimulate growth and reduce poverty among the population of poor countries.
in writing. the european parliament adopted a report on the impact of european development policies by very close votes (sometimes by a few votes). several positive points: the use of a financial transaction tax to achieve the 0.7% gni target, including for development aid; the need to remove obstacles to development such as agricultural dumping, the illicit debt burden, capital flight and unfair trade; the need to address the root causes of food price speculation and land grabbing in the area of food insecurity; the demand to end the seed monopolies; the need to tackle climate change by first reducing greenhouse gas emissions in europe, by increasing the targets in member states, rather than in developing countries. with this strategy for european development policy, parliament is not using either the language of the wood or neo-colonialism; it highlights the real problems and the measures that need to be taken. it remains to be seen when the council and the commission will take account of its positions. the doubt is real.

for the greens/efa group mr president, mr prime minister, mr commissioner, you have intervened in this debate by focusing your speech on economic governance, that is to say on the package of six directives that are currently being negotiated. the purpose of this report is to integrate this work, but it is also to go beyond it. it is also to point the way, a vision that goes beyond the very short-term discussions in which you are legitimately involved. but take the time to read this report because it outlines a majority view. this is not just the view of the socialists, the greens, the liberals or the epp group. it is a vision that has been the subject of a compromise, a majority compromise. look at what's in it and you'll take a breath of fresh air from the current situation. what is at stake today? the question is who will pay the bill for the crisis, who will pay the 20 points of public debt accumulated over three years to save the markets, the banks and europe from a very serious recession. by continuing to focus on the public finance issue, you're targeting the fireman rather than the arsonist. if the governments have spent 20 points of gdp on additional public debt, it is not for the pleasure of spending it, but because they had no other choice. by considering only the consequences and limiting yourself to a european policy focused on managing the consequences of this crisis, rather than on the causes, i think you are missing the point and you are very clearly weakening the pro-european sentiment in european public opinion. and we know that today we are threatened by this tendency and this withdrawal. the second major question that this report seeks to answer concerns the balance of power between states and markets. the euro was built, in part, to prevent markets from speculating on our currencies. that's what we saw in the '90s. we are now at the point where we have to prevent the markets from speculating on our public debt, and to do this we have two tools. the first is eurobonds; it is about pooling our debts to ensure a deep, liquid market, so that we can no longer speculate against this single market of public debt. the function of the second tool is to limit the capacity of financial markets to speculate on government debt through a number of instruments. that is the path that a majority of this parliament is prepared to propose to you. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter.

in writing. if there is one thing i cannot be accused of, it is of not recognizing the importance of border controls. on the contrary, it is well known that i am in favour of the full restoration of the sovereign rights of the member states to define the conditions of entry and residence on their territory and to organise compliance with these conditions. but unfortunately we are in the schengen area, and the states are supposed to ensure that their own external borders are controlled for the benefit of all. the proposal for a decision establishing a list of travel documents which may be covered by a visa is therefore not, in itself, absurd in this context. what is important, however, in terms of security and the fight against illegal immigration, is to leave it to the commission to draw up this list and to consider, if the member states had not taken a decision on the list within a short time, whether they would recognise it as valid, in the 'no consent' mode. on the contrary, it should have been assumed that such silence automatically amounted to a refusal to recognise a document as legal. this is called an implied decision of rejection, a common concept in public law. that is why i abstained on this report.
in writing. i abstained on this report on the development of broadband in the union which, while containing many references to competition and the liberalisation of broadband services (a sector which is already too liberalised), also contains a number of positive proposals. among these, the commitment to provide, by increasing public investment in infrastructure, the maximum number of citizens with full broadband coverage by 2013, which is essential especially for citizens in remote areas, while maintaining access quality and without excessive user charges. the proposal to ensure open access to public institutions in order to guarantee the free flow of knowledge and improve public online services, the desire to guarantee net neutrality, the use of open standards, data protection and respect for citizens' privacy, and, finally, the need to combat the digital divide with particular attention to the most vulnerable populations, such as people with disabilities, people from immigration or people with modest incomes, can also be noted. but once again, beyond words, we expect action.
in writing. while social networks have become a daily part of life for a majority of europeans, 30% have never had access to the internet. the vote by our assembly is aimed precisely at closing this digital divide: the objective is to cover the whole of europe's broadband territory by 2013. this strategy is all the more important as the internet has become a determining factor in society as a whole. the successful implementation of this plan would meet various objectives, such as social cohesion, the fight against unemployment, the right to information and the right to access culture. initially conceived as a network created for the use of the military, this tool has also become, by increasing the efficiency and economies of scale of our companies, an indispensable vehicle for economic growth. this is a competitive advantage which we must build on, as must american companies. to turn this strategy into smart, sustainable and inclusive growth, we will need to make investments that are up to the challenge, put in place a legal framework to ensure the safety of internet users (fight against cybercrime, protection of private data) and pay fairly to all net actors.
in writing. in may 2009, the european commission launched an evaluation of the 1995 directive on the protection of personal data. the commission is to present a legislative proposal to amend this directive by the end of the year, without excluding the possibility of adapting other legal instruments to the new general data protection framework. the last 15 years have been marked by the internet revolution and, more generally, by the increasing use of new technologies. the resulting collection and processing of personal data is on an unprecedented scale, enhanced by the globalisation of trade. the report highlights some of the main features of the future reform: the increase in the right to information, improved data transfers, particularly in the context of judicial or police cooperation, harmonisation of the status and powers of the national authorities responsible for data protection, etc. as a strong supporter of the right to be forgotten and of the security of internet exchanges, i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. access to data by european citizens, right to information on the use made of our data, explicit consent to the processing of our data, right to amend, right to delete, right to be forgotten, data lock, etc. these are the guarantees to which every citizen is entitled in the context of the protection of his personal data and which the european union must respect and, moreover, promote and protect. improvement of data transfers, harmonisation of the status and powers of national data protection authorities, securing of exchanges on the internet, protection of vulnerable persons and in particular minors, especially on the internet and networks, raising awareness of citizens and young people on data protection issues, severe european sanctions in case of misuse of data, etc. these are all clear elements, measures and rules which the european union must put in place and encourage in order to guarantee these rights to citizens. i therefore supported this report which responds to my concerns and contains a strong message for the european commission in its work to revise the 1995 directive on the protection of personal data which now needs to be updated in the face of the rise of new technologies and the globalisation of data exchanges.
in writing. i supported sending a strong message to the european commission with a view to the revision of the directive on the protection of personal data. several points are particularly important to me. firstly, it is about protecting vulnerable people, especially minors, who are known to be increasingly surfing the web, especially on social networks, where they easily share their personal data. in the face of this, we demand that young people be made aware of responsible behaviour! in addition, i strongly support the right of citizens to be able to easily delete, correct or block their data, and to be informed of any misuse or error that may be made in data protection. this seems obvious, but there are still obstacles that need to be overcome. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of personal data, in particular by ensuring that the data subject is able to access the data in a secure manner.
in writing. the increased use of the internet and the development of social networks, profiling practices and 'cloud computing' are creating new challenges in the protection of personal data. i therefore support efforts to strengthen the protection of personal data and to harmonise the application of the european rules on this matter. the free movement of personal data must be accompanied by safeguards for citizens who must be able to know, free of charge, how their data can be accessed, used, rectified and deleted, enjoy a high level of protection in their online and offline activities both in the european union and in third countries, and be able to defend their rights through class actions in court. in particular, young users should be protected from the threats posed by uncontrolled use of new technologies, for example by integrating media literacy into school curricula or by imposing a high level of data protection as a default setting. the 'right to be forgotten' also seems to me to be a key concept to be developed for the protection of personal data.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on data protection because it is necessary for europe to establish clear and common rules for all member states on access to, retention of and deletion of european citizens' personal data. the current legislation (dating from 1995) needs to be updated and modernised in the face of the emergence of new information and communication technologies. i will also ensure that the commission's future legislative proposal establishes a genuine 'right to be forgotten', that is, the right under which individuals can, under certain conditions, have their data no longer collected, analysed, processed or used in any way, and that it can be deleted, particularly in the world of social networks on the internet.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the european approach to data protection, as it contains many positive points: strengthening of certain rights of individuals over their data, protection of individuals irrespective of their geographical location, strengthening of the powers of national data protection authorities, appointment of data protection officers in companies, reference to the 'right to be forgotten', notion of explicit consent for data processing, expansion of the list of sensitive data, etc. however, there are still gaps, some of which are even cause for concern. this is the case with cloud computing (storage of data on platforms outside personal computers), the scope for self-regulation by companies, and agreements on the international transfer of data. those agreements should reflect the union level of protection of personal data. we know that this is not the case, particularly in the united states. i therefore regret that this report was adopted without debate in plenary when it sets out the framework for the forthcoming revision of the data protection directive. i hope that the forthcoming debates will enable us to fill these gaps.
in writing. the development of new technologies is one of the major objectives of the europe 2020 strategy and has a growing impact on the daily lives of european citizens. the importance of these tools in our personal and professional lives represents a tremendous opportunity to develop the sharing of knowledge and know-how. this must, however, be accompanied by adequate data protection so that europeans can express themselves freely, while respecting personal information. i welcome the adoption of this report, which sets out a clear legislative framework, which considers that the best use of the technologies of tomorrow must not infringe individual freedoms. making information accessible to the greatest number of people is a challenge that europe must meet. this ambitious objective must be accompanied by harmonisation and legal certainty to provide our citizens with the highest level of protection.
