in writing. i welcome the court of auditors' intention to introduce the notion of efficiency into its work, with the novelty this year of including a chapter in the court of auditors' report entitled 'getting results from the eu budget'. this is all the more important in the difficult times we are going through, when we must be particularly vigilant in how we manage the public sector, by respecting the financial regulation, but more importantly by committing ourselves to using european contributions in the most efficient way possible. on the contrary, i am disappointed with the information which has become increasingly lacking over the years in the court of auditors' special reports for agencies and joint undertakings. on the contrary, these decentralised agencies, which are present in various member states, deserve particular attention.
on behalf of the verts/ale group. – mr president, the eu committed itself to help developing countries reach the millennium goals, achieving 0.7 % official development aid by 2015, and committed itself on aid effectiveness, debt, climate, finance, etc. the eu has not reached the 0.7% target and, with the crisis, is unlikely to do so in the near future. the greens believe in a change of policy, addressing tax havens and tax evasion, with binding measures, implementing article 208 of the lisbon treaty on policy coherence, by matching words with actions, with coherent policies between trade, agriculture and fishing, addressing farmland acquisition by foreign investors with the risk of undermining food security, such as in africa, and putting in place fair trade rules to break the vicious circle whereby developing countries are locked into dire poverty despite agricultural and mineral resources. the trade pattern where developing countries export raw materials and buy manufactured products from industrialised countries has to change. the next report on the eu’s accountability should include the abovementioned policy changes as well as its financial commitments.
madam president, i would first like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr kaczmarek, on his excellent work. it is important that the european parliament should take stock of the work of the acp-eu joint parliamentary assembly each year, since this assembly plays a decisive role in strengthening the north-south dialogue and in implementing a development policy based on partnership and exchange. 2010 was a rich year for the apa, which met twice, as my predecessors said, in spain and the democratic republic of congo, to discuss, among other things, the impact of climate change in the acp countries, the impact of the global crisis, media freedom and independence and food security. but in 2010, the app also sent its first election observation mission to this legislature. i had the honour of co-chair ing this mission to burundi for the presidential elections with my colleague assarid, member of parliament from mali. this election observation mission was a real success. we were able to meet all the political actors concerned and, thanks to the dual origin of this delegation, both acp and european, we embodied a different legitimacy from european or african missions. i therefore invite the bureau of the acp to renew this experience, which makes it possible to put into practice the solidarity and the special relations which unite the european union and the acp countries.
on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, when we speak of culture at european level, we always refer to the sum of the cultures of the different member states which each one must discover and appropriate to himself, but we rarely speak of a common heritage, a european heritage which goes beyond national histories, reflecting the intense interactions and rich exchanges which have bound us together for centuries. the european heritage label was originally an intergovernmental initiative which already reflected europe's cultural roots. what were the sites marked? the acropolis in athens, the birthplace of the first democracy in the world. cluny abbey, the crossroads of roman civilization, which gave birth to european humanism the gdansk shipyards, stronghold of the solidarność trade union, whose courage changed the face of europe. the home of robert schuman, political visionary and founding father of the european union. all of them are places where our common history and the values we stand for together are read. tomorrow we will vote to turn this intergovernmental initiative into a community project, to strengthen the credibility, visibility and prestige of this label by establishing transparent and rigorous selection criteria. i would like to thank chrysoula paliadeli and the open-mindedness she has shown in defending a quality label awarded every two years, which encourages cooperation to promote transnational sites, which has an independent jury of experts appointed fairly between the institutions, and which rewards not the beauty of a site or its architectural quality but its symbolic value for european integration. jean monnet, the father of europe, is wrongly credited with the quote: "if i had to do it all over again, i would start with culture". the success of this formula is based on the idea that our union was first economic, then political, but never cultural. yet europe was the home of painters, philosophers, artists and writers long before the ecsc or the treaty of rome. it is not a question of creating an artificial european culture but of recognising the heritage we share. the european heritage label is an essential initiative for the development of cultural europe, because it allows for this recognition, this pedagogy and this outreach.
president of the european council. − mr president, it may at first sight appear strange to be addressing the issue of longer-term reforms to our system of economic governance when we have not yet completely dealt with the immediate difficulties which are the legacy of past mistakes. yet these are two sides of the same coin: short-term solutions will not be credible in the absence of a longer-term perspective. the longer-term perspective also presupposes that we can turn the corner on the current crisis, but in today’s debate i will focus, as parliament has suggested, on the longer term. as you are aware, the conclusions of the eurozone summit of 26 october 2011 charged me, in close cooperation with the president of the european commission and the president of the eurogroup, to identify possible steps to strengthen the economic union to make it commensurate with the monetary union, focused on strengthening economic convergence within the euro area, improving fiscal discipline and deepening economic union, including exploring the possibility of limited treaty changes. i will present an interim report to the december european council, which will include a roadmap on how to proceed while fully respecting the prerogatives of the institutions, including the european parliament. a final report will be finalised by march or june 2012. the task i see for us is clear: we have to bring the economic and monetary union to a solid end-state. i relish this opportunity to listen to your views. in discussing this, i think it is first advisable to look at what we have already done over the last 20 months and then to see where it is desirable to move further. at that point it will become clear whether or not such further advances need treaty change and, if so, what changes. what is it that we have achieved so far? it is often overlooked and underestimated, not least by the outside world and the markets, and we need to be extremely vigilant in implementing it. we have in fact put in place a multi-faceted reform, combining institutional pressure, peer pressure and market pressure. i mentioned these in the debate last month, but allow me to be more detailed now. institutional pressure has been strengthened, also thanks to your parliament, through: the establishment of the three financial sector supervisory authorities and the european systemic risk board; the reform of the stability and growth pact, providing for shorter deadlines, a greater focus on debts (and not just on deficits), and making it easier to sanction a member state not fulfilling its obligations; adding a new macroeconomic surveillance procedure looking at other macroeconomic imbalances – after all, that is only a part of the wider economic picture – and finally, establishing the efsf (and the long-term esm) capable of providing support in return for strict conditionality. conditionality is a powerful tool, as is now becoming clear to all those who follow these matters. at the same time, peer pressure has been enhanced. to give a few examples, for a start all governments now realise much more acutely how the conduct of another country can have an enormous economic and financial impact on their own. peer pressure will also be exerted at the highest political level through regular euro summits. the events of the last weeks show how effective this can be for some countries. the european semester provides an annual cycle of intense macroeconomic, budgetary and structural policy coordination. finally, 23 of the 27 member states have agreed to go further and work together in the euro plus pact on structural reforms that have a bearing on their competitiveness, over and beyond the important europe 2020 programme. market pressure will complement the above because institutional and peer pressures will also have an impact on the market, amplifying their political effect. markets may now be over-reacting, but they will not go to sleep again! indeed, the combination of these three pressures is already producing results. at their summit last month, eurozone member states entered into a number of additional commitments, notably the following: to translate the stability and growth pact rules into national legislation, preferably at constitutional level or equivalent, by the end of 2012; to ensure that national budgets are based on independent growth forecasts; to consult one another and the commission before the adoption of any major fiscal and economic policy reform plans with potential spillover effects; and also to stick voluntarily to the recommendations of the commission and the relevant commissioner regarding the implementation of the stability and growth pact. finally, a number of member states have adopted further reform measures, not least as a result of these pressures. it was also agreed that for euro area members in an excessive deficit procedure, the commission and the council will be able to examine national draft budgets and adopt opinions on them prior to their adoption by the relevant national parliament. the commission will now bring forward proposals on closer monitoring to the council and parliament under article 136. the commission has already strengthened the role of the competent commissioner in this field, and i would like to congratulate olli rehn on his elevation to the vice-presidency of the commission. the eurogroup of finance ministers will, together with the commission and the ecb, remain at the core of the daily management of the euro area, as is explicitly mentioned in the conclusions of the eurozone summit. as you know, the treaty provides for the eurozone finance ministers to elect their own president, currently jean-claude junker, to whom i want to pay tribute today for his work and his engagement. when his mandate expires next year, a decision will be taken on whether his position should become a full-time one based in brussels. the eurozone summit – and i quote – ‘will define strategic orientations for the conduct of economic policies and for improved competitiveness and increased convergence in the euro area’. in the same way as the european council does for the union as a whole, we will also organise a better coordination among the eurozone institutions and strengthen the existing administrative support without creating new bodies. does this strengthening of cooperation among the 17 – i repeat among the 17, no more, no fewer – create a two-tier europe? there has been much exaggerated talk about this; it is time to de-dramatise this debate. after all, it is perfectly natural that those who share a common currency take some decisions together. indeed, the existing treaty already provides for that with a special chapter containing provisions specific to member states whose currency is the euro and other provisions where only members of the council from euro member states can vote. it is thus a perfectly normal part of our current institutional arrangements, a specific working method. as i said to you last month, the eurozone is not a derogation from the european union, it is part of the european union. the treaty is quite clear: it is the member states who have not joined the euro which are referred to as member states with a derogation, and of course most of them will in due course join the euro. it is in the interest of the non-eurozone eu members that its financial stability is organised and secured. a better structured euro area is in everybody’s interest while ensuring coherence among the 27. it is my intention to organise eurozone summits as a rule in conjunction with european council meetings, if possible following them. this will enable all 27 to contribute in the full european council meeting and make points, should they so wish, on the issues to be discussed among the 17, and likewise the commission and the parliament will continue to play their substantial roles involving their members from all member states. i will report to parliament on eurozone summits. i wanted to outline all this to you because it shows that the steps taken over the last few months, each one perhaps small in itself, amount cumulatively to a significant change already in our governance structures. it is clearly the starting point for any reflection on where to go further. in doing so, it is my intention to examine the ‘what’ before the ‘how’. we should examine the goals, and only afterwards the legal instruments required to get there, including limited treaty changes should these prove necessary. a lot can be done within the treaties, including the use of instruments such as enhanced cooperation. for treaty changes, a unanimous ratification is needed by every single member state. institutional changes are no substitute for dealing with the immediate financial crisis, so we have to get the different time perspectives right. however, improvements of all kinds are possible and in themselves desirable. it is useful too to give the public and the markets a sense of our medium-term direction. some of these areas in which improvements to our economic governance could be envisaged are obvious; others less so. let me mention the three issues in the mandate from the euro summit statement: strengthening economic convergence, improving fiscal discipline and deepening economic union. firstly, as regards strengthening economic convergence, we need to examine whether to go beyond the ‘six-pack’ in terms of further macroeconomic surveillance, how to strengthen the framework for commitments under the euro plus pact, and whether there are areas in which enhanced cooperation is desirable among the 17 in areas of economic policy that are crucial for competitiveness. secondly, in terms of improving fiscal discipline, should we go further in terms of the automaticity of the sanctions provided for under the excessive deficit procedure? should we provide, in extreme cases, for further sanctions such as suspension of voting rights, suspension of structural funds or other payments, or power for a central authority to intervene in national budgetary procedures? thirdly and finally, in terms of deepening economic union, is there a need for harmonisation in certain areas such as taxation or even some social fields? should there be a limited mutualisation of public debt, and what further regulations are needed for the financial sector? again, all these questions are interlinked and changes in one respect cannot always be assessed independently of changes in others. this crisis in the euro area does require us to do more. we have come a long way from the empty, and now discredited, toolbox i discovered when i took office – which i still consider as a major error, all the more so that during the convention warnings were given by lucid observers. we now need to go further, and we need both fiscal discipline and economic and fiscal integration focused on growth – not only to punish the sinners but also to link our policies, to demonstrate that we share a common destiny. we need to acknowledge that this means a sharing of sovereignty for all members of the eurozone, and not only a loss for the countries in difficulty. we need to find the right balance between intrusiveness and legitimacy, discipline and incentives, effectiveness and accountability. this will guide my thinking on the fundamentals of the economic and monetary union in the months ahead. but above all, today, i want to listen to your views, your ideas and your suggestions; this parliament has always been a rich source of ideas, a laboratory of proposals for the development of our union. i look forward to hearing them.
president of the commission. − mr president, the european commission’s recent economic forecasts are further proof that the backdrop against which we are all working is indeed pressing, and extremely challenging. economic recovery has hit a standstill. since our last fully-fledged forecast in may, global economic conditions have worsened. investment and consumption are stagnant, and are being damaged by a persistent lack of confidence. growth forecasts are low and unemployment is set to remain at around 10% for the next two years, at 23 million people across the european union: a terrible situation. added to this are the continued turbulent events in the sovereign bond markets meaning that our challenges are of a greater magnitude today. it is precisely for the restoration of confidence that our work on fiscal consolidation, on structural reforms, on strengthening economic governance and on boosting growth is more important than ever before. that is why the commission is advancing its work and taking its responsibilities with the utmost seriousness. as i said to this house on the day after the euro area summit on 27 october, the commission will advance its second annual growth survey on policies for growth and jobs in the european union for 23 november. at the same time, we will come forward with our proposals on further strengthening the economic governance of the euro. the purpose is to continue the comprehensive approach i set out in my state of the union address to this parliament, and also in the commission’s roadmap to stability and growth two weeks later. we need more discipline, but we need more convergence. we need more responsibility, but more solidarity. we need financial stability, but also economic growth. and this is the pact we are proposing to the european citizens. we cannot do this only through responsibility; we need solidarity. we cannot do this only through financial stability; we need economic growth. the commission’s second annual growth survey will provide a first assessment of progress in the implementation of commitments made in the first european semester, including country-specific recommendations and those under the euro plus pact, and constitutes the starting point for the second european semester. let me make two remarks on the annual growth survey. the first message will be the importance of staying the course and implementing what has already been agreed. consistency in implementation is key. we cannot change our plans all the time. we have to be consistent and deliver concretely the commitments that have been made. the problems we will face in 2012 are even more systemic and urgent. we should continue to deal with them robustly and not be diverted from the direction we have set ourselves. the downbeat economic perspectives do not mean we can allow ourselves to reduce our efforts in fiscal consolidation or in promoting growth. they must be stepped up, because we are reforming for the long term. the second remark is that the experience of having completed one full annual growth survey and european semester, combined with the strengthened rules we now have on economic governance, means that our decisions need to be reinforced and adapted in certain respects. not least to take account of the persistent and pervasive nature of the crisis. we are indeed now facing a truly systemic crisis that requires an even stronger commitment from all and may require additional – and very important – measures. for 2012, the annual growth survey will focus on five key areas. first, on pursuing stability through fiscal consolidation. second, on further strengthening the financial sector. i would like to thank this house for its support for the 27 proposals on the financial sector that the commission has put forward over the last months. i count on you in 2012 to support the financial transaction tax and the proposal we adopted yesterday on credit rating agencies. third, on boosting growth by reducing fragmentation in our markets and making europe a more attractive place to create and invest. in the year ahead, i count on the support of this parliament to fast-track a number of measures on the table, namely the single market proposals. let us not forget that we have to liberate the full potential of the single market, because the key to the response to the current crisis is growth, and without growth there will be no way out of this crisis. we can do much more – through structural reform – to achieve the goal of growth. fourth, on nurturing our human and social capital. i am thinking here specifically of young people unable to find meaningful work in europe, and all that can be done to help them. fifth, on modernising our public administrations, which are a determining element of competitiveness and productivity. today we are invited to discuss economic governance. for some, it may seem frivolous to discuss this topic at a time when urgency demands action. and yes, let me be clear: all levers of action must now be used without delay. discussing governance, including treaty change, must not be an excuse not to take action now, because action is needed now. having said that, governance matters: it defines the parameters within which action can – or cannot – be taken. in this respect, we have been held back by the intergovernmental approach that has been predominant in many of the decisions, because the intergovernmental approach puts a premium on the slowest and the most reluctant, not on the most decided and the most engaged. take the european financial stability facility, for example. it must be as flexible as possible. the unanimity rule has held back its development for too long, until we finally came to the decisions of 27 october, and this is one of the problems. today the markets, the investors, are not only looking at the deficits, at levels of debt, but also at the capacity of the euro area and the european union to take decisions. that is why having a stronger governance of the euro area is vital for the survival and the reinforcement of our common currency. markets and investors demand stronger governance in the euro area – it is not just a political issue for those, like me and many of you, who share a passion for a stronger europe. it is indeed now just a matter of common sense to have stronger economic governance in the euro area, and of course in the european union. reforms at national level must be completed with appropriate structures at european level that will give weight and resonance to the economic decisions. on 23 november, i expect the commission to adopt, and to send to this house, two initiatives on further deepening european union and euro area economic governance in line with the roadmap for stability and growth that i presented to you on 12 october, and which was largely endorsed by the european council. these initiatives are based on article 136 of the current treaty. in addition, the commission will present a green paper on stability bonds, which i know is eagerly awaited by this house. this will be followed, before the end of the year, by a communication that deserves special attention: a communication on the external representation of the euro area, based on article 138(2) of the treaty. it will make proposals towards a more consolidated european voice and representation in international fora and institutions such as the g20 and the imf. in strengthening our integration, we must also strengthen our voice and strengthen our credibility worldwide. the initiatives based on article 136 that vice-president rehn is now completing will address two issues. on the one hand, the need to increase surveillance, especially for member states that put at risk the financial stability of all. the first regulation is for enhanced surveillance of euro area member states that are experiencing severe financial disturbance or requesting financial assistance. it will provide an interface between intergovernmental financial assistance and treaty-based surveillance – in other words, bringing it into the community framework. it will step up surveillance for euro member states receiving precautionary assistance and assistance under an adjustment programme, and will also ensure post-programme surveillance. the key here is to ensure coherence between reinforced governance in the euro area and the overall acquis of the 27 member states of the european union, thereby increasing convergence in the 17 members of the euro area without damaging the interests of all the european union. the second regulation is for enhanced surveillance for euro area member states in excessive deficit procedure, thereby translating one of the commitments of 26 october. it will set out graduated steps and conditions for monitoring national budgetary policies. it should enable the commission and the council to examine national draft budgets ex-ante and to adopt an opinion on them before their adoption by the national parliaments, requesting a second reading in serious cases. in addition, the commission will monitor budget execution and, if necessary, suggest amendments in the course of the year. but in connection with this, i want to be clear about one thing in particular. the final say on national budgets will remain where it belongs, with national parliaments. but national parliaments have to be made much more keenly aware of the european rules which their governments – and they themselves – have agreed to respect. increased surveillance by the commission will lead unavoidably to a greater role in domains previously restricted to national governments or parliaments. but this is necessary and indispensable if we want to have a common currency. here, i think, the european parliament can play an absolutely vital role, in particular through interparliamentary dialogue and cooperation. the final part of our package is the green paper on euro stability bonds. it will present and assess the options for the joint issuance of bonds in the euro area. it will also explore reinforced economic governance options that would need to be developed, depending on the decisions taken. i believe that euro stability bonds will be seen as natural when we achieve our goal of reinforced governance and, of course, discipline and convergence in the euro area. they will be a concrete demonstration of the principles of responsibility and solidarity. i should like to summarise by saying a few words on the principles behind this package. the increasingly systemic nature of the crisis has made it clear that we must progress with greater integration of economic governance, especially within the euro area. this crisis has exposed weaknesses and gaps in terms of surveillance, intervention and decision-making. some of these can now be addressed thanks to the recent successful conclusion of the ‘six-pack’ negotiations, for which i thank this house for its excellent cooperation – more than that, for its decisive commitment. the ‘six-pack’ will come into force in around one month from now and, as vice-president rehn has stated, the commission will use its provisions from day one. but, as we could see from the conclusions of the euro area summit on 26 october, there is full consensus now to go further, and this is a very important development. member states are now accepting what some time ago would be considered unthinkable. euro area member states must now consult the commission – and each other – before adopting any major fiscal or economic policy reform plans. they have committed to respect the commission’s recommendations in implementing the stability and growth pact. and they have entrusted the commission with the lead role in monitoring the implementation of the second greek programme and the reforms in italy. that is why this package, and in particular the regulations based on article 136, will address problems that have become more visible and more acute in the sovereign debt crisis, namely the risks of contagion and spill-over from countries experiencing severe financial disturbances. reinforced surveillance is absolutely crucial in bolstering confidence among the general public and market participants. while this reinforced discipline is now recognised as entirely necessary, the commission is committed to going further to make sure that changes in economic governance are done in a transparent way; in a democratic way; in the community way. these regulations will be based on the principle of full transparency. both regulations will of course be subject to codecision. and we look forward to continuing the excellent cooperation with this house which we saw, for instance, in the ‘six-pack’ negotiations. the instruments we have developed and are still developing will be essential to ensure that we do not face again the kind of situations that made europe so vulnerable to the crisis. they insist that member states, especially in the euro area, live up to a long-standing obligation. it is, to quote the european union treaty, that member states must – ipsis verbis – ‘regard their economic policies as a matter of common concern’. this is the fundamental lesson of the crisis: it is the lesson of interdependence. it is the lesson that, when things go wrong, the consequences are felt far beyond national borders. and the hardest lesson is this: when things go badly wrong, the impact is felt by every european taxpayer and by far too many european workers, whose prosperity and livelihoods are put at risk not only by their own governments but, sometimes, by someone else’s government. that is why we need to learn these lessons, to do all we can to rebuild our structures and revise our rules in a unified way that takes proper account of our interdependence and the responsibility that places on all of us, including of course the european institutions. a key way to ensure this is – as i have said many times to this parliament and also to the european council – to insist that the community method and the community institutions remain at the heart of our response to the crisis. they must be at the core of how we shape the european union to make it stronger and fitter for the future; to make it more efficient, but at the same time to uphold its democratic principles. it means governance for all and by all, not only by a few. in the future, we will need to go even further on strengthening integration. this will require treaty changes. let me be clear: i am in favour of treaty change if the treaty change is to reinforce the european union, the community method, the european institutions and the sense of a common purpose. but let us not fool ourselves. treaty change takes time and should not be seen as the immediate solution for the current crisis. let us discuss it seriously, with due reflection and with due involvement of relevant actors and institutions, namely this european parliament. as president van rompuy has mentioned, there will be a report to the next european council. the president of the european council was asked, in close cooperation with the president of the commission and the president of the eurogroup, to identify possible steps on further strengthening economic convergence within the euro area, improving fiscal discipline and deepening economic union, including exploring the possibility of treaty changes. but this should be seen as just the beginning of a process in which the level of ambition, democratic participation and involvement of the representatives of the european citizens is absolutely crucial. i am committed, and i will make sure, that this process will be conducted in close collaboration and cooperation with you, the european union citizens’ representatives. the community method and the community institutions remain at the heart of the process and they must also remain at the core of how we shape the european union to make it stronger and fitter for the future. this also shows that for the euro – if we are committed to the community approach, and if we are committed to respecting the treaties – we do not need another commission, another parliament, another court of justice. the euro is a central part of the european union, not something separate or apart. (applause)the euro is not an opt-out from the european union. this is why we should implement the community approach when we deal with the euro. we will not make the euro stronger through the fragmentation of the european union. as i have stated several times to you and also to the european council, the economic government of europe in matters of european union competence is the european commission. its accountability is to this parliament. this is the responsibility of the full college, not a part of it. i have given vice-president rehn special responsibility regarding euro governance and we have made sure that economic analysis is done in the most objective way. but let us be clear: in matters of political decision, the responsibility of the commission is collegiate. we need to respect the rules. we need, more than ever, strong community institutions and strong governance. this is also part of rebuilding confidence. any revision of the treaty should be for deeper integration of the euro area, but also for a stronger european union, in full respect of the community method and, of course, the prerogatives of this parliament. reinforcing the governance of the euro is also reinforcing our union. there should not be any divide between the current 17 member states on one side and 10 on the other; most – almost all – of which have a vocation to join the euro. all member states are full members of the union, and all should be committed to fulfilling the objectives of the treaties. the member states of the euro area have committed to completing the monetary union with an economic union, but this must also be completed with a political union, and with the political unity to move forward together. the community institutions par excellence – this parliament and the commission – have never left in doubt their determination to tackle this crisis head-on and to work for a stronger european union. i know that i can count on you and you can certainly count on the commission to continue doing precisely that. (applause)
president of the eurogroup. - mr president, mr president of the european council, mr president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, i understood that the debate we are having today should be about the governance of the euro area, and should not therefore concern the substance in the first place, but should concern first and foremost our working method and the interlinking of our different working methods. i do not really distinguish between form and substance, because in europe i have often found that form is the substance that comes to the surface. if your working methods are intergovernmental, it is because your will is not entirely community-based, which of course explains many working methods. i would like to review very briefly some of the elements of our working methods: macroeconomic surveillance and the european semester first. i do not believe, to be honest, that we can draw any definitive conclusions from this first experience of the first half of the year. i am not disappointed with the results of the first half of the year, but i believe that the results are definitely improving. i think it is quite normal that in a first, rather superficial, hasty experiment, we cannot draw all the possible conclusions. i believe that when governments present their draft budgets for 2012, this exercise of ex ante and a priori consultation will enable us to check whether or not governments have followed in full or in part the recommendations addressed to them during the first european semester. in general, i would like this exercise to become more political, more inclusive and less technical. if we are to be the economic government of europe, we must have the ambition of a government. it is obvious that all the different council configurations must be better involved in the exercise centred around the european semester and that all the sensitivities which are expressed through the different council configurations must be better heard. i do not believe that economic governance, since it is not simply the budgetary management of things, cannot be in the exclusive hands of ecofin and the finance ministers. (applause) and i would like to see in all our approaches, our working methods become more political. in fact, after a fairly long experience of community affairs, i find that very often, at the level of finance ministers, sometimes at the level of prime ministers, we endorse texts which we have not prepared ourselves and which we have not discussed among ourselves. it is a bit like some of the committees of the european parliament, but in our case it is more ... political. i would like to see more detailed discussions on the specific situations of the various member states at the level of ecofin, as well as at the level of the other council formations and at the level of the european council under the presidency of mr van rompuy. i would like to see a government that is able to say yes or no to recommendations and the others to enter into a virtuous dialogue with the government of the country concerned, because we are not a government if we cannot have a rich debate among ourselves on the essential political choices that we must make together but that we must apply individually in our different countries. i would like the european parliament to be involved as closely as possible in our approach to budgetary and macroeconomic surveillance. i in writing. i voted in favour of the report establishing a single european railway area. almost 10 years after the first railway package, which opened up and liberalised the various european railway operators, we have won the case on guarantees which are essential for the protection of employees and train users in europe, including the rejection of the total unbundling between infrastructure managers and railway operators, and the disappearance of the minimum service requirement in the event of a strike. a 'meeting clause' with the european commission is also planned, which will allow a further debate on the legal framework for this single european railway area, and in particular on the status of employees in the sector.
in writing. with the first railway package adopted in 2001, a first attempt was made to reverse the decline of rail transport, ensure the integration of the sector and improve its attractiveness compared to other modes of transport. unfortunately, this first reform did not bring about any significant improvement in his situation. the adoption of this proposal for a directive was therefore urgent. merging three existing directives, it contains provisions on the appropriate financing and charging of railway infrastructure, conditions of competition on the railway market and the organisational reforms necessary to ensure adequate market surveillance. i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on the single european railway area. rail transport still has great potential which we tend to overlook. the aim is to make this sector more dynamic and competitive. this requires the removal of the technical, legal and political obstacles to a european railway area. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the safety of rail transport. by improving the conditions of competition in the railway market, this report will make it possible to offer our citizens an efficient and diversified railway network service that best meets their expectations. it will be easier and cheaper to travel by train within europe.
in writing. it's about time. it had been 10 years since europe had set itself rules for moving towards a single railway area. but nothing had really moved forward. the railroad expansion has been slowed. in fact, rail has become the only sector to lose market shares in recent years. the explosion of low-cost short- and medium-distance services is a major factor. the train, however, meets several of our requirements: more environmentally friendly modes of transport (europe 2020 objectives), more cost-effective, which contribute to the sustainable development of our territories while offering solutions to the increased need for speed and intermodality, both for passengers and for goods. today we have come to realize that the train is a safe and valid mode of transport. the appropriate legal instruments must now be put in place. that is the spirit of this legislative package.

in writing. i voted in favour of this report, which recalls the european union's responsibility for financing development in third countries. the report calls on the member states to respect their own objectives in financing development aid. however, these are not unsustainable: each state must contribute 0.7% of its gross national income (gni) to this aid. we are now only 0.43%. this is a multi-billion euro shortfall in countries whose urgent financial needs in implementing health and education policies are known. the economic and financial crisis has given the countries of the north, and in particular the european countries, a duty to the people of the countries of the south. the aid to these countries should show that europe's values are those of solidarity, human progress and openness to the world. europe should finally be up to the challenge of development aid. there's still a long way to go.

in writing. the eu-us cooperation is that of two economic giants which should be strengthened, especially in a context of crisis. the resolution, adopted ahead of the 28 november summit, calls on the eu and the us to work together to implement the g20 commitments, particularly on jobs and growth. it underlines the importance of our cooperation in the energy field. it also welcomed the progress made in the area of freedom and security, in particular with regard to the protection of personal data. that is why i voted in favour of this resolution.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution because i believe it is important to strengthen transatlantic cooperation in the context of the economic and social crisis affecting our two continents. on the more specific question of security and the fight against terrorism, i believe that we must try to convince our american partner of the merits of an approach which is proportionate, which leaves no room for arbitrariness and which is more respectful of individual freedoms, unlike the approach advocated so far by the united states. it is with this kind of approach in particular that we must approach the continuation of the negotiations on a european union-us pnr agreement.
in writing. i supported this resolution in plenary because the transatlantic partnership is a driving force for the entire world economy. i regret, however, that there is no mention of international trade. the united states is indeed intensifying its protectionist policies. one example: the passing of the buy american act a few months ago. this us legislation requires companies bidding for a public contract to use only us materials. the united states and the european union are both members of the wto's agreement on government markets, which prohibits such practices. with other colleagues we recently asked the us authorities how this legislation will affect european businesses. we await a clear and complete response and will remain vigilant as to any further action to be taken in this regard. the transatlantic partnership is working well, it is important and beneficial for both economies. we will not allow this crisis to destroy the good relations that they have.
in writing. i voted against this resolution because it makes cooperation and the relationship between the eu and the us the alpha and omega of the conduct of international relations. this resolution is moving between good intentions and pious wishes, in disagreement or in contradiction with the declarations of the eu or the united states, but above all with the principles and values displayed and constantly contradicted by the acts. this resolution reaches new heights in terms of the eu and us responses to the financial crisis, welcoming the latest g20 and in terms of data protection, as with the pnr agreement which tramples on european principles and law in this area. the acta agreement has been ignored, as has the durban climate change conference! the credibility of transatlantic relations must be based on new political foundations and must first of all turn its back on a bilateral vision in which the west rules the world, imposes its choices and is unable to apply on its own territory the values of human rights and freedoms which it claims to impose on the world, including by military force.
in writing. there are many obstacles in the internet domain, such as the prioritization of traffic according to price. these obstacles are often orchestrated by the operators themselves for commercial purposes. in fact, parliament adopted a resolution, which i supported, in favour of an open and neutral internet. in accordance with the principle of competition, consumers must be able to choose freely their operator at reasonable prices. the protection of personal data must also be guaranteed.
in writing. the internet is an important part of the daily lives of european citizens. it is therefore right that it should be regulated in accordance with the principles of neutrality and openness, as is the case with the telecommunications sector. healthy competition must be applied in this area if european consumers are to benefit from the best available services. the commission must also be attentive to the quality of internet traffic management and ensure that connections are not disrupted by network congestion. in order to respect fundamental rights, the commission will have to ensure that internet service providers cannot block, disadvantage, affect or reduce the ability of anyone to use a service to access, use, transmit, post, receive or offer any content, application or service made available via the internet - with the obvious exception of child pornography sites.
in writing. i supported the resolution on net neutrality because it is a balanced text, which recalls the commitments made under the telecoms package and which emphasises consumer protection, particularly in terms of switching providers or access to information.
in writing. i voted in favour of this resolution. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to cover the whole of the eu, including the eu's external borders, and to extend the scope of the directive to cover the whole of the eu. however, i regret the economic approach of the resolution, the lack of reference to the acta negotiations and above all the ambiguity of the resolution as to the possible interpretation of restrictions by operators on mobile internet access in the event of network congestion. the resolution reaffirms various principles, such as freedom of expression, respect for privacy and warns of the risks to the promotion and respect of human rights in the use and access to the internet. we must be vigilant with the ngos and ensure that any new community legislation is evaluated swiftly and that the european commission legislates if this is the conclusion of this study. together we must uphold and respect this political commitment of the european parliament to a free, neutral and democratic internet.
in writing. i voted in favour of a resolution in which the european parliament reiterates its support for the convention on cluster munitions, which prohibits states parties from using cluster munitions because of their irreversible consequences, which primarily affect civilians. parliament called on the commission and the council to introduce a clause prohibiting the use of such weapons, as is already the case for weapons of mass destruction, in agreements with third countries.
in writing. digital is a growth-enhancing sector for the european economy and contributes to the achievement of the europe 2020 strategy's objectives for sustainable, smart and inclusive growth. the european parliament's resolution on the modernisation of vat legislation, which was tabled by my colleague marielle gallo and which i supported, provides for measures to stimulate the digital single market, such as a reduction in vat on cultural goods. for example, digital books should benefit from a reduced rate as paper books.
in writing. i did not vote in favour of modernising the vat legislation on digital cultural goods. in the difficult economic times we are living through, the first priority is to combat deficits and a reduction in vat on any category of products does not go in that direction. digital cultural goods differ from 'classical' cultural goods, particularly when it comes to books: the production costs (material, staff) of digital books are much lower than those of paper books. finally, a lower vat rate on cultural goods could contribute to a further fall in purchases of paper books, a sector which is already experiencing considerable difficulties.
in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution on the modernisation of vat legislation because it stresses the need to strengthen the european digital market and to put an end to the shortcomings identified that are hampering its growth. a particularly important point for me is the possibility of reducing the vat rate for online cultural services (tv, books, magazines, music, newspapers) so that they can benefit from a more favourable tax regime, similar to that of their 'paper' versions, and thus put an end to the discriminatory treatment of services according to the medium used (electronic or physical).
in writing. the digital revolution, combined with globalisation and the acceleration of trade, is forcing us to rethink our cultural and economic model. with the internet and digital technologies, cultural works can benefit from tremendous dissemination tools if we can adapt the regulatory framework of the single market. however, the development of the digital book in europe, for example, lags far behind its international competitors. european legislation prohibits reduced vat rates for services provided by electronic means. the minimum vat rate is 15%, while the physical book may be subject to rates of up to 5%. we end up with a system where the transaction details matter more than the content. but a book is a book! the disparities in taxation create distortions which are all detrimental to the competitiveness of european enterprises. americans have long had a competitive advantage. will europe react? i'm aware that public money is running short. however, if we do nothing, we will not only miss our appointment with the digital future, but we will also be deprived of a lever for growth, competitiveness, cultural diversity, and employment.
in writing. i abstained on the resolution on the modernisation of vat legislation to boost the digital single market. this modernisation is based solely on reducing vat on cultural goods sold in the digital space and subject to low consumption. unfortunately, this proposal is not based on the idea of the distribution of works as a public service for the greatest number of people, nor even on the logic of vat as an unfair tax that must be reduced to reduce the burden on the incomes of the poorest. instead, this resolution is based on the desire to stimulate a digital single market, treating cultural goods as any other marketable goods. the negotiators who put the compromise in place did not even dare to address our political group.
in writing. convinced that the european neighbourhood policy contributes to the strengthening of democratic principles and good governance and stability in our immediate neighbourhood, i voted in favour of the lisek report. under the european neighbourhood policy, the eu is linked to a number of countries, including georgia, by action plans. the association agreements are the first step in bringing them closer together. parliament recommended that the negotiations be based on the establishment of the rule of law, the gradual establishment of a free trade area, the preservation of the territorial integrity of the country and the de-escalation of russian-georgian relations.
in writing. this report was adopted by the committee on foreign affairs. it reiterated georgia's commitment to democratic values, which are essential to the success of the negotiations and the proper implementation of the association agreement. nevertheless, georgia must continue its efforts, particularly in the areas of good governance and respect for human rights. it is a good report, and i have decided to support it.
in writing. enshrined in article 2 of the lisbon treaty, gender equality is a fundamental principle. in his report, mr gustafsson calls on the european parliament to promote this principle in all its policies and activities. the report highlights the need to increase the representation of women in parliament's decision-making bodies as one of the priorities. as president of the association "women at the centre", i am deeply committed to respect for gender equality. i therefore supported the resolution.
in writing. i voted against the report on an integrated approach to gender equality in the work of the european parliament. throughout my political career i have been a constant campaigner for equality between men and women. this report presents some interesting ideas, and it is essential to continue to affirm the importance of gender mainstreaming in public policies to contribute to gender equality. however, i could not reasonably support article 12 which gives disproportionate attention to transgender people in european policies. i'm all for tolerance. it is not appropriate for the european parliament to commit human and financial resources to the evaluation of european policies on transgender people at the present time. so i had to oppose the report.
in writing. as the world's largest market for fishery products, the eu is the first to be affected by illegal fishing. globally, 15% of marine catches are considered illegal. however, in a context of declining fish stocks at sea and the gradual degradation of the marine ecosystem, it is important that the eu takes a leading role in international debates and proposes strong measures to combat illegal fishing. these measures will include increased transparency to better detect undeclared vessels. it is imperative that the eu respects its own rules (respect for fishing quotas) in order to set an example and lead to convergence of good practice at international level.
in writing. i voted for the lövin report on combating illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing. this report makes concrete proposals to combat this scourge at world level, particularly within international organisations such as fao. the report also proposes to improve the traceability of seafood, in particular through the use of catch certificates for fish sold on the international market.
in writing. i voted in favour of the report on illegal fishing worldwide because its objective is unquestionable. illegal fishing is unfair competition for legal fishing and is often accompanied by dramatic social conditions. there is no international framework today to share common standards. it is therefore essential that the european union should be a force for good in the bodies of which it is a member. in the forthcoming cfp debates, however, i will be vigilant on the issue of sanctions, which is raised in this report. the resolution calls for the withdrawal of european subsidies for offenders. this proposal will require consultation with local stakeholders before it can be considered. the entry into force of the point permit is also welcomed, which i cannot support in the current implementation arrangements. in addition, in view of the recent decision by the uk government to stop subsidising security in the channel, i have made it clear in this report that the union would need to improve its own functioning, in particular by creating a european coast guard service, for better coordination and greater efficiency in our actions.
in writing. this report was adopted by the committee on fisheries. this is an important report because illegal fishing is one of the most serious threats to biodiversity. the report calls on the european union and the member states' control authorities to provide themselves with sufficient resources (human, financial and technical) to be able to fully combat illegal fishing. the report also calls on the commission to identify and sanction operators who violate eu legislation, to create a european coastguard function, to guarantee the full and effective traceability of fishery products and to increase the resources allocated to the fight against corruption and organised crime. i supported this report in the vote in plenary.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report which reaffirms our commitment to make the union a leader in the fight against illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing. as the leading importer of maritime products and with one of the largest fleets in the world, i am convinced that the union must set an example to rally the entire international community. since two thirds of the world's marine areas are located on the high seas and are beyond national jurisdiction, only a global and concerted solution can be effective. iuu fishing represents more than 15% of catches and threatens the sustainable management of fisheries resources and the whole sector. however, the instruments to combat this scourge already exist within the united nations food and agriculture organisation (fao) and the union. i therefore regret that the only thing lacking today is the political will to apply them in a general and responsible manner. it's up to us to act now to save our oceans. all actors must contribute to this effort: fao member states by respecting their commitments but also citizens by consuming these dwindling resources responsibly.

this result. thanks are due also to vice-president vidal quadras and the members of his team, as well as to the successive council presidencies, culminating in the agreement under the polish development partner. we would also be unable to pursue cooperation in some key areas with our strategic partners. therefore, the commission welcomes the agreement covering the short period left between now and 2013. this compromise allows the commission to immediately start implementing the budget for the ici plus initiatives and the banana accompanying measures. for this reason, the commission is grateful for amending budget 6/2011, agreed on 18-19 november between parliament and the council. the additional eur 13.4 million for the banana accompanying measures means we can start implementation as soon as possible. the actions to be funded will improve the projection of the european union’s interests at international level and comply with the development commitments made in geneva to finally end the long-standing banana dispute in the wto. the compromise text addresses parliament’s request for more clarity on the financial allocations in broad terms. at the same time, the proposal respects the council position that the legislation should not include specific financial allocations for individual countries and regions. turning specifically to the banana accompanying measures: the compromise text includes additional information on the three criteria to be followed by the commission in determining the financial allocations per country. it also includes an indication of how the criteria will be applied. it also adds an explicit reference to the commission’s intention to come forward with a formal implementing commission decision on the indicative country allocations. this will give parliament and the council the opportunity to express their views on the financial allocations. the accompanying measures promised in the framework of the banana trade agreements are important for the acp countries. the tariff cuts have already started kicking in, and the acp countries have requested this additional support. last but not least, i would like to the remind the house that the funds we promised to the acp countries’ banana producers in geneva must be additional and cannot be taken out of the european development fund. moreover, as we are also at the end of the 10th european development fund financial protocol, there is no margin of manoeuvre left within this instrument. a few words about ici plus: under ici plus, minimum percentage floors for the three priority areas (public diplomacy, economic partnership and people-to-people links) and a maximum percentage ceiling for administrative costs have been included in the text. the four percentages add up to less than 100%, leaving sufficient margin to decide on final allocations during programming. this gives the necessary flexibility to take account of developments and needs on the ground. at the same time, it provides for involvement of the co-legislators in overall priorities for ici plus. mr president, to conclude, the commission therefore looks forward to the final approval of the package by parliament.

on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, commissioner, today is world aids day. it was very important for our parliament to adopt this resolution to send a strong signal. because if the aids epidemic is going down around the world, it may be less visible. but we must not let our guard down, because today is still a plague. more than 12 million young people aged 15 to 25 are affected, including 500,000 in europe, which is why we must bring all our political forces together. the european commission - commissioner dalli has just said this - has adopted an action plan on the fight against hiv for the period 2009-2013, and it is important that at the mid-term we can take stock of the situation and see what progress has been made. in fact, more than 50 000 new hiv cases are diagnosed each year in the european union and neighbouring countries. in the eu, nearly 30% of hiv-positive people are unaware of their infection and in several neighbouring countries this figure is as high as 70%. this is a serious problem for us as policy makers. half of all hiv-positive people continue to receive treatment late and reach advanced stages of infection before being diagnosed and starting treatment. in addition, it has recently been shown that an hiv-positive person who takes antiretroviral medication after diagnosis, rather than when his health begins to decline, can reduce the risk of transmitting the virus to uninfected partners by 96%. it is therefore essential that the european union remains committed to ensuring that the progress and investments already made are not eroded. we must strengthen prevention and training. we need to improve surveillance. we must constantly establish networks linking all those involved in the fight against this scourge. and we need to encourage the dissemination of good practice and get, among other things, very easy, and of course effective, tests for citizens. if these tests are widespread, i think it will be much easier for everyone to know if they are actually infected with the virus. that is the work we must do. i think it is important that we do not let our guard down and that we continue our efforts to fight hiv/aids.

in writing. 52% of young people who leave school without a diploma find themselves unemployed. the current dropout rate is intolerable. that is why i supported the adoption of this resolution to call on member states to undertake educational reforms that target the children most at risk of dropping out of school, and who are - more often than not - children from poor and disadvantaged families or from migrants. particular efforts must be made for roma children, 20% of whom are not in school at all and 30% of whom are in a situation of dropping out of school. the success of the 'second chance schools' experience should be supported to help reintegrate young people who have dropped out. finally, different learning methods could also contribute to this reversal, as could the promotion of courses which reward practical knowledge more.
in writing. i welcome the adoption of the report on school drop-out, which affects 6 million young people in europe each year. this report is consistent with the priorities of the european union's europe 2020 strategy, which has set itself the objective of reducing the school drop-out rate to below 10%. in france we have set ourselves the ambitious target of bringing the rate down to 9.5%. it is essential to tackle the root cause and prevent these young people from being marginalised. i therefore fully support the recommendations in this report, which stress the need to identify and support young people at high risk of dropping out from early childhood. it also recommends that the personalisation of courses and training be made more widespread, that alternating training be developed, that consultation with parents be strengthened and that the impact of social inequalities be taken into account.
in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution on combating early school leaving. this text recalls one of the main objectives of the europe 2020 strategy: to reduce the school drop-out rate to below 10% by 2020, which would have a positive effect on reducing youth unemployment and improving the employment rate in the union (more than half of europeans who left school early are currently unemployed). this is all the more important to achieve as the number of jobs available for the low-skilled and unskilled labour force will continue to decline in the coming years. the resolution also highlights a worrying situation: one in four young europeans currently has difficulty reading. it is clear, however, that reading is an indispensable tool for progress in all school subjects, for integration into the world of work, for understanding information, for communicating properly, and for cultivating oneself. so back to basics: specific measures to address the gaps in reading are urgently needed. and let us advocate early learning of ict (new information and communication technologies), such as languages, which young people have the advantage of being able to assimilate quickly.
in writing. i supported this report in plenary because it tackles a real scourge, which most often affects young people in an already precarious situation. it is undeniable that, in many cases, school dropout is linked to poverty and social exclusion. so fighting one is fighting all the others. the report sets out simple guidelines: early detection, increased support, personalised approach. these solutions are known, but few states today are willing to make their implementation a priority. but enabling more young people to take full advantage of education raises the overall level of skills and therefore employment opportunities. a final word on reading: the proportion of 15-year-olds with reading difficulties in the member states is 24.1%. if we have to choose an angle of attack, this is it! reading is, in my opinion, the indispensable key to all knowledge, all knowledge. we must ensure that all young people, whether they leave the school system on time or early, have this key in their pocket!
in writing. i voted in favour of this report on the fight against school drop-out, which persists and even worsens in all the member states of the union. the proposals in this report are positive: the need to identify 'at-risk pupils', the call for a personalised and inclusive approach to education, the development of free public education and care services, especially for young children. we need a school that will truly be a school of equality, inclusion, of all and all, and academic achievement. it is up to the member states to translate these proposals into action, while austerity policies are primarily targeting public education services.
in writing. the european development cooperation policy granted the african, caribbean and pacific group of states trade preferences on agricultural products such as bananas. denounced by the world trade organisation (wto), this preferential trade regime was the subject of a banana agreement negotiated between the eu and the latter. although tariff preferences have been revised downwards, the eu has not abandoned the acp banana-producing countries. in fact, it has put in place a programme of measures (2010-2013) to support them in their adaptation efforts. these measures were the subject of an overall compromise with the council. i voted in favour of the goerens report which recalls that the treaty of lisbon places the european parliament on an equal footing with the council as regards the approval of strategic priorities in the programming of cooperation funds.
in writing. i voted in favour of this agreement which will support the acp banana economy while respecting wto rules. this is to help countries whose economic development is concentrated in specialised sectors.
in writing. i voted against this report on the creation of a new financial instrument for development cooperation which provides for support measures for banana producers in certain acp countries following the reduction of their tariff preferences. i am of course in favour of this aid programme with a budget of eur 190 million and in favour of the granting of accompanying measures in the banana sector because this sector is of crucial importance for our acp partners. i am, however, totally opposed to the council's attitude on this matter and its refusal to recognize any power whatsoever in our parliament. under the lisbon treaty, the european parliament has equal power with the council to approve strategic priorities and financial allocations in the programming of european funds, including those for development cooperation. by its rigid attitude and its threats to block the whole legislative package, the council has shamefully denied the mandate given to the european parliament's negotiating team led by my colleague charles goerens, who himself asked to have his name removed from the report, to show his displeasure. for these reasons i voted against the report.
in writing. i voted against this report, of course, not because i am opposed to the idea of giving financial aid to the acp banana-producing countries which have been affected by the reduction in customs duties on bananas from latin american countries. on the contrary, the aid of eur 190 million to be distributed over 10 countries over 4 years seems to me to be entirely justified. i am very concerned, however, about the way in which parliament's powers have been denied throughout the negotiations on this text. while, since the adoption of the treaty of lisbon, parliament can be placed on an equal footing with the council in the control of the commission's implementing powers, the council has demanded that it simply inform parliament of the implementing measures which will be taken following the adoption of this text. this refusal by the council to allow parliament to exercise its legitimate right of control is absolutely unacceptable. to denounce this refusal and to avoid setting a precedent in future negotiations on financial instruments, i have opposed the adoption of this text by parliament.
in writing. this dci/bam text wipes out the mandate given to parliament's negotiating team: to respect the spirit and the letter of the lisbon treaty, to put parliament on an equal footing with the council on all programming decisions concerning the choice of strategic priorities and financial allocations, and not to set a negative precedent for parliament before the next negotiations on the future financial instruments for external aid 2014-2020. with the application of article 291 of the feu treaty to strategic programming decisions, parliament will therefore have even less power of control than under the comitology procedure in force under the old treaty. all this is the result of shameful blackmail by the council, which threatened to block the whole package of measures if parliament rejected even one of the four texts put to the vote. i therefore voted against this text because our parliament had to defend its rights under the lisbon treaty, while showing that its plenary remains sovereign in the face of attempts to destabilise the council.
in writing. i voted in favour of this report because the community funding provided for in the regulation as negotiated with the council will support economic, financial, technical, cultural and academic cooperation in the partner countries. it will also strengthen economic links with these countries. another important point for me is that this new regulation will strengthen the role of parliament: it will finally be involved in the programming, evaluation and notification of the programme. it will therefore no longer be able to simply give its opinion after the fact but will actually be able to give directions. that is why i hope that it will come into force as soon as possible.

in writing. the kaliningrad enclave is the only enclave existing within the territory of the european union. the council and the european parliament adopted in 2006 a regulation laying down rules on small-scale crossborder trade at the external land borders of the member states which allows for derogations from the general rules on border controls laid down in the schengen borders code for persons residing in a border area. this regulation allows member states to conclude bilateral agreements with neighbouring countries which are not part of the european union. the small border traffic makes life much easier for people living close to the external land borders. there is little evidence of abuse. the application of the normal rules for defining the border zone would artificially divide this enclave. the text authorises the extension of the 'border zone', thereby facilitating and increasing economic and cultural exchanges between kaliningrad and the main centres of northern poland. i voted in favour of this amendment to the rules of procedure because i believe that european laws and regulations must be adapted to the realities on the ground.

in writing. croatia is unquestionably a european country, with its geography, culture, history and population. and each of us should appreciate the close relationship we can have with her. however, the european construction as it stands cannot be the framework for these relations. it is in fact moving dangerously towards a centralized supranational state, bypassing the peoples and national parliaments, imposing its ultra-liberal and globalist dictates, arrogating to itself the right to dictate the budgets of the states, and thus all their actions, with an eye riveted more on the satisfaction of markets than on the well-being of men. i understand the symbolic value for the croatian people of membership of the european union. but i also know that these people will soon be unhinged. the benefits will be far less than expected, and the stresses far more unbearable than expected. ask the greek, irish, portuguese people what they think of it today! i'm not selling a friend a ticket to the titanic. that's why i abstained.
